A most beautiful morning. Wind about W. Wrote to WBS. Dined with H Hurry. At the Pig & had oysters & spent the evening at the Albion
A beautiful morning. Wind W by N. Took a drive with the Doctor to Tynemouth. H Hurry dined with me. At Tynemouth again in the evening

Delightful autumnal & harvest weather. Wind WNW. Went with H Hurry by steam up to the Regatta at the Kings Meadows. Never was out in a more beautiful day. A most lively & animated seem, the river covered with boats & the banks with gaily dressed people & carriages. Finished at the Albion & H Hurry's
A fine morning. Wind SW. Walked to Tynemouth. H Hurry & Dr Fenwick dined with us. At Tynemouth again in the evening. H Hurry suppered with me
Fine weather, rather foggy. Wind SW. Received a letter from WBS. Began & continued to rain very heavy at 11 o'clock. Dined with H Hurry. Finished at the Albion

A fine morning after the rain. Wind W by S. Walked to Tynemouth. Dined with C Cockrill at the Custom House. At the Pig. Tea with CG. At Tynemouth again in the evening. Finished at the Albion & Hurry's
A dull cloudy day with a little rain. Wind N by E. Sea high. Dined with J Tinley & walked to Tynemouth in the evening
A foggy morning. Wind SSW. Walked to Tynemouth. Dined at home. Do again in the evening & the Albion
A beautiful morning. Wind NW. Received a letter from WBS & answered it. Took a long walk with J Cunningham. Drank tea with J A Richardson & finished at the Albion
A dull morning. Wind SE. Turned out foggy & very damp. Walked to Tynemouth. Went to church in the afternoon. Dined with J Tinley
A fine morning. Wind N by E. Went up to Newcastle by steam. Walked out to Benton. Dixon engaged out to dinner. I dined & stayed all night. Fanny Brown there

A dull day. Wind NNE. Spent the day at Benton. Dixon shot from Fawdon where he had been all night. Homewards to dinner but had poor sport. The foundation stone of the new church was laid behalf by Lord Porgdon
A fine morning. Walked from Benton, home. Dined at home. At the Albion in the evening

A beautiful morning. Wind S by W. Received a letter from WBS. Wind changed to SE. Went to Whitby & had a run of the beagles but poor sport. Dined with C Cockrill, walked to Tynemouth. At the Musical Meeting & CC
A rainy morning. Wind SSW continuous heavy rain all day. H Hurry & Lockesill dined with me at 4 o'clock. Called at the Albion latter in the evening
Finer weather. Wind NW. Walked to Tynemouth. Dined at house at 4 o'clock. At the Pig and Albion in the evening
A dull morning. Wind NNE. Walked to Tynemouth. Dined with H Hurry at 3 o'clock. At J H Richmond in the evening
A mild morning with rain Wind SSW. Cleared up in the afternoon Dined at home & having a cold went to bed early

A wet and unpleasant day. Wind N & N by E. Breakfasted with J Tinley & drove the two young horses to Newcastle & returned to dinner Mr Day & I Wright dined with us Misses Watt, Kelso, Carr, two Mr McCarrs & Mr Hutchson in the evening
A fine morning. Wind NE. dined with H Hurry on board the Choice. Walked to Tynemouth. Tea at Southerns. At the Albion
A dull morning. Wind SE. Took a long walk round by Hawkeys Lane, Preston, Cullercoats & Tynemouth, home to dinner. Called at the Doctors & finished at the Albion
A most beautiful morning. Wind WNW. Dined with the Doctor. Walked to Tynemouth & spent the evening at Holroyd at Billy Mill being his birthday
Beautiful weather. Wind WSW. Went out with the hounds & had good sport. Dined with H Hurry on board the Choice. Met Bess. At the Musical meeting
A fine morning. Wind about West. Walked to Tynemouth. Dined with the Coui: of the United Club at the Albion
A beautiful morning. Wind WSW. Wrote to WBS. Called at the Doctor at dinner time. Went & round the bar in the Choice. Landed at Tynemouth & had something to eat at Southerns. Met Bess
A rainy morning. Wind about West. Dined with H Hurry. At the Albion in the evening
Finer weather. Wind N by E. Received a letter from WBS. Walked to Tynemouth. Dined at Southerns with a party. Met Bess. At the Albion
A dull morning. Wind about West. Walked to Tynemouth. Wrote to WBS. H Hurry, C Cockrill & E Charlton dined with me at 4 o'clock
A fine morning. Wind W by S. Took Physic. Dined with C Cockrill at the Custom House. At the Albion in the evening
A dull & wet day. Went to church in the morning & heard Mr _____ the new lecturer of South Shields preach an excellent sermon for aid of the dispensary. £22.10/ collected. Dined with I Tindley
A dull morning. Fresh breeze at SW. Took in long walk round by Preston & Tynemouth. Wind suddenly changed to N with rain. Dined with H Hurry. At the Card Club. No meeting. At the Musical meeting

A beautiful morning. Wind WNW. Went by coach to Newcastle & attended the Inspection of the NNVCaraly on the town moor when they went there this evolution remarkably well. Dined at the George with Mr Richardson & returned in the evening with Mr R & omnibus
A beautiful morning. Wind WNW. Dined at home. Went out fishing with the Doctor, but had no sport. At the Pig, Albion
A dull morning & rain. Wind SW. H Hurry & Charlton dined with me. At Tynemouth in the evening. Very unwell came home early
A fine morning. Wind WNW. Very unwell. Lay in bed till 12 o'clock having taken medicine. Not out
A rainy morning. Wind NW. Cleaned up. Confined to the house all day
A fine day. Wind SW. Again in the house
A fine morning. Wind SW. Still confined to the house. In physic. WBS
A fine day. Blowing hard at N. Sea up. Still confined to the home
A fine morning. Cold NW wind. Fresh breeze. Still confined. Wrote to WBS of the averages bill busy paid into G & Co. Cockrill, H Hurry & C Ridley spent the evening with me
Rather a fine day, wind in the morning NW but changed again towards afternoon & variable at N. N by E with rain at night. Received a letter from William. Had a hifetable at home
A fine morning. Wind SW. Went out to the Newsroom at 2 o'clock. Dined & spent the evening with C Cockrill
Wind WNW with showers. In physic. Still confined to the house. An attack of rheumatism in the left side. H Hurry & J H Richmond called & spent the evening
A fine morning after a stormy night wind variable from SE to NW. At home all day
Had leeches applied to my left side & lay in bed till 4 o'clock. E Chartton called to see me
A raw wet & cold morning. Wind NNW. In the house all day. Suffered much from my side

A gale of wind at NNE & sea high. Had 14 more leeches applied to my side & took much blood & felt relieved. Dr Fenwick & I Lewisked called to see me. The former stayed all night. A dinner given Mr Young today
Rain and wind NNW. Laid in bed till late. Found myself much better. H Hurry called
A fine morning & warm. Wind NW. The doctor gave leave to go out a little, but did not feel inclined. H Hurry dined with me
A fine mild day. Wind WNW. Went out & walked to Tynemouth. Dined with H Hurry. J H Richardson there. Back to Young
A fine morning. Wind NW. Went out & had a look at hounds. Dined with C Cockrill & spent the evening

A cold day with showers of rain & some hail. Wind N & NNE a few ships got to sea at considerable risk with steam boats although it was high. The Hilton Lolifte & United Kingdom Steam Boats arrived after a long and stormy & long passage from London, the latter put in for a supply of coal & sailed again. Dined with I Tindley & in the evening walked to Preston & took tea with Miss Kilse
A beautiful morning & Wind WNW. Went out. Attended the Maystrabs Hunting. Dined at home. Met Bess
A dull morning & fresh breeze at W by N. A gale. H Hurry dined with me. Called at the Albian & I spent the evening at Mr Cruddas
A dull morning & a gale at W by N. Wrote to J Small & cut him some trope. Dined with H Hurry. Met Bess. At home
A fine morning. Wind WNW. Walked to Tynemouth. Dined at home & in the house all the evening
A fine morning & fresh breeze at West. Walked to Tynemouth. Dinned with H Hurry at 3 o'clock. The doctor , Cunningham & Cockrill at the Albion in the evening
A fine morning after rain. Wind WSW. A large fleet arrived. Walked to Tynemouth. Dined with H Hurry who afterwards went to Newcastle to fix the Choice. Met Bess. At home in the evening
A fine morning. Wind WSW blowing hard. Dined again with H Hurry. At the Albion in the evening
A rainy morning. Wind WSW. A letter from WBS. H Hurry & JH Richardson dined with me at 4 o'clock

A dull morning. Wind W by S. Walked to Tynemouth. At Chapmans. Got in bills for £50 on WBS merchant & returned to him. Dined with J Tinley & accompanied him & party to the amateur concert in the evening, which went of successfully well & was crowded being 360 there. Suppered at Tim Ligs afterwards
Most boisterous weather. Wind got round to ESE blowing a gale with heavy rain. Wind changed in the afternoon to SW & finer weather. Dined & spent the evening at home. Met Bess
A Finer weather. Wind still from the same quarter N & N by E & sea still high. Received a letter from Mrs Scott that she will be at home on Monday. Wrote to her & Dined with J Tinley
Blowing hard at SW. Dined with A Bartholomew on board the Dalsy aplins
A dull morning with showers. Wind NE & sea high. Dined with H Hurry. Went to the Catholic Chapel & spent the evening at JH Richardson
A fine morning with cold NE wind. Sea high. H Hurry dined with me. Met Bess
A fine cold day. Wind NE. Tom Smith came & stayed all night. H Hurry & C Cockrill dined with me
A fine morning with cold SE wind. Went with Tom Smith to Newcastle by steam & walked from there to Benton, dined & stayed all night with D Dixon. Received a letter from WBS to send him £60

A dull cold morning with a little snow. Wind NW. Walked from Benton to Shields. Dined with H Hurry. Attended the weekly amateur practice. A bad account received today from Lloyds of Fallon being washed ashore on the coast of Jutland supposed to be the

A beautiful morning, rather frosty. Wind NW. Walked out to Tynemouth & saw the hounds. Dined at home. Took wine with h Hurry & spent the evening at JH Richardson who had the Albion Whist Club & supper. Met Bess

A beautiful morning & frosty. Wind NW. Wrote to WBS & cancelled been £60 a £50 pot No 4803 & £10 No 18895. Very Lame having had my knee injured last night by being thrown down an area by My Downie. Dined at home. Took Bess to the Abby & afterwards called on H Hurry
A fine morning. Wind NW. Took medicine. Very lame. Walked to the newsroom. Dined with H Hurry & went to the Catholic Chapel in the evening
A fine morning. Wind NW. Dined at 5 o'clock. The King dismissed his ministers on Saturday. At Mr Reeds with a large party. Called at H Hurry
A fine day, rather cold, wind got round to SE in the afternoon. Dined with J Tinley. Walked to Tynemouth in the evening
A fine morning. Wind NW. Dined at home at 4 o'clock. Met Bess. At home in the evening
A dull foggy morning. Little wind at NW. Dined at home at 3 o'clock. At home in the evening

A fine morning. Wind SE. Dined with C Cockrill at 5 o'clock. His brother & Mr Foger & I attended the musical Practice at the George in the evening. A party suppered with me & Mr Cockrill stayed the night
A fine morning & cold wind E by S. C Cockrill left. Dined with C Cockrill at the Custom House at 2 o'clock. Spent the evening at H Hurry's
A dull morning. Rather wet, wind NE. Dined & remained at home all the evening
A rainy morning. Wind NW & N by E. Walked to Tynemouth. Dined with H Hurry & C Cockrill
A fine winter's morning. Wind NW. Walked to Tynemouth. Dined with H Hurry
A fine morning. Rather foggy & frosty. Wind NW. Hurry, Cockrill, Richmond & Hrldray dined with me.

Beautiful weather. Air frosty. Wind from the West. Walked to Tynemouth. Let the farm on Tuesday to Potts & her son who trace Leus Hello ground. At £150 a year. Dined with H Hurry. At home in the evening
A fine morning. Wind WNW. Dined with C Cockrill at 4 o'clock. Attended the weekly practice of the musical society

A fine morning. Wind WSW. Douralled J Tinley about Bowles impossibility selling the manure off the farm. J Tinlet wrote him a letter threatening proceedings if he did not bring it back or pay the value & also said that he would not charge us with the expenses but get them from Bowlls & Souther. Dined at home. Suppered with the Albion whist club
A damp morning. Wind WSW. Dined at home. On board the Brodnick. At H Hurry & home in the evening
A beautiful day. Wind NW. At church. Walked to Tynemouth. Dined with J Tinley.

Blowing hard at W & shower. Received a letter from WBS about his insurance out at & will a letter to Chapmans. Saw them & wrote to WBS with their answer. H Hurry dined with me. Spent a pleasant evening & suppered with J Cunningham
Very boisterous weather. Wind NMW. Walked up to J Holdroyds with JH Richardson, dowery, Grnddas, H Hurry & Cockrill. Dined and suppered
A fierce day. Wind NW. Dined with H Hurry. At the Albion in the evening

Beautiful weather. Wind SW. Dined with h Hurry again to help him away with the cold beef. JH Richardson there. Went to Mr Jewson's concert in the evening, which was very well attended & performance good. Suppered with J Jury
Most beautiful weather. Wind SW. Walked to Tynemouth. Cherlton & I dined together at the Northumberland Arms at 2 o'clock. At home in the evening
Extraordinary weather. Mild as a May day. Wind WSW. Walked to Tynemouth. H Hurry & J Cunningham dined with me. At the Albion. Gave Tygack & Dobson an order on WBS for £15.3/- for the Hope
A dull rainy morning. Wind varying between ENE & SE. Changed on the afternoon to SW. Dined with JW Lowery at Cheston Fields with JH Richardson

A fine day. Cloudy with wind SW Several ships got to sea in the morning. In the afternoon a few light ships got down after a 12 days passage amongst them the Hope, went on board at ½ past 4 o'clock, when off the Black Middens & got her papers. Went to Newcastle & fixed her for Carr's Walls before 6 o'clock either on my own account or 10/- freight, optimal to give an answer tomorrow.
A fine morning. Wind WNW. In the house all day
A fine morning. Wind WNW. Dined with JH Richardson & spent the evening
A fine morning. Wind from the N & W. Went by steam to Newcastle & from there walked with D Dixon to Benton's where we met Dr Fenwick who went home in the evening. I stayed all night.

A most beautiful morning. Wind NW Walked from Benton's, called at Wallsend to see Potts, who has been long ill. Saw the hounds, had no sport. Walked to Shields. Dined with C Cockrill. Called at the Albion. At home in the evening
A dull morning. Wind SSW. Walked to Tynemouth. Dr Fenwick & H Hurry dined with me
A dull damp morning. Wind N by W & NNE & so continued during the day with an unpleasant damp mist. I dined with H Hurry. At Tynemouth in the evening
The weather much the same as yesterday morning. Wind NNE. Walked to Tynemouth. Dined with Cockrill at 2 o'clock at the Pig. Met Bess & went to the Abby. At home
A beautiful day. Wind NW. Walked to Preston. Saw the hounds. Dined with JH Richardson
A dull morning. Gale of wind NNE. Sea high. Continued blowing hard all day. With rain. Dined at home. At H Hurry's in the evening
A cold cloudy morning. Wind about NNW. Went to Newcastle & agreed to take 10/- freight. It turned out a very wet day. Dined with J Tinley. Ship went to the spout. Gave Stephenson £40
Fairer weather again. Wind NE & sea much fallen. Wrote to WBS yesterday with Rent account. Turned out a rainy day. JH Richardson, Cockrill & H Hurry dined with me at the Albion in the evening
Finer weather. Wind N by W. Dined at the Groom & Gypsey Club & had a very pleasant meeting & admitted Craig a member. At the theatre & suppered at the Albion
A fine morning. Wind NW. Walked to Tynemouth. H Hurry dined with me. At the Albion in the evening
A fine morning. Wind NW. Air frosty. Dined with H Hurry. Called at the Doctors
Beautiful weather. Rather frosty. Wind NW. Received a letter from WBS. Sent him by the Shields Stephenson on a round of beef. Dined at home. Met Bess. At the Albion
Fine weather & hard frost. Wind NW. Took a long walk round by Preston, though the fields to Cullercoats & Tynemouth home. Dined with C Cockrill & finished the evening at the Albion
A fine morning. Rather frosty. Wind WNW. Walked to Tynemouth with Lowery & Richardson after writing to WBS. Dined at Hurry's. At home in the evening
Xmas Day. A fine morning after rain. Wind about N. Walked to Benton & spent the day with Dixon Dixons
A fine mild morning. Wind about West. Went yub accompanied by Dicks shooting but had poor sport, the birds wild, killed a hare & one bird. Mr & Mrs Atkinson & Mr Berley dined with us

A very dense fog. Little wind at NW. Walked down to Shields. JH Richardson & H Hurry & I dined with the Doctor & left him about 7 o'clock where the above gathered & Mr Cruddas came & drank wine with me.
A rainy morning. Wind WNW Did not go to church. Went in the afternoon Dined with I Tindley.. Hearing they wished to load their ships before us, I called upon J Carr about it. Suppered with him
A fine mild morning. Wind SW fresh breeze. Walked to Tynemouth. Dined with H Hurry. At JH Richardson's in the evening
A fine morning. Wind WSW. Walked to Tynemouth. Took the hare to Mrs Richardson. Dined with H Hurry. At the theatre in the evening
A Fine weather after rain. Wind SSW. Dined at home with h Hurry at 2 o'clock 7 spent the afternoon with Mr Henderson at Tynemouth
A fine morning. Wind WSW. Received a letter from WBS. H hurry. JH Richardson & on Cockrill, Bartholomew & Charlton dined with me. At the theatre in the evening. At the Albion & πολ Jarvis
A fine seasonal morning. Very queer from last night's dissipation. Did not get up till late. Walked to Preston. Dined with JH Richardson at 3 o'clock. At πολ Jarvis again
A hard frost. Wind NW. Suffering from the effects of last two nights. H Hurry, Charlton & I dined at the Northumberland Arms & went to the theatre in the evening & finished at the Albion
Beautiful day. Very hard frost. Wind NW. Walked to Tynemouth. Dined at home at 4 o'clock and remained in the house
Hard frost. Wind WNW. Had a 2 o'clock dinner with H Hurry & went to Tynemouth in the afternoon. Spent the evening at Southerns

A fine day. Hard frost. Wind NW. Six Charles Grey came to the George having offered himself for the borough. His Addressed the election in a beautiful & eloquent speech & declined coming forward this, but explained his determination to do so the next election. Dined at the George with his committee & spent a pleasant day. Jn Liver Kill too unwell to attend

Turned out at 3 o'clock. A dismal & wet morning, blowing hard from the east. Had not light enough to get us underway until about 4 o'clock, when the whole fleet were in motion, fortunately, at last with a fair wind. Being excessively wet & unpleasant I got into bed again & lay till ½ past 10 o'clock & then found the ship off Leigh above Southend & still raining hard. Brought up off Greenwich at ½ past 3 & o'clock landed with ...

A fine spring morning. On going out, found the harbour in dreadful state of confusion & much damage done in consequence of the immense land floods driving the ships adrift. Rode to Newcastle with J Tinley, saw W Chapman. He offered to take my bill at 6 months with another approved name to it, for 1000 or 1200. Refused & dined with J Tinley. Wrote to William. Wind SW. Many ships got to sea.

Got up at 4 o'clock this morning Went to the spout. Brought a lot of beef on my way up at 40/- Returned to breakfast & went by steam to Newcastle where I learned that the act gave them the power of loading any ship under 6 keels before larger vessels. Dined with J Tinley. Mrs Scott got from Toyston

Called upon Chapmans for £10 for self & gave Stephenson a draft for £26.18.5 being the balance of his account for the last voyage. Paid into Chapmans WBS balance not foe £30.5/-. Paid entrance & expenses up to the end of the year to the whist club £1.13/-
Could not attend the oyster supplier at the George in consequence. Gave Goe Slops 20/- on account of his wages.

... in the morning. Packed my cloths up. H Harry & I walked to Tynemouth in the evening & took some gin punch with Daises. Took leave of Mrs Scott & slept on board the Hope. Our from all passengers. Anne Stoke also on board.
Petersburg voyage commences

... we did see of the town, we were much pleased with. The houses are good and exceedingly neat & clean inside & out & the inhabitants appeared to be a very respectable orderly set of people.

Bob, JnoG [John Galbraith] & I took a stroll even in the rain & found our way into the church, where we remained some time. There was a large assemblage of children who were undergoing some examination by their chargeman. He appeared to be cajoling them, hard a great deal, but undeserved not a word that we saw, so came away as wise as we went. The alter was very splendidly ornamented & the whole had a very grand imposing effect.

The Captain was employed during the morning purchasing such stores as the ship required.

At ½ past 1 o'clock pm we sat down to dinner & were very hospitably entertained by W Chapman & his father, too much so could, for we got rather too much wine & I found myself pretty well screwed by the time (5 or 6 o'clock) we had to go on bord again.

Reached the ship at about ½ past 5 o'clock taking our pilot off with us with the intention of getting under way & running down to Copenhagen road, but it [was] blowing a gale of wind, as it had been all day. & having a foul birth from the number of ships. Lying about us, we could not get our anchor excepting at the risk of doing damage, so we determined to lay still until the wind abated.

Between 9 & 10 o'clock turned in for the night.

... sails set. Perfectly astonished at the exceeding beauty of the coast, so finely wooded & rich. ‘tis impossible to imagine scenery more splendid.

At ½ past 6 o'clock am came to an anchor in Copenhagen roads about ¾ of a mile from the entrance to the harbour. Dressed ourselves & got on shore about ½ past 7 o'clock. The mouth of the harbour is protected by a story battery (an island) called the Crown Battery, on both sides of which vessels can pass in, but on that side next to Elscaeur is the deepest water. We were obliged to stop at a platform where the Zuarantan Officer is on the right hand side after passing the battery, where after being asked several questions, we were given a pass without which we should not have been allowed to land. The expense of this is one dollar for each person on board. Equal to about 2/3 a price.

Upon landing, we were assisted by a person who proved to be Mr Chapman's agent at Copenhagen. He undertook to do what was necessary for us, such as paying the dices for & sent a person who accompanied us to their counting house. The firm, Heeksher, Peterson & Möller from whom we met with every attention.

Called upon Mr Ryan, a personal friend of Mr Chapman, who had given us a letter of introduction to him. From him we also met with much pontificating. At 8 o'clock went to the Hotel D'Angleterre & had our breakfast & afterwards proceeded, accompanied by a clerk of Mr Ryan, a very intelligent young Dame who talked English fluently. Arrived at the town by the ramparts. As our time would not allow us to see much more than the town itself, but with it we were as touched & delighted without exception. Taking it all together, it is the most beautiful city I ever saw. Most of cities have their St Gales Bellengales & but here there does not appear to be anything of the sort. ‘tis all alike most ...

Turned out at ½ past 7 o'clock & most delightful morning, with a fine breeze from NW. been going 5 & 6 knots all night. After breakfast going 6 knots & steering an ENE course. At few of our companions, the dragon flies still with us. At 12 o'clock took observation & by it, with in lat:56.36. long: 18.41

... debt. I should also mention that before the ship got to the mole, party of customs house officers came on board & immediately scaled down all the hatches& everything on board in the shape of a trunk or parcel belonging to us as passengers. The masters & crew's trunks & cabin lockers & draws being examined, the seals to remacer upon the karabis until the collector came on board to search the ship.

In the evening we walked about the town which is perfectly good for the plaice & the fort exceedingly strong being covered with cannons & having a garrison. I know not of how many men. I should think not numerous. The mole where the merchants vessels lay is a fine reservoir or wet dock capable of containing several hundred ships & water enough for them to take in the whole of their cargos. There is also another mole for the men-of-war. We strolled about the town the whole of the evening & when we looked at our watches much to our astonishment we found at nearly 12 o'clock & quite day light. In fact it is light all night here in summer. We returned to the ship, had our glass of spirit & water & turned in.
... some prayer. Returned to the ship about 11 o'clock. Had a glass of cool brandy & water & went to bed

... trip. On board we met Mr Fordeson who was also going up. Our papers were taken from us by an officer, who it appeared gave it to the master of the boat & his duty I understand is to deliver them to some officer in Petersburg. We had a very pleasant passage aft of three houses & landed about a mile below the city at the wharf of a Mr ____ a Scotchman & proprietor of the steam boats. He was the first who started steam boats in Russia under an agreement with the Government that for a certain number of years no other boats were to be allowed to oppose him. He has thus accomplished a large fortune.

Taking a donkey & cart for our luggage we drove to a Mrs Welson, a widow who keeps a boarding house in that part of the town called Backline. Here we found a room & after lunching, Bob & I strolled out to endeavour & find out the gentleman to whom we had letters of introduction. The first person we called upon was a Mr Dye, a friend of Inspector Hodgson whom we found a very pleasant gentlemanly fellow residing in the first line, upon the Island & in very elegant quarters. He gave us an invitation to dinner for tomorrow.

We were struck with the magnificence of everything we saw. It not possible to summarize the splendour of the streets & various buildings you see on every side as you pass along every house is upon a large & noble scale & whichever way your turn your eyes ...
A fine morning. Wind SE Called & paid Spence & Foster for the main mast £20.13/-. Walked to Tynemouth. A heavy thunder shower in the afternoon. Dined with Mrs Scott

... took a long stroll down the New Ky Prosped, the fashionable & finest street in Pitusby. It is about 3 wests in length & having trus on each side between the froth pavement & road which adds much to its beauty. Returned to our lodgings about 11 o'clock completely knocked up & foot sore.

... long there as it threatened another storm, we therefor got into our boat, but had not been long on board before the rain came down in torrents with most awful thunder & lightning. It however cleared up again before we reached our landing place. These gardens are about two miles or more from Petersburg & where the people flocked to in thousands on a Sunday. The walks upon this & neighbouring islands are beautiful. We fortunately had a boat with an awning over it.

On our return took a glass of grog & went to bed

... city of Petersburg, it contains only three very small rooms, something after this plan [See figure] Here is also to be see the boat which he built himself. How it is made known he was an excellent carpenter & used to row in. In the Citadel church there are some beautiful things in ivory of his turning & workmanship.

Dined with Mr Gillibrand only his wife & Mr Lindsey there. Spent a very quiet day & left early being foreign port day, which over the water & took tea with a friend of Mr Lumleys & Bob & I afterwards had a stroll down the Mews by Prospect to see the people & illuminations for the Emperors birthday. They don't as with us place candle & light in the windows etc, but feet what they call fat pots along the street upon the edge of the pavement & most horrible effluence they send forth. We got to bed about 12 o'clock

... the Petershoff Road, but being plagued with my toothache & my jaw much swollen, I was obliged to let Bob go by himself & dined at the club with Mr Lindsey. He & I in the evening each got a horse of Me Webster who keeps excellent cattle & took a very pleasant ride down by Catharinoff & round home by the Petershoff Road. After having our grog, retired to bed between 11 & 12 o'clock, exceedingly stiff & fatigued.

... intended for the foreign ambassadors when the court is there.

In the grounds we took lunch & at the same time had the pleasure of being most unmercifully bit by mosquitoes.

From this we drove to Parlousky another Palace the residence of the late Dowagn Empress the widow of Paul & mother of the present Emperor. It is a handsome building but nothing splendid in its appearance. The interior we did not see. The grounds though not as extensive, I think more beautiful than Jarskoi. There is more variety of scenery, hill & dale nature has dome much for it. The other is obliged to ask. In these grounds are some very fine statues & near the Palace is one of the most splendidly executed things I ever saw, these female figures upon a pedestal in marble as large as life, supposing an usn a ne plas lettra of statuary.

After taking some brandy & water at the top of the waterfall to quench our thirst, we again got into the carriage & drove homewards, stopping at a fine fountain on the road where we dined, having carried what prog & drinkables we wanted with us.

When at Jarskoi we saw the Emperor's cows, pastures and fine animals & the breeds of all nations. This establishment the late Emperor Alexander took great delight in, and it is kept up at considerable extent. The cows are dressed the same as horses & in fine condition.

... took a walk in the summer gardens of the Palace. On our return had a glass of grog with Mr Lindsey & got to bed at 12 o'clock.

Got admission into the premises where they are building the new Isaac Church & now engaged in erecting the granite pillars for the Portico & they use of an immense size most beautifully polished. The finest & longest in the world, brought from the quarries in Finland, their circumference about 30 feet & height upwards of 50 & although they weight ___ tons, they raise them in 20 minutes

... filled with ancient armour, arms & belonging to various nations and exceedingly curious, colours & standards taken battle, models of fortifications, cannon & mortars, the cloths, arms & accoutrements belonging to peter the Great, the late Emperor Alexander & several Generals etc. etc. etc. all very curious & well worth seeing, particularly the funeral car for the late Alexander, a most magnificent vehicle.

After leaving the Arsenal Me Lindsley accompanied us to the market near the Cesan Church where we purchased several articles as presents for the Lees etc.

Came home to dinner, Mr Lindsley with us had Sadaek for dinner, these fish and another called Saggee are fine flavoured & most excellent.

The pay of the Russian soldiers & officers is very trifling. That of a Saballere £16 a year & a private 11 Rubbles, not much more than 9/- English. The private of the bodyguard have 13 Rubbles

Being rather tired in the evening we only took a short walk down the Newsky Prospect

.. in the vapour bath, which we looked into, but that was all for it was, so intolerably hot we were glad to draw back, others afterwards having part oiled themselves & perspiring most copiously at every pore were employed scouring & pumping upon each other with cold water, all of course en buff. We next took the liberty of paying the ladies a visit, whom we saw the same way employed & in the same state of nudity. Their moderately poor innocents did not make them shrink at all from our scrutinising gaze. Indeed they seemed to enjoy the fun as much as we did. I think there were from 30 to 40 of them. We didist not venture to look into the ladies vapour bath, for we could not get to without passing through ducking guard & we were afraid they might favour us with a sousing.

We then proceeded to the market & purchased several pairs of slippers etc & returned home by the summer gardens. Took a couple of glasses of iced grog & went to bed
... humour to go on shore. Obliged to go to bed. The pain & opium making me exceptionally drowsy. Bought some flannel & hartshorn in the evening which I put upon my face when I went to bed

... not inhabited. They are all within a stone's throw of each other. After passing Ertholmene, we had a most delightful sail under the Island of Bornholm & a good view of it. This is one of the richest and most beautiful islands that can be imagined. It is in fact a perfect garden & to us had all the appearance of a gentleman's park. The soil is good & exceedingly productive yielding as much in one season as would keep the inhabitants several years. A boat came out to us from the shore & we purchased of them four ducks ¾ score of eggs & 2 pounds of butter for which we gave only 6/6

When we reached the west end of the island then wind took us all at a lk, but soon favoured us again. In the evening it became quite calm. At ½ past 8 o'clock the captain, Bob & I as usual had our grog & being in the humour, had some supper & had a regular jollification, blew a cloud & got to roost between 12 & 1 o'clock

A very fine day. Wind SE Engaged in the office with Robert. Walked to Tynemouth & took a warm bath. Dined with Mrs Scott. Walked in the evening to Carr's Wall Spout The Hope got under it in the morning & to come off at night with 13 or 14 Keels. The remainder to follow

.. glass of wine with him & I don't know how to account for it, excepting it was drinking upon an empty stomach but I really got muzzy of which I was sensible enough to feel heartily ashamed when I had to appear in the presence of Mr ships Chapmans. Got on board a little after 12 o'clock after one or two adventured before we left the town H French's ship, the 3 Brothers & several other vessels passed us upward bound between Copenhagen & Elsinore

... the stateroom scuttle light, wet my bed & I did not expect to have had one to sleep in tonight, indeed had the gale continued I should not have cared about it, but I contrived by placing canvas between the bed and sides of the vessel to fortify it pretty well from the wet & thus gained a better nights rest than I anticipated.

My face beginning to swell again, but no pain.

... get at them. Bob & I much annoyed having made certain of having a comfortable dinner & bed on show & talked over our plans of future proceedings. He having determined to stay a few days at Shields & take his passage in some other vessel.

The wind & sea being right aft, we soon passed Huntcliff foot again & at 8 o'clock left Flamborough Head bearing west distant 2 or 3 miles.

A great many light ships in Burlington Bat as we passed.

Ship made a great deal of water during the day

... struggled hard to prevent it escaping. I felt that "Richard was himself again" & no longer the prospect for the present of ruin & a jail before me. At 4 o'clock pm we brought up abreast of the Navy Hospital, within a short distance of the shore, blowing a heavy gale from the SW & rejoiced that we had got into such a snug roadstead, instead of being at sea at night

Such tempestuous & unsettled weather for the time of year I don't remember. This is the fourth gale we have experienced since leaving Elseneur & although it is such a short distance to the river, I almost despair of reaching without some disaster for bad luck seems to thwart us, whichever way we steer.

Bob & I turned in a little after 8 o'clock. The gale rather encased with rain

... were compelled to give the ship the whole chain. Wind WNW & cloudy. Dismal weather with rain. A light ship close by us drove & another broke his chain & sun down the river. Continued blowing hard all day with heavy showers of rain & squalls & towards evening the wind got to about N by W but the tide not answering. Till near dark, we lay still, indeed it blew too hard to think of getting under way & one or two vessels that weighed were soon obliged to bring up again

... since I had the pleasure of seeing him. We afterwards took a Greenwich boat & went down to the Hope upon Dowslands way where we dined off cold mutton. At low water looked at her bottom & gave orders for her to go into the dock to be caulked. Turned out an exceptionally wet evening. Had our tea on board & afterwards took a Mackware stage to Leadenhall Street & then walked to New Inn. Bob Marsh at the theatre.
Rather showery. Called at the New Inn. Put my portmanteau & bag into a cab & drove up to Nottingham Place. Spent the evening quietly at home.
... Peggy laying at the wharf at Purfleet. Young White of Wordland near Durham, a 4th mate in the company's service also joined us. Blew a cloud or two & turned in.
Wrote to WBS about the Harrisons average bills, which are ready for delivery. Drank tea & spent the evening at Tynemouth
Cargo of the Crisis, H Nicholson. If so it is a feared the ship & crew are lost

A beautiful day. The Hope got safe down from the spout having taken in 13 keels & 6 char. The remainder followed her down & we got to sea about ½ past 1 o'clock PM wind about NE but very little of it so that we did not get much beyond Sunderland before dark. Gave Richardson & Davidson notice of appeal against the land tax for the property in Shields & Preston. Wrote to William

Quite calm during the whole of the night Got up at 8 o'clock & found we were only off Hartlepool A heavy rain early in the morning & a change of wind to about S. A large steam boat passed us for Leith at 9 o'clock. The weather fine but still little wind & continued moderate all night

At 6 o'clock am off Whitby. Wind about SE by S & SSE during the day heavy squalls with rain & a little thunder & lightning. Obliged to take in sail until at last we only carried two close reefed topsails, reefed trysail & fore topmast staysail before dark the wind got to W by S & WSW when off Robin Hood's bay & increased to a heavy gale & tremendous sea which lasted all night, continued on the starboard tack until 6 o'clock Sunday morning. Still blowing a gale with heavy sea. Up all night

At 6 o'clock am rose. Ship a little to the north of Flamborough Head & stood in on the eastbound tack. Wind about W & W by N. Made Robin Hood's bay at 11 o'clock am tacked & stood to the southward again wind & weather now moderate, set main staysail. At 12 o'clock let a reef out of top sails at 1 o'clock set main sail. Turned out a beautiful summers afternoon with a fine breeze, about 6 o'clock lay too under Flamborough head, unbent & repaired foresail at 8 o'clock, again got underway with a fine westerly breeze to cross the Dups. Drank a glass of porter, smoked a pipe & turned in between 9 & 10 o'clock

Got up at 8 o'clock. Found the ship off Dunlengton Church with a fine leading wind from W by S about two points worse than last night. A fine morning, towards evening began to blow fresh. Found the fore topmast backstay spring, secured it with a tackle & took in a reef being rather squally Turned in about ½ past 9 o'clock

Looked out a little after 4 o'clock am. Found we had got a change of wind about 2 o'clock from about WNW. An agreeable change for us, making all sail. The ship passed the floating light at 3 o'clock, reached Cromer at ____. Passed through Yarmouth Roads at 11 o'clock & brought up being high water, at ½ past. Off Golaton, the Dalryaple & Nancy in company. Wind about W & by S. The latter ship from Archangel Captain Stormont came on board to dinner. At 5 pm being low-water got underway with a light breeze from the W by S & sailed out of St Nicholas Gateway & beat to the southern water highwater between 12 & 1 o'clock, when we brought up for the tide between the reefs points about 4 miles to the south of Southwold, between 1 & 2 o'clock am. After supper, turned in for the night.
A fine mild day. Wind SW. Went to church in the morning. Dined at home

Got up between 9 & 10 o'clock having a slight cold & a little rheumatism upon me. A fine warm summers day we have had for the last five weeks. Wind about south, but little of it, between 10 & 11 o'clock. The United Kingdom steam ship passed us bound to London at ½ past 11 o'clock. When off Orford the [wind] changed to the east, a fair wind, but we want a little more of it. I hope it will continue. The breeze continued & we got down to the south end of the Middle Sand where we brought up for the night, not being able to run through the Shoe Hole in the dark. After we got to bed, the wind increased & blew hard with a heavy swell, a great many ships around, which gave us a foul berth extremely dangerous in that part should a gale come on from the ESE. & cause of the loss of so many ships and lives we had in the March gale about five years ago.

... the ship papers, entered her & went up to Richmond's, a very unpleasant walk. Richmond was going out to dinner. Got my boots etc. dried & then went to Millers coffee house, Red Lyon Square, where I found William and Bob Marsh & had my dinner. They not a little surprised to see me. Slept at Nottingham Place

A fine morning. Wind WNW Took the Greenwich passage boat at the tower & went down to the Hope off Greenwich & found her just getting underway for the pool, on my return pesance conveyances much surprised at meeting Watt. Carr's Walls such a bad coal than none of the Hope was sold today. Wrote to Mrs Scott. Dined with Richmond & met Tom Griffeth. Played a few rubbers in the evening & lost £3.15/- Got home to Nottingham Place at 2 o'clock am Saturday

Another fine day. Wind SW Went to the city as yesterday on the Paddington coach. Engaged during the morning with Captain Dawson of the Dalryaple swearing affidavit respecting timbers etc. walked out of the city. Called upon Bob Marsh. We went with Mr Vincent, hired a boat & rowed up to Putney, where we had tea, mutton chops etc. & returned to town at 9 o'clock after a very pleasant evening

A dull morning. Wind SW with rain during the day. Bob March breakfasted with us. Went to the chapel in Vere Street. I afterwards walked round by Gower Street & called upon the Lumleys, they [had] gone down to Stanmore for the day. Continued upon and saw the Linskills in York terrace, Regants Park. Walked round by Hyde park, very little to be seen. Town exceedingly dull. Took a beef steak at the Blue Posts in Cork Street & drank wine in Nottingham place

A Beautiful day. Wind SW Went into the city this morning by the Paddington stage about 80 fresh ships got up to market, 2 or 3 of Carr's Walls? The coals bear such a bad character on the market that we could not sell any of the Hope's cargo. Walked out of the city, called upon Bob March, dined at the Blue Ports & took wine in Nottingham Place

A glorious day. Such a change. Quite cheering after the stormy weather we had. Wind WSW Did not go into the city. At 12 o'clock walked down to Hartley the dentists in mags Building & had my teeth examined & cleaned. Called at fosby's & Bob March's & afterwards walked home with William to drufs. Dined at 7 o'clock with Mr Linskill, met Mrs & Miss Payin Mr Ro Bill & spent a pleasant day. Lady Campbell came in to tea

A beautiful day. Wind SSW Went into the city by a Paddington stage. A few fresh ships up. Could not sell the Hope. Bob March, Mr Vincent, William & I went down by water & dined on board. In the evening at English Opera House
A very wet & disagreeable day. Wind SW. Took the Paddington coach into the city. Called at Lees & left the policy of the Hope Club. Dined at I Loblengs, a large party

A showery day. Wind from NW to N Went into the city at ½ past 11 o'clock by the Paddington stage. With some difficulty got the Hope sold at 30/s Walked out of the city with William & dined with Richmond, met Rob Jobling Played at whist & won 4/-
An extremely fine mild day. Wind varying between SE & W. Dined at home Agreed with the washerwoman to take my cloths by the quarter at 1 ½ guinea

A very fine day. Wind West Walked round the Regents park. Took an early dinner with Richmond who afterwards drove me down to Stanmore to stay the night. Left town at ½ past 5 o'clock. A beautiful evening. Took tea and went to bed in good time.

An exceedingly fine Day. Hot summer weather. Richmond & I after breakfast took a long walk. Upon our return found Mr & Mrs Lumly had arrived. Mr & Mrs Griffiths also came down before dinner & Jobling came after we had sat down. We spend a very aggregable & pleasant day & returned to town in the evening.

A hot day, wind west. Went into the city by a Paddington stage. On the market, coal lower. Walked out of the city. Dined at 6 o'clock with Mrs Whenbury in Gower Street; a quiet party only Richmond there. He & I went in the evening to Vauxhall Gardens to meet Bob Marsh, Vincent & William. A great many people there, but of the inferior classes. Got home between 1 & 2 o'clock.

A fine day, but exceedingly hot. Wind SE. Breakfasted with Richmond who afterwards drove me into the city & then to Stone Stairs & we went on board the Hope. Took a Paddington stage home. Dressed & dined at Joblings. A large party.

Another beautiful day. Wind SE. left town at 9 o'clock am. By the Portsmouth coach with Bob Marsh, where we arrived at ½ past 5 o'clock, crossed over by the steam boat to Ryde to stay with Mr Lee. Dined between 7 & 8 o'clock. Mr Lee living at Navarino House, beautifully. Situated about ½ a mile west of the town, upon the side of the hill which descended to the sea of which it commands a most beautiful view, with the mainland, Portsmouth

A glorious day. Wind east. Got up before 7 o'clock & bathed. Breakfasted at Mr Lees at Navarino House. At 11 o'clock went on the pier to see the Regatta, but dull work, being small boats. Dined with Mr Lee & afterwards attended the Ball at the Library, a very poor one & company bad. Not a pretty girl in the room.

A very foggy morning, wind NE. Cleared up towards 12 o'clock & turned out a delightful day. Rebecca Captain & Mr Lewis, F Barclay, Bob Marsh, William & I went in a sailing boat to Portsmouth to see the Victory & much pleased with our trip. The wind being against us, we were obliged to land & walk about two miles to Gosport. Returned to Navarino at ½ past 7 o'clock to dinner
A remarkably fine mild day. Wind W & W by N. Dined at home. In the evening at a Quadrille party at Mrs J Tenleys. A very pleasant dance. Upwards of 100 there & kept it up till 3 o'clock

Rather cloudy in the morning. Wind NE but afterwards turned out an exceedingly fine day. Started at ½ past 10 o'clock am with the following party in two sociables & a gig upon a tour round the island viz: Mr Rebecca & Laura Lee, Captain & Mrs Lewis, F Barclay, Bob Marsh, WBS, self & two servants. Stopped & saw Shanklin Chine, called & left our luggage at Ventnor. Drove on to & saw Appuldurcombe the seat of Lord Yarborough containing several fine paintings & finely situated. Returned to Ventnor to dinner & slept. A very pleasant & agreeable party

A pleasant morning but rather cloudy. Wind NE. F Barclay & I got up early & bathed. Started after breakfast & travelled along undercliff & saw the difficult gentlemans seats. Most beautiful & romantic well wooded & cliffs very grand. Stopped at Blackgang Chine, immense high cliffs with waterfall, continued our journey through a beautiful & well cultivated country to Freshwater Bay, where we had lunch about 4 o'clock. Captain Lewis & the ladies went by land to see the Needles. F Barclay, Bob Marsh, WBS and self & two servants went by water & got very well to the Needles which with the cave & majestic chalk cliffs, were very grand. But our return was attended with much unpleasantness to say the least, having an ebb tide & strong wind against us & being in a bad and cranky sea boat, we all got most uncomfortably wet by the spray of the sea. With much difficulty got back to Freshwater Bay to an 8 o'clock dinner. This is a very retired & pretty place

A fine morning. Wind still from the NE. F Barclay, WBS & I bathed & after breakfast started for Newport where after passing through a pretty country, we arrived about 2 o'clock, stopping to see Carisbrooke Castle on the way. After lunch continued our journey to East Cows, where we dined. For Previously crossing the water to see West Cowes & in the evening, after a most delightful tour & favored with most beautiful weather. We all returned safe to Navarino House much pleased & satisfied. Expenses of the tour £3.10.

A continuance of fine weather. Wind fresh from the NE. After taking an early breakfast F Barclay, Bob Marsh & I embarked in the George IV steam boat & went to see Southampton, stopping ½ home at Cowes on the way, & after spending a very pleasant day returned to Ryde to dinner. William left for Town
Still delightful weather. Wind variable between NE & NW but returned to the old quarter NE in the afternoon again. Strolled about the town & pier all day. Dined at Navarino

A beautiful day. Wind NE. Changed to NW & N with thunder & lightning & apparently heavy rain in Hampshire, but returned to the old quarter at night. F Barclay left us this morning for London. Sorry to loose him, a pleasant fellow. Mr Lee & Laura in the chaise & the rest walked to Binstead to see the abbey of which there is little remaining, after lunching on the grass with difficulty & getting our feet covered with mud. We returned home by the beach.

Delightful weather. Wind SE. Sea quite calm. Captain & Mrs Lewis, Bob Marsh & I took a boat & amused ourselves four hours fishing. Great success having caught 89 what they call whiting pacets, a small fish. Took a walk on the pier after dressing & dined at Navarino. The two young Wainwrights dined with us

Still fine weather. Wind variable between SE & N. Spent the morning Lewis Marsh & I in taking a walk to St John's towards St Helens & home in the afternoon. On the pier blowing very fresh. The Samarary frigate sailed & an Indiaman brought up off Ryde
A continuance of fine weather. Wind ESE. Attended divine services in the morning. The afternoon walked on the pier. Never was at such a dull place on a Sunday. Scarcely a soul to be seen.
Another fine mild day. Wind W & WNW. Took a walk to Tynemouth. Dined at home. In the evening at the theatre

A fine day. Wind ESE blowing fresh. Took a walk after breakfast with Captain Lewis & Marsh across the Daffers to the wood from which is a very beautiful view. Played a few games at billiards with the Captain. Spent the evening as usual at Navarinos

A pleasant morning, after heavy showers in the night. With a change of wind to SW a slight shower or two during the morning. The Valorous frigate arrived from the West Indies at Spithead after four years absence. Twice on the pier the only walk today. At Navarinos.
An exceedingly wet day. Wind E in the morning & afterwards changed to SW blowing fresh. Walked about the town and pier.
Wind still blowing hard from the SW but finer weather. Received a letter from William & wrote to Turner at London about the packages. Took a walk with Rebecca & Laura & Bob Marsh over the Daffers
A showery morning & blowing hard from the SE. Walked into town after breakfast & played at billiards in the afternoon. Turned out fine. Attended the theatre. Mrs Hugh Barclays bespeak, a fair house.
Precisely the same sort of day as yesterday.
A very cold day & blowing a gale of wind from ENE. Did not go to church being unwell with the toothache. Walked upon the pier in the afternoon
A beautiful day. Air sharp & frosty. Wind ENE. Walked upon the pier. Played a few games of billiards. Still trouble with the toothache

A continuance of uncommonly fine weather. Wind SSE. Captain & Mrs Lewis, Laura, Bob Marsh & I took a sail to & up Portsmouth Harbour round all the men-of-war. Went on board the Royal George Yacht and returned to dinner much gratified & delighted with our excursion.

Fine weather. Wind ESE. We amused ourselves in the morning making a large kite for the boys & in the afternoon walked on the pier. Received from William by George Lee two £5 notes with a letter from Stephenson of the arrival of the Hope at Shields after an 8 day passage on for journey

A fine mild day with showers in the morning. Wind SW. Walked to Tynemouth in the morning. Called upon the Miss Ildertons at Mr Sibbs, Mrs Dixon, Bell & Hanna Smith came down & lunched. Dined at home. Tea at Mrs Harrys & whist club in the evening. Heard from & wrote to William
Extraordinary fine weather . Wind about east. Finished & set the kite up. Lounged about the town in the afternoon.
A continuance of fine weather. Wind about SE. Passed the day much in the usual way.

A beautiful day. Wind SE. After breakfast Rebecca, Mrs Lewis, Lee and the girls & I went in the Isis to Portsmouth on board the Melville man-of-war. Captain Hill & much gratified & pleased with the beautiful order she was in & after lunching with Mrs Hill, returned to Ryde, delighted with our sail. The 1st Lieutenant got his promotion this day after 21 years hard service.

A most beautiful day. Wind SW. Went to church in the morning & heard a very poor commonplace sermon from a Mr Moors. Walked upon the pier in the afternoon. Mr & Mrs Gve Lee & Miss Jane Lee dined at Navarinos. Wind changed with a some rain at night

A fine warm day. Wind SW with a few light showers in the morning. Bob Marshes & I had a most delightful bath after breakfast. The Brocklebank steamer arrived from Brighton on an excursion of pleasure loaded with passengers between 2 & 3 rd, principally trades people in appearance. Lots of vulgarity, pipes & "heavy wet". Played a few games of billiards.

Beautiful weather. Wind SW. Remained in the house until after lunch. In the afternoon strolled about the town. Went to a Quadrille party at the library in the evening. Very well attended & good company. Wrote to William
A continuance of most extraordinary fine weather, with wind SW. Strolled about the pier & town

A glorious day. Not a cloud to be seen. Wind SW. After breakfast Lewis, Fanny, Bob Marsh took a boat & sailed round to Brading Harbour. Much pleased with the views of the country & coast & delighted with our sail. Got back at ½ past 3 pm. Received a letter from William of the arrival of the Hope but too late for yesterdays market.

A beautiful day. Wind SW to W. After breakfast walked to Binstead parsonage, about 1 mile, from Naravinos. In my opinion the prettiest & most picturesque place in the island. The grounds laid out with great taste & kept in the highest order. The views from them very fine. Wrote to William of my intention to be in town on Sunday.

A wet morning. Wind NW to SW. Cleared up before 12 o'clock & turned out a pleasant day. Booked outside place by the Rocket coach from tomorrow morning. Received a letter from William of the sale of the Hope at 32/3
A continuance of mild weather. Wind NW. Opened two accounts at chapmans WBS & JRS Executors & JRS private. Dined at home & drank tea at Mr Deightoughe , not well

A good deal of rain in the night. Wind SW. Left Ryde at 9 o'clock am. Steam for Portsmouth. Took an outside place in the Rocket coach & arrived in London at ½ past 7 o'clock pm having had a few showers of rain on the road. Got a bed in Nottingham Place. William out of town at his friend Oliphants. Found a note from him that Stephenson had been obliged to leave the Hope & return to the North in consequence of the illness of his uncle. Spent a very pleasant month with my friends, the Lees at Ryde& sorry to leave there.

A fine day. Wind SW. Went into the city by a Paddington Stage. Saw William. Attended the market & afterwards went down the river and dined on board the Hope. Walked home in the evening on our way drinking tea with Oliphant at Cockspur Street.

A dull morning during the day showers of rain. Wind SW. Walked into the city. Brought a new hat of Oliphant. Paid £3 for the Hopes ballast & took a Greenwich boat into the pool to her. Gave the mate charge for the passage to Shields. Returned to the city & had a basin of turtle soup at Bleadens. Afterwards took a Paddington Stage & went with William to see the Zoological Society garden in the Regent park. Well worth the walk. In the evening went to the Argyle rooms & was much amused with Fumtas chin

A fine day. Wind SW. Walked into the city. The Hope not to be out, the country craft having been sunk. Met Mr Carr who went out of the city with us, dined at the Blue Ports & in the evening went to Covent Garden Theater & saw at ½ price the latter part of Hamlet & Peter Welkins

Still fine weather. Wind SW & SSW. Went down to the Hope, only to do 10 ½ cha today. Dined on board. Walked up & went to Drury Lane Theatre to the pit at full price & saw "A cure for the heartache" & XYZ. Very much entertained.

Fine weather. Wind SW. Now & then a shower of rain. Walked into the city. Attended the Coal Exchange. The Hope not to do anything today. Watt called, took a boat to Hungerford. All dined at the Blue Pasts. Lent Watt 20/- Received of WBS £2.16. Balance of Hopes after her 3rd coal voyage.

A very wet morning. Wind WSW. Cleared up towards the middle of the day & turned out a fine afternoon. Went down to the ship about 1 o'clock pm. Found her nearly out. Watt came on board. Sailed about 3 o'clock & got below Woolwich & brought up, where Watt left us. A breeze springing up got underway again about 9 o'clock against the flood but obliged again to let go our anchor about 11 o'clock for want of wind! For the night William slept on board. Brought today a life preserver for 18/- Some white & coloured neckcloths for £2

A beautiful morning. Wind South. Got underway from off _____ at 11 o'clock am with a fresh breeze, landed William at Gravesend. At 1 o'clock pm. At 4 o'clock passed through Shoe Hole 8 o'clock abreast of Harwich & 10 o'clock off the Lowestoft Light & turned in for the night. Blowing fresh.

Blowing hard all night with rain towards morning. Got up at 8 o'clock am. Wind just changed to WNW, rather squally. Ship off Cromer. At 11 o'clock abreast of the floating light. Blowing hard from West. Ship under foresail & reefed topsail, mainsail & double reefed main topsail & reefed trysail. At 2 o'clock pm double reefed fore-top-sail. At 3 o'clock made the Spurn [Point] being off the floating light. Still blowing strong from the West

About 7 o'clock got bound. Flamborough Head at 10 o'clock. Off Robin Hoods bay blowing hard with squalls at 11 o'clock between the bay & Whitby met a fleet of London vessels. Blowing hard. Nearly run down one vessel owing to his own obstinacy or keeping a bad lookout. Stowed trysail & main sail & took in jib. Very dark ahead. At 12 o'clock or little after it, clear weather but continued to blow off Hunt Cliff Foot. Turned in for the night.
Dockwray Square, North Shields
A fine day. The air rather cool. Wind NW. Went over the water & called upon Mr Heatley . Dined at Mr Tibbs, Tynemouth

At 5 o'clock am off Sunderland with fine weather. Wind about WSW. Got a pilot on board. At 6 o'clock brought up off Shields Bar, turned out dressed & landed in Tynemouth Haven. Breakfasted in Dockwray Square. Mrs Scott not up being rather unwell. Went up to Newcastle but the Carrs busy from a fortnight to three weeks, returned to Shields by steam & fixed the Hope to take Burdon main to be load up under the spout on Friday. The ship towed safe into the harbour by a steam boat. Blowing a gale of wind from about WSW. Dined with Mrs Scott. Wrote to William

A fine day. Wind NW. Received a letter from William with the Hope's Balance Note for £63.18/- Engaged all the morning on board ship. Got the ballast out. Dined at home. Mrs Scott not well. Spent the evening at J Tinleys. W Temple there. Won 10/- at whist. Several ships got to sea.

A very fine morning. Wind NW. Made the Hope's book up. On board the ship under the spout. Got some keels in. Set the new for-topmast backstays. The Lady Jane arrived from Greenland with 15 fish, a full ship. Gave Stephenson £30. Made an agreement with the washerwoman for the quarter at 1 ½ guinea. Dined with J Tindley. Won at whist 4/-

A fine day. Wind WSW with a shower of rain at 1 o'clock. Mr Mark went on board the Hope with me & had some soup at 4 o'clock pm. The Hope load up & at 5 o'clock got to sea with a fine leading wind & beautiful weather & prospect of making a quick passage. Burdon Main loaded her for 15 keels & 6 char. Dined with J Tinley, J Dale, mark & Temple there. Won at whist 16/6 Gave Stephenson 35 to pay pilotage etc. with.
A beautiful morning. Wind about WNW. Went to Newcastle & saw the Dixons, Smith of Joyston & returned with J Tinley to dinner. Wrote to William of the sailing of the Hope. A few ships got to sea.
A fine & extremely mild day. Wind W by S. At church morning & afternoon. Dined with Mrs Scott. Went in the evening to the Quakers meeting to hear a woman preach; a tolerable discourse.

A pleasant and warm morning. Wind WNW. Went over the water to see Bowlby respecting the money he was to endeavor to get for C Harry from P Laing not received. Dined with Mrs Scott. Wrote to William about a Scotch coal freight for J Fenwith's Fidelity. At a party in the evening at Mrs Mathews. Wind changed in the afternoon to NE
An exceedingly fine day. Wind NNW. Engaged the whole of the day writing in the office. Dined at home & spent the evening writing.
A pleasant day. Wind NW. Called to see Mrs Ferguson's paintings. Prepared for going to Togston. Dined at home
A delightful day. Wind NW. A little swell upon the bar. A few small ships got to sea. Played billiards most of the morning. Dined with Mrs Scott. Wrote to William
A rather damp morning with appearance of rain. The wind blowing fresh from WNW kept it off. At church in morning. Walked to Tynemouth. Dined with Scott

A most beautiful morning. Wind NNW. Left Shields at 8 o'clock am after breakfast & got to Newcastle at ½ past 9 o'clock. Received a letter from William before I left Shields of the arrival of the Hope, but not sold. Wrote to J Fenwick of Preston Villa from Newcastle what William says about freights for Elgin coals & also sent J Tinley the part of the letter relative to N Birds debts to W & JS. Then left Newcastle at 10 o'clock by the Alnwick coach & got to Felton about 2 o'clock. The day much changed, being very cloudy & beginning to rain at ½ past 2 o'clock. After having some lunch, started for Togston to walk in the rain & arrived there at 4 o'clock. Found only Mrs Smith & Emma Galbraith at home. The rest of the family in Alnwick to attend the Jessions Ball. 2nd & 3rd voyages received for manure £3.17.6

A fine mild morning. Wind WNW. After breakfast, Emma & I walked to see the new colliery sunk by Tom Smith & others & afterwards went down to Amble & the sands & returned about 2 o'clock after a most pleasurable walk. Tom, Fanny, Anna & Bell returned from Alnwick to dinner at 5 o'clock

A beautiful autumnal day. Wind WSW. Drove Fanny, Bell & Emma Galbraith down to Warkworth church. Called upon the Miss Watsons. Saw the Chatterbucks etc. In the afternoon took a walk with Tom to the colliery. res Matt Culley came to dinner at 5 o'clock
Another fine day. Wind N by W. After breakfast went out shooting. Birds very plentiful. Got a great many shots but only killed a brace and a half. Got home at 4 o'clock. Dined at 5 o'clock
A continuance of beautiful weather & very mild for the season. Wind SW. Out shooting all the morning. Killed a 1 ½ brace of birds. Mr Culling also out & killed 2 ½ braces & a hare.

Beautiful weather. Wind SW & WSW. Mr Culley left us this morning. Out shooting from 12 o'clock to 3 o'clock towards Amble & killed 2 ½ braces. Shot very well today. Tom & Fanny drove this morning to Brinkburn. Fanny remained there & Tom returned in the evening. Sent a brace of birds to Mrs Scott and a brace to J Tinley

Weather exceedingly fine. Wind SW. Out shooting all this morning. Birds very wild. Did not kill one. Shot a hare. Sent it with 2 ½ braces of birds to Mrs Scott, I Tinby & Mr Mark. Tom also out today & killed 1 ½ braces. Mr Elliott dined & spent the evening
A fine day Wind SW. At home all the morning, reading and writing to J & B Galbraith
Fine weather. Wind SW. Out shooting. Got 1 ½ braces of birds.
A most beautiful day, rather frosty, wind NW. Dined with Mrs Scott. At the theatre in the evening. Last night of the Company's performance; a very full house
A beautiful day. Wind SE. At church in the morning. Called upon Mrs Cluttesbuck. Mrs & Miss Watson & Mr Bruce. Returned to Toyston to dinner.
A fine mild day. Wind SE. Out shooting & killed a pheasant & leveret & lost 1 ½ of birds. Tom Smith left us early this morning for Newcastle fair. Sent a letter by him to Rev Snowdon
A pleasant autumnal day. Wind ESE. Out shooting. Birds wild. Killed nothing
A beautiful morning. More like spring than autumn. Out for two hours shooting. Very hot. Birds exceedingly wild. Killed nothing. Tom got home in the evening
Fine weather. Wind north & rather cool. Mrs Dixon, F Smith & F Brown drove down from Brinkburns. After lunch Mrs Dixon & F Brown returned. Received a letter from Mr Vernon & the boys
Continuance of fine weather & wind NNW. Out shooting & killed 1 ½ braces of birds. Wrote to Mr Vernon & R Snowdon

Fine weather. Wind NW. Out shooting, no sport, the dog being tired by having been at Warkworth & the birds wild. Dined at Mr A Moises. Amble & spent a very pleasant day. The party consisting of Major Mr & Miss Clatterburn, Mr & Mrs Moises, Mr Elliott, Tom & Fanny Smith, self & Mr I Ord. Received a letter from master of the Hope being to sail on Thursday from London

A most beautiful day. Wind NNW. Went to Warkworth Church in the morning. Called upon Mr & Miss Watons. Drove Fanny & Bell Smith & Emma Galbraith in the afternoon. Robert Brown walked down from Brinkburn, dined & stayed all night. Spent a jolly evening.

A delightful day. Wind, but little in the morning at NW, afterwards changed to SE. Robert Brown left us for Brinkburn. Tom Smith drove him beyond Felton. Went out shooting but had no sport. Birds wild & scent bad.
A cool morning & thick weather. Wind SE. Walked twice to the colliery. Miss M Watson came up & dined at Togston. Played at whist in the evening
An exceedingly fair day, rather cold. Wind SW. Dined at home. At the assembly in the evening. A very pleasant one, but not numerously attended, about 60 there. Got home at 4 o'clock. Wrote to William

Got up at ½ past 6 o'clock am. A fine morning. Wind at SE. Breakfasted & rode to Morepeth with Tom Smith, market & fair day there. Left Morpeth by the Shields coach & got home at 4 o'clock. To dinner. Mrs Scott very well. The Hope arrived this afternoon & fixed for Wellington to be loaded on Tuesday. Received a letter from William, the sale with balance now for £73.18/-
A cold day. Wind about SSE. Called upon J Tinley. On board the Hope & gave Mr Stephenson £35 to pay wages. Dined with Mrs Scott & in the evening at the whist club of which I've been elected a member.

A cool day. Wind SSE blowing hard. A great many laden ships put back. Mr Mark & Mr Ferguson dined on board the Hope with me. Hauled her upon the shore to get her ballast out & look at her bottom. Took coffee with Ferguson .

Weather still cold & wind SSE. Received a letter from William to attend Birds meeting at Newcastle. Went up but the commissioners would not allow our claim. Returned home to dinner. Drank tea at J Tinleys.
A very cold day. Wind NE. At church in the morning. In the afternoon walked to Tynemouth. Dined with Mrs Scott,
A winters day. Very stormy with sleet & hail. Wind in the morning NE & changed to SE. On board the Hope. Tom & Fanny Smith & Emma Galbraith arrived from Togston.
A very frosty cold day. Wind WSW. The Hope got 4 keels down today. Dined at home. Robert made a bad collection of rents.

A very unpleasant & raw cold day. Wind SSW. The Hope got all her coals today, but being thick weather and poor prospect, did not go to sea. Mrs Matthews & Miss Liddell drank tea with us. Gave Stephenson £8. To my astonishment a writ of arrest was opened against me by Bland, Dunn the tailor partners . Very unhandsome conduct as William had called upon him to settle the account before I left town.

An exceedingly cold damp unpleasant day. Thick weather & wind SE & SSE. The Smiths left us for Togston. Wrote to William. Dined with Mrs Scott. In the evening at the card club. Won 4/-. The Hope not got out. Wrote to William

A raw damp day. A few loaded ships got out [in] the morning tide with a poor prospect. Wind SE blowing fresh all day. Several light ships got down. The Hope still in the harbour. Wellington coals 45/- at Wednesdays market. Only 7 ships there
A fine day but cold. Wind SSW. Dined at home.
A continuance of cold weather with rain. Wind SE. Mr Mark dined with me on board the Hope. No ships got to sea this day

A heavy fall of rain with wind at ESE in the afternoon. It got to E & NE with a deluge of rain. Dined at home. No ships sailed. Received a letter from William of his having paid Bland, the tailor my bill with costs £35.9.10
A very wet day. Wind NNW. A large fleet of small ships got to sea. The pilot refused to take charge of the Hope there being a heavy sea upon the bar. Dined at J Tinley with a small party.

A damp day with a little rain & wind in the morning. NE afterwards changed to SE & heavy sea upon the bar. The Hope still not able to get to sea. Dined at home. Attended the new whist club for the first time at J Tinleys. Won 20/-

A very fine day. Wind NW & sea down. A very large fleet with the Hope sailed with a fine prospect. Walked to Tynemouth & called upon Mr Marks of the 5th Regiment. Dined at Mr Mayne. Met Captain Bunbury of the 80th Regiment. Mr Hopkins, Mr Mayne & Mr Ferguson.

A fine day. Wind WNW. A few ships went to sea. Engaged all the morning in the office. Wrote to William. Paid Barthewan an advance of £5.5.4. At the whist club in the evening. Paid into Chapman £50 rents on acct of executors

A beautiful day. Wind SW. Several ships got to sea. Gave Reaerby the painter a draft for £6.7.6 for painting the Hope. Dined with Captain Bunbury at Tynemouth & spent a very pleasant day. Borrowed £50 of exors & placed to Credit of private account at Chapman
A fine day. Wind WSW. Took a walk round Cullercoat fields & Tynemouth. Dined at home. Spent the evening with the whist club at Mr Metcalfs
A fine day. Wind SW & cold. Went to church with Emma in the morning. Walked to Tynemouth in the afternoon. Dined at home.

A pleasant day, but blowing hard from SSW. On board the Amity. Went over the water to see Mr P Laing respecting Che Harry's account, but did not see him, he being in London. Dined at home. Suppered with H Harry. Received a letter from William.

Another fine day & mild. Wind SSW to WSW. Engaged in the morning in examining my father's old papers & accounts in search of the Ariel's vouchers and burning such papers as were out of date & useless. Dined at home & at the whist club in the evening.
An exceedingly pleasant day. Wind W by S. Employed all the morning in unpacking the tenure books we brought from Ireland. Dined at Mr Craiges, a large party.

A fair day. Wind W. Received a letter this morning from William of Frys & Chapmans failure which surprised me much, the consequence was a run upon Chapmans House here, but which I believe ended towards the evening. The bank are otherwise not affected by Frys failure having known for a fortnight it was to happen & consequently preparing for a run, they suffer no losses. At the theatre in the evening. Much amused.

A cold morning. Wind NW to W & WSW towards the evening. Took a walk with Emma & called upon Mrs Paul & Sharp. Wrote to William but forgot to put the letter into the post. At the whist club in the evening. No run upon Chapmans today. All quiet & business going as usual.

A fine mild day. Wind about West. Attended a meeting of the Commissioners under the new act to appeal against the rate of the House in Dockwray Square & got it reduced from £50 to £45. Took a walk with Emma & showed her the glass exhibition. Received a letter from William. No account of the Hope. Drew upon Chapmans for £5 for self.

A dull day. Wind ESE. A few light ships got in. Finished a long letter to William a continuation to that which I forgot to put into the post on Thursday & enclosing Turner's letter from Carlow, sent them off. Dined at home. Attended the whist club at Mr Allens. A very wet afternoon & night.

A very stormy & rainy morning with a gale of wind from ESE to E by N. & high sea upon the bar. I went to church in the morning. A continuation of rain & much heavier. Dined with J Tinley. Received a letter from William of the Hope's arrival. Old Mr Metcalf of Tynemouth died very suddenly this morning during church time.

Early this morning it blew a very heavy gale of wind from the NE & ENE with showers of rain & heavy sea. Towards afternoon the wind abated but continued from the east. Engaged in the office the principal part of the morning. Wrote to William. Dined at home. Mr Wheatley buried a son & daughter Mr Gun today. They died of consumption.

A dull morning. Wind N by S towards evening the wind got up & increased to a perfect gale from the S by W & excessively cold. Understand that several ships, all on shore, some near Sunderland. Walked with Mr Mark & called upon Captain Bunbury & Mr Hopkins. Dined at home. In the evening went to the Commercial to see Mr Ildeston who was waiting there for Mr Tibbs. Received an invitation & suppered with the committee of Association for prosecuting felons. Sat rather late.

A fine mild day and wind about W by N. Walked to Tynemouth called at Tibbs upon Mr Ildeston who returned to Shields with me. Dined at home & in the evening met Mr Ildeston at Mr Baskers to take wine. Mr Mark there.
A fine day. Wind WSW. During the morning at home reading. Dined at home & in the evening at the whist club. Bad accounts of losses in the Monday morning gale upon the Yorkshire coast.
A fine day. Wind WNW & rather cold. Dined at home
A pleasant day, but rather cool & wind SW. Dined at Mr Tibbs at Tynemouth. Mr & Mrs Tinley, Miss Hewson, Mr & Mrs L Fenwick, Mr & Mrs I Fenwick, Misses Drury, Captain Bunbury & self the party

A most beautiful day. Fresh breeze from SW. The two Mrs Dixons came down from Benton, lunched & took Emma back with them. Dined at home. In the evening attended the whist club at Greenhows. Towards night it began to blow very hard. Mr Harry, H French, Mr Mark & I took wind at the George. Ps Subscription 1G to newsroom

Blowing a heavy gale of wind all night from S by E. This morning SSW & towards afternoon got to W by S. Received a letter from William informing me of Jon Young demanding payment of their claims. Attended morning service. Dined at home. In the evening took wine with Mr Harry at the Albion.

A pleasant winters morning. Wind NNW which changed in the afternoon to about WSW. Got £5 from the bank for own use. Dined with J Tinley. Went to the theatre at the Prince. Mrs Metcalf of Tynemouth buried today
A pleasant day. Milder wind WSW. Dined at home.

A fine but cold frosty day. Wind WNW. Went to Benton by the coach in the morning. Walked there from the turnpike & afterwards onto Newcastle where I wrote to William to sell the Hope. Missed Dixons, walked out to Benton again to dinner. Mr Colonel Dixon staying there. Mr Allinson dined with us
Rather a stormy day & cold. Wind WNW. Walked into Newcastle with Dixon. A great day at Gosforth guns firing etc etc. Mr Charles Bell married one the Miss Brandlengs. Returned to Benton to Dinner.
A beautiful mild day. Wind WNN. Out greyhound coursing. Ran 8 or 9 hares & killed none. The dogs out of wind not having had any exercise lately. But had some pretty running.

Exceedingly fine mild. More like summer than December. Walked with Dixon to Newcastle. Spent the morning there, took the steamer boat & got to Shields at 3 o'clock. Dined with J Tinley in the evening at Mr Harry's. Then whist club. At night the wind got round to the east.

A very foggy day & unpleasant day. Wind about S by E. At church in the morning. Tinley, Mr Brereton of Liverpool & I walked to Tynemouth in the afternoon. Dined at Tinley's. Met Mr Brereton & a Mr Smith of Oporto.

A fine day, Wind WNW & a slight frost. Dined at Mr Reeds, a large party. Received a letter from William with gratifying intelligence that Lees & co had agreed to let me take the Hope upon mortgage the price £1250 to pay all expenses incurred in the last two years making her stand me in about £1350. Wrote to William

A dull day but dry. Wind about S. Received a letter from William of the sale of the Hope at 34/6, a miserable price = 8/6 freight. After laying a fortnight at London. Dined at home. Wind changed to about SW in the evening.

A fine day. Wind S & SW. Went at Williams request to look for Baxter Arthur of the amety, but he had gone to sea. Called upon Junior Carr & gave him William's letter to pay me the balance of the Hope's freight account. Dinned at home. Wrote to William. Payed into Chapmans £15 rents on account of executors

A little rain in the morning. Wind W & SW. A pleasant afternoon. Dined on board the Combatant, Captain Barnes. A ship of the Tinleys, an agreeable party consisting of J Tinley, A Harry, Mr Boswell, Captain Webb, W Barnes, Mr Richardson & self, went to the play at ½ price to pass an hour but returned home at 10 o'clock at which hour Mrs Scott had made up her mind I should be in. Her conduct towards me so pointed & bad that I have determined to go to lodgings as I neither have nor do I wish to give her any annoyance at the same time. I don't choose to submit to it myself, for it seems her temper & disposition neither to be happy & comfortable herself or to let others be so.
A very fine day. Wind WNW. Took a walk to Tynemouth. Dined at home. At the whist club in the evening

Blowing a gale of wind from NW with a little rain. Captain Bunbury, Mr Mark & I went over to Sunderland & dined at the mess of the 80th Regiment & spent a very agreeable day, the dinner given to colonel Cookson who was for many years commanding officer of the regiment in India. Slept at Joyscys Inn
A fine mild morning. Wind about W by N. Blowing strong. After breakfast, called at the Barrack & afterwards returned to Shields. Dined with Mrs Scott & in the evening at the whist club at R Pearts
A damp foggy day. Wind W & WNW. Went to church in the morning. Dined at J Tinley's

An exceedingly wet day. Wind about W or W by S. Received a letter from William & answered it ordering by W Taylors desire the Morning Journal & Morning Herald newspapers. At 5 guineas for the Newsroom. Dined at home.

Rather a damp day. Wind E & ESE. Dined at J Tinleys. A pleasant day. There Captain Bunbury, Mr Hopkins 80th Regiment, Mr Parr & Doctor White. Afterwards went to the ball. Very well attended for the first time. Upwards of 60 there. Danced with a Miss Paine of Faversham, a very fine girl.

Paid apprentices one quarters wages, £1.8.9 Repaid executors £50 borrowed of them. Gave Stephenson £25 to pay wages
A fine mild day. Rather damp with rain in the evening. Wind SE. The Hope arrived safe in the evening ½ past 6 o'clock. Dined at home. Received the Hope's accounts along with a balance of £51.11/-
A beautiful day, Wind WSW. At church in the morning. Walked to Tynemouth in the afternoon with J Tinley & boys. Dined at home
