Xmas day. A fine day. Wind SSW. Went to church in the morning & afterwards walked up to Benton to dinner & stayed all night. Wrote to William to take the Hope off risk of British Club

A beautiful morning & sharp frost. Wind SSW. Walked into Newcastle. Took the Hope on for a turn of townley & gave notice to the Hope Club of my intention to lay her up. Received from Carr & Co £21.6/- on account of WBS. Balance of freight acct o/s Hope. Came down to Shields to dinner & in the evening attended the whist club. The Hope got under the crane to take her manure out for Mr Junior Finewick of Preston Villa. Gave Mrs Scott a draft on Chapmans for £75 her annuity.

A fine seasonable day, rather cold & frosty. Wind S by W. On board the Hope all the morning. Along side the crane getting manure out for which I received of Mr Fenwick £2 there being 80 tons. The people engaged unbending sails & taking down running rigging etc preparatory to laying ship up. Dined at home. In the evening at the whist club at Tom Weights

A foggy morning & a heavy fall of rain during the whole day. Wind W by S. Cleared up in the evening. At church in the morning. Miss Heevson dined with me. Wrote to William informing him of my having received of Mr Shakers £10.11.2 on account of Messrs Lees, which I carry to WBS Cr. Spent the evening at J Tinleys.
A fine weather day. Excessively cold. Wind SW. Engaged in the morning drawing & on board ship. Dined at home. Took wine with Mark Cunningham & Boswick at the Albion
A fine day. Rather thick. Wind SW. Dined at home. Paid into Chapmans on my own account £10.11.2

A pleasant day. Wind WNW. Engaged in the morning drawing & on board of ship. Sails all on shore at Mr Hearns. Ordered the running rigging to be taken to Mr Sharps, as there's nothing safe on board from the nightly visits the thieves pay. Thus ends the year, a very poor one for ship & owners. I for one can safely say that I have not made one farthing. I only hope the next year will be productive of more good or I know not what will be the consequence. Dined at home & in the evening attended the theatre. The bespeak of the Subscriber to the Assemblies. A very fair house, as things are.

A most beautiful morning. The air rather frosty. Wind WNW. Walked up to Beaton. Dined & remained all night.
Another fine day . Wind NNW. Walked from Beaton to Wallsend. Called upon & dined with Mr Potts in the evening. Walked to Shields & attended the whist club

Another fine mild day. Wind WEW. On board the Hope. Got the cabin & half deck stoves on shore to repair. Dined at home. In the evening gave Mark, J Harry & R Peart a bowl of punch and a rubber of whist at the George

A fine day. Wind NW. On board the Hope. People engaged smoking her. Dined at home. In the evening at the whist club at the Craiges. Paid Geo Slops apple the balance of his wages 18/3 & advances him 3 weeks lodging money & 10/9 cash. Tom Wright junior married today to his grace of Felling.
A fine winters day & cold. Very appearance of a change of weather. Wind NNW & N. Went to church morning & afternoon. Dined at J Tinley's. Geo & Mrs Heddek there.

A fine winters day. Wind NE. Cols & sea high at night, a little snow & frost. Dined at home. Received a letter from William. Engaged most of the morning in the office writing. Mrs Dixon brought Emma home.

A cold day with frost. Wind NE & sea high. Walked to Preston with Robert & Emma to talk to Moor about arrears of rent. Went on board the Hope. All safe. Dined at home. Mrs Marr called in the evening with whom we agreed to send Emma to school the next morning. Suppered and smoked a few segars with A Harry. Wrote to William.

A fine day & cold. Wind ENE & E by N. Attended a general meeting of the ship owners & entered into resolutions relative to the rate of timber freights for the ensuring years & agreed not to take less than 45/- for Quebec, other ports in proportion. The meeting from the conflicting interests could come to no resolution with regard to the coal trade. Dined at home in the evening. Took wine & suppered with A Harry, A French & A Nicolson at the Albion. Called at the Mulstream.

An unpleasant day. Ground very wet & dirty from the snow not laying. Wind variable during the day. Between the E & S. Once or twice it was at SW for a short time. Dined at home. At the whist club in the evening. Called at the Mulstream.

A very unpleasant day. Cold with Sleet. Streets excessively dirty. Wind about N & sea high. Paid Barnes £1.5.6. Clark £1.16.6 & Alder shoemaker 10/6. Dined at home in the evening at the Albion whist party, rather a noisy party. At the Mulstrum
Fair weather but cold. Wind SE & ESE. Sea high. Several light ships got down. Dined at home. In the evening at Tibbs whist club. Paid Reed apprentice I Weeks board lodgings 7/-
A thick dull day, but dry. Wind variable. At church in the morning. Received a letter from I & B Galbraith & Mr Vernon. Dined at home. In the evening at the Mulstrum.

Finer weather. Cold with a little hail. Wind ESE & sea high. Several light ships got in. Dined at home. In the evening called & took wine with Tom Wright upon his marriage. A great many there. Spent a pleasant evening.

Here I find myself once more in my native place after misfortune unlooked for & unmeritted & two years of anxiety and in settling our affairs, the disgraceful conduct of our attorney (Baily) & his clients, proceeding from ignorance & stupidity, I believe caused the delay, but which however has ended by the various amendments & and alterations in the deeds suggested by William & myself, much more to the advantage of ourselves & all parties, than could possibly have been anticipated at the commencement. I now trust this is the beginning of a new life, where in its course will be attended with prosperity & happiness both to my brother & myself & that he may soon have it in his power as I'm sure it is his wish & intention to "render unto every man his due" he may have committed errors but this I know, they have been errors of the head not of the heart. If he had a fault, it was too great a desire to serve others without perhaps prudently asking himself whether he could do so, without committing an act of injustice to himself his family or those who were next to those connected to him by the nearest & dearest ties, however "Expereentia docet". Here's oblivion to the past & may prosperity attend the future. As for myself, I feel as every ...
A fine mild day. Wind WSW. Dined at home. Engaged Mr Stephenson as master of the Hope, having a very high character from Mr Hogg. Wages £9. per voyage
A cold day. Wind E by S. A few ships arrived. At the court for Taverne the principle part to the morning. Dined with the Liberal club, Commercial Hotel & spent a pleasant day. A large party.

A fine day. Wind NW with a slight frost. Walked to Tynemouth with Mr Boswell * took a warm bath. Dined at home. In the evening joined a party to drink a little punch at the Mulstream. Lots of fun. Got home at 10 o'clock
A very fine day with a hard frost. Wind variable between SW & NW. Walked to Tynemouth with Boswell. Dined at home & in the evening at the whist club. Called at the Mulstrum.

A dull day with snow & wind variable between W by S & SE. At night got to west again. Drew £10 out of Chapmans & paid Cluigh for G Slofs cloathes £2.14/0. Dined at home. In the evening at the Albion whist club. Called at the Mulstrum but did not stop long.

A fine winters day. Ground covered with snow, but not much of a frost. Wind at NNW. Called upon Mr Ferguson & got some drawings for copying, engaged in it all afternoon. Dined at home. Mrs Scott down stairs in one of her bad humours & very disagreeable. Attended the whist club at Drewgs. Paid Reed apprentice 7/- cost week board & lodgings.
Another fine day with frost & showers of snow. Wind N & NNW. At church in the morning. Dined at home. Mrs Scott downstairs. Went to Stowells Chapel in the evening. Called at the Mulstrum.
An exceedingly fine day. Hard frost & wind NW. Engaged the whole of the morning at home drawing. Dined at home. Suppered & spent a pleasant evening with A Harry & his sister.
A continuance of frosty weather with snow showers. Wind NW, changed in the afternoon to east, with thaw. Dined at home. Wrote to William

A beautiful day & frosty. Wind E by S & changed in the afternoon to W by S. A great many light ships arrived. Walked to Tynemouth with W Ferguson & called upon Captain Bunbury. Dined at home. In the evening at the theatre ½ price. Mrs Grose's benefit £17 in the house. Paid average Elizabeth. Choice to Hope Club £28.19.2

A fine day. Exceedingly cold. Wind SE blowing fresh & sea high. A King ship came in in the. Dined at J Tinley's & went to the apunbly in the evening. A most delightful Ball. Suppered afterwards. The dancing at ½ past 2 o'clock & Kept it up till 6 o'clock.

A beautiful day. Wind SW. Changed towards evening to East. Engaged all morning on board the Hope. Having two men employed in overhauling small ropes running rigging to which we found in a much better state than could be expected. Mr Carr late master must have been very careless to say the least, having left some sails, bread, flour & bags & a cask of provisions with the head knocked in & compass as on board which were all destroyed & rotten
A cold day. A continuance of frost & snow and a gale of wind SE & SSE, sea high. A few loaded ships put back. Dined at home. Spent the evening at J Tinleys. Paid Reed a week's lodging 7/-.

A continuance of frost & snow & a gale of wind from SE to SSE. Went to Newcastle to endeavour to get something for the Hope, but did not succeed. People not willing to do anything until after the meeting of coal owners. Dined with J Tinley, a party, Captain Morins & 2 Lieutenants of the childers, C Milners & sister Miss Atlen Lieutenants 80th Regiment
A fine day. Hard frost. Wind NW. At church in the morning. Walked to Tynemouth. Dined at home & took wine with A Metcalf

This morning a thaw commenced, early at blew a gale of wind with sleet. Wind blowing E by S & S by E. Excessively wet & sloppy walking. Dined at home. Spent the evening & suppered with Mr Allen. A very pleasant party. Got home at 1 o'clock. Engaged a new washer woman by the quarter.

A continuance of thaw with heavy rain. Much of the snow disappeared. Wind SSE. Went to Newcastle but no freights or anything offering. The fuller obsheiate. On my return found Mr Watson of Walkworth here. Dined at home. Spent the evening at J Tinleys. Miss Nicholas, Miss Allen and Captain Moorers there.
A unpleasant day. Rainy & very wet & dirty walking. Wind NE in the morning which changed to NW. Dined & spent the evening at home.

Finer weather. Wind ENE. Mr Watson left us for Newcastle. Went up to Newcastle to attend the annual meeting of the Hope Club. No material alterations made in the rules. Took Mr Boswell up to dine with me. Returned in the evening & attended the whist club. Reduced my investment in the Hope Club to £500. With Ana Gallop for the first time.
A wet day. Wind N by E. Offered the Hope to the Liberal Premium Club for £500 Insurance. Dined at home. At Mrs Grenlows in the evening, a large party
Finer weather with a slight frost. Wind NW, changed in the afternoon to SE. Dined at home. Met Ana Yallop. At the whist club in the evening at I Dales. Paid E Reed a weeks lodging 7/-
A fine frosty day. Wind W by N. A large fleet of colliers went to sea. Attended church in the morning. Dined at home. In the evening at the Mulstrum. A French, Boswell & Nicolson. Jane Muston
A damp morning, but turned out fine. Wind S by W. On board the Hope all the morning got cables upon deck, found them in fair order. Dined with Dr Drury. Whist club in evening

A fine frosty day & sharp frost. Wind W by S. Engaged part of the morning drawing. Took a walk round by the ship. Found all right, Stephenson on board waiting for Mr Cleths to survey her for the Premium Club. Dinned with Mr Chapman of Elseneur at the Commercial. A French & W Boswell came and took wine. Went to the theatre, Crooks benefit, a fair house& the last night of performance for the season. Got £5 of Chapman for self.

A beautiful morning & hard frost. Wind W & W by S. A French & I walked round the town with Mr Chapman of Elseneur to call upon his friends. Dined at 2 o'clock with A Harry. On board the Choise, A French, A Nicholson, Drewing, Cunningham, Mark ____, self & Captain ____ Mr Bradshaw came on board. After dinner we spent a very pleasant day.

A damp morning. Wind West. Passed part of the morning in drawing & writing to William with Robert's account of seats. Attended a meeting of shipowners & masters for the purpose of establishing a asylum for aged & infirm master mariners, an excellent institution & long wasted the meeting most respectfully & numerous attended & then business well conducted & a most liberal feeling persuading every person as the donation & subscriptions best testified. Read a letter from Geo Dunn to know if I intended loading the Hope. Answered in the negative unless fieghted or upheld. Dined at home. Mrs Scott very unwell, but downstairs. Saw arr γαλλοπ
Weather rather damp & foggy. Wind from W to N by S. Passed the first of the morning in drawing. Dined at home. Saw ann γαλλοπ. At the whist club
A fine mild morning. Wind W by N. Paid Brown for oakeun & for Hope's buffet & the year £21. Dined at I Fenwicks, Preston Villa, a party of 18

A beautiful mild morning. Wind NNW. Employed the first of the morning in drawing. Went to the news jbetenaid room. Dined at home. In the evening at the club at J Tinley's. Mr Walowstegs ship that Fenwick fixed by Mr Allen in Quebec & East coast at the shipowners rates.

A damp morning, having been a great deal of rain during the night. Wind NNW. Mrs Scott very ill. Wind variable during the day between NNW & N by E. At church in the morning. The newspapers countenancing the speeding in Parliaments of the news as to declaring their intention to grant Catholic emancipation which caused a great sensation here, but particularly to the incomcas to it in both houses of parliament. Dined at J Tinley's. The two Carrs there.

A fine mild day. Wind NW. Engaged in the morning drawing. Dined at home. Went over the water & joined H Harry, Boswell, French & Nicolson at Bullocks & took wine. Went to the theatre in the evening at North Shields. Received a letter from William. Mrs Scott suffering dreadful pain.
A pleasant morning & wind NW. Mrs Scott in great pain last night. Got £5 from Chapmans for private use. Walked to Tynemouth. Dined in the Commercial, the Limited & Eligible Clubs. Sat very late.

A beautiful morning. Wind NW. Attended the meeting of the Master Mariners, when the rules were read over & adopted. Walked up to Milburn's Place to see the ship. Dined at home. In the evening at the Mulstrum.
A very fine day, Wind West. Brought the Hope down to the Low Light shore to get her ballast out and agreed with a man to repair & refit all the rigging for £10

A mild morning, but damp having been a great deal of rain in the night. Wind NW. A meeting held of the committees of clubs to demand an explanation of Joe Elder for fixing his ship below the rates of freight determined upon by shipowners. It is not the first time he has been guilty of such dishonest practices. He could not explain himself & unless Mr Bell cancels the charter, which will be known tomorrow, Eldess ships will be turned out of the clubs, the proper way of treating such fellows. Dined at home. In the evening attended the whist club & afterwards went to a large bridal party at Tom Wrights

A most beautiful morning. Quite mild & spring weather. Wind WNW. Took a walk to Tynemouth. Dined with the Friendly club at the George Tavern where we had a handsome dinner & spent a pleasant evening. Saw Ann Mallot

A fine morning. Wind NW. Went by coach to Newcastle. Called at D Dixons. Found Mrs Dixon about to set off for Shields to see Mrs Scott. Called at G Dunn & Sons & refused to load their coals without being upheld. Afterwards walked down to Shields. Dined at Mrs Reeds with a large party. The bridal party Mr & Mrs Tom Wright there. Attended the whist club at A Metcalf. Paid R Brown the account £4.10/-

A mild morning with the appearance of rain & blowing fresh at WNW. Mrs Scott in a devil of a humour blowing every person up right & left. I think her mind must be affected. Went to church. Took a family dinner with A Harry. In the evening at the Mulstrum. Met Bell Jervis for the first time.

A fine morning & calm wind about West. Walked to the ship & ordered the sails & small stones on board. About noon it turned very thick weather & the wind suddenly changed to NE with heavy rain that lasted all night

A damp morning it having been a great deal of rain & sleet during the night. Wind NNW changeable during the day to ENE & NE. Went down to the ship. The committee on board surveying stores for the Hope club. Dined at J Tinleys with a party of gentlemen. We all afterwards went to the ball. Only 52 there, but a pleasant dancing ball. Ordered a new mainstaysail for the Hope.

Rather a dull morning. Wind WNN & looks like more rain. Turned very cold towards afternoon & wind changed to SE & S by E. Went to Newcastle but everything very dull & could do nothing for the Hope. Returned home to dinner.

A cold morning. Wind SW. Has been some rain in the night. Received a letter from the committee of the Hope Club ordering us to get a new lamp & next winter a new foresail. Also now four new ballast shovels. Engaged all the morning writing to William & the Galbraiths. Found Mrs Craig in a chaise & went to Walls to dine with Mr J Wright, a large party of 18. Spent a pleasant day & had the best port wine I ever tasted in my life. Got home at 12 o'clock.
A beautiful morning. Wind SW. Mr mark & I took a walk along the Herd sand. Dined at home. Suppered at Mr Bradshower

A fine morning. Wind SW At 10 o'clock am wind suddenly changed to SE with thick fog & very raw and cold. Went to Newcastle by coach but could not get anything for the Hope. Called at Mrs Dixon's. Dined at home. In the evening at the whist club at A Dales. Received a letter from J Young demanding payment of their claims upon W & J Scott which we shall most certainly not accede to, he having agreed to take the comporation with the other creditors.

A cold day, Wind SE. On board the Hope in moorings. Got the rigging all down, a fire lighted in the cabin & hold partly scraped & cleared. Dined at the vicars & met a very pleasant party. Received a letter & wrote to William
A fine morning. Wind E by N. About 10 o'clock am it began to rain very heavy & continued all the morning. Went to church. Dined with J Tinley

A fine morning. Blowing fresh from the WNW & lo. Wrote to J Young requesting a few days to communicate with my brother. Walked up to the ship with J Tinley in the morning, who wrote to Netern to send down the deed of release. All letters be relative to our composition. Dined at home. In the evening had an ryotes supper at the Northumberland. Won a bet lost by Locklder & Mr Holroryd. Sat down 13 & spent a pleasant evening

A fine morning. Wind NW & afterwards changed to East with snow. Walked to Tynemouth. Attended a sale of old furniture at Mr Lenskerths. Mrs Dixon came down to see Mrs Scott. Dined at J Tinleys. A large party.

A fine morning. A hard frost. Wind E by S. Has been a little snow in the night. Last night the mews room was on fire but was discovered in time to get put out before much damage was done. In a short time it would broken out & spread that the whole building would have been destroyed. The floor rafters and ceiling of mews room partly burnt. Walked with Boswell to Tynemouth. Dined at J Dales. Met a large party & spent a pleasant day.

A fine morning & blowing fresh from E. Received a letter from William with a copy of his answer to J Young. Paid Morton & Thompson for the Hope's bowsprit pump for £25.7/-. Dined with H Dale, Mr Mark & Mr Jackson of the 80th regiment. Spent a pleasant evening. Walked to the ship in the morning. Turned out a very wet night. Sleet
A dull wet morning. Wind SSW. Dined at home. In the evening attended a large party at Mr J Fenwicks, Preston Villa, about 120 there, a dinner.

A raw cold foggy morning. Wind SW. Drove up to Newcastle with Mr Tinley, called upon Mrs Dixon, went to the Quay side, but could not do anything for the Hope. Returned to Shields by steam boat. Dined with J Tinley & went to the whist club at Mr Richmonds in the evening.

A beautiful morning. Wind SW & cool, rather frosty during the night. Went to church. On my return found Mr Dixon, Bell Smith & Tom had come down to see Mrs Smith. In the afternoon walked to Tynemouth & called upon Mr Jackson 80th regiment. In the evening at the Mulstrum. Had all Laserio

A fine frosty morning. Wind SE & E by S. Went to Newcastle by steam. Could do nothing for the Hope. Walked up to Westgate Street & the billiard rooms. Returned to Shields to dinner. Spent the latter part of the evening at J Tinleys

A very fine morning. Wind NW. Went by steam to Newcastle. Nothing to be done for the Hope. Dined with Dixon Dixon. In the evening went to the theatre. Met the Ildestons there. A very thin house. The high sheriffs benefit. The Dixons & Tom & Bell Smith went to a ball given by the offices of the dragoon quarter at Newcastle.

An extremely cold & frosty day. Wind SSE & every appearance of bad weather At church in the morning - Young King preached. Dined at home. At night blew a gale of wind. A heavy sea on the bar. Wrote to Bessy & Captain Lewis
A raw cold morning. Wind NE. Tom & Bell Smith started for Togston. I returned to Shields by steam to dinner. Went to a small party in the evening at Mr Marks

Finer weather. Wind NE. Wrote to J Young that we were made to pay him & his father's lie leaedind but no more. Added a postscript to J Tindley's letter to William. Dined at home. Attended the whist club in the evening.

A fine morning. Rather cold. Wind NNE. Walked up to the ship. George Slofs employed rigging her with only the apprentice of the little boy Ned Reed. For a very fine young man, only been seven coal voyages & is as good as any man. Dined at home. Saw poor Richard Brown who I much fear has not long to live.

A pleasant morning. Wind NW. Went by coach to Newcastle but evening continues very dull & could do nothing for the Hope. An immense number of people at Newcastle, having been to see the unfortunate woman Jane Jameson hanged for the murder of her mother. Returned home by steam to dinner. Attended the whist club at J Dale's. Met Jane Thompson for the first time at Jenny Maxwells

A fine morning, but rather dull. Wind NW. Took physic & could not go to church. Wrote to Mr P Lacing respecting C Harry's claim. At the grange man Sunderland. Dined at home. The newspapers today filled with Mr Puls expositions of the measures of ministise for the relief of the Catholics. Took wine in the evening with H Harry & J Lunning have at the Albion. Afterwards called at the Mulstrum & saw Bell Jarvis !!!!

A fine morning. Wind NW. On board the Hope. Brought some beef 6.0.6 at 4 o'clock. Dined at Mr Allen's & suppered in the evening at the George with a party. An Oyster supper. Kept it up very late. Paid £1.4/- entrance for Friday C Club. Got £5 of Chapmans
A pleasant morning. Wind NE. A little rain during the day. Walked up to the Ship. Dined with a large party at J Tinley & in the evening a party at Mr Barretts
A pleasant morning. Wind NW. Amused myself the best part of morning with drawing. At the billiard table & dined on board the XYZ with Mr Harrison. Saw Bell Jarvis in the evening.
A fine morning but rather cool. Wind W by S. Walked up to the ship. Sent Master Scott Crathorn £2. Dined at home. At the whist club in the evening.
A cold morning. Wind NNS & N by E. A heavy sea on the bar. Paid Clark, coopers for the Hope £1.9/- Dined at home
A very stormy cold day with a heavy fall of snow. Busy with the rigging at the ropery. A heavy sea upon the bar, Wind SE by S. Dined at home. Wrote to Messrs Lees & Co

A fine frosty morning. Wind NW. Went to Newcastle by steamer. Ordered the Hope's coal down. Returned home to dinner. At the whist club in the evening at Allens. J Tinley received a letter from H Dale stating that he had C Young & Sons orders to proceed against us for their debts.

A very fine morning & frosty. Wind NW. Changed during the day to NEE & SE. Went to church in the morning. Walked to Tynemouth in the afternoon. Dined at home. In the evening at the Mulstrum with Bell Jarvis

A fine morning but cold & Wind SW. A great number of light ships coming in. On board the Hope. Moved her from the Quay (Smiths) & laid her upon the shore to have her keel surveyed for the Liberal Premium Club. Dined at home. Mrs Dixon down to see Mrs Scott. With Bell Jarvis at her sister Mary's

A fine morning & blowing fresh from the SW & cold. Another large fleet coming in. Borrowed off Robert £5. On board the Hope. Two keels alongside. People engaged lending sails. Walked up to the spout/huroonaschs & took lunch on board the 3 Brothers with A French, H Harry, Allen, W Harrison, J Wright there. Dined with J Tinley a party & in the evening went to the ball which was thinly attended but a very pleasant one.

A pleasant day. Wind SW. Paid E Reed's mother £1.8.9 being ¼ years wages. On board the Hope. Got 9 keels in. paid Fenwick for making main stagsail & foretopmast sturingsail £2.9/-. Dined at home. Spent the evening at J Tinley's

A damp morning. Showers of rain & blowing fresh from SSW. Attended a meeting of the parishioners at the church respecting the burial ground at Tynemouth. The board of ordinance having given orders that no more interments shall take place. A most arbitrary & unjust proceeding & which the parish considers they have no right to do, it having been the parish church & ground for time immemorial. Dined with Mr Allen & afterward went on board the Hope. Got six more keels on board today. In the evening at the whist club. Paid Geo Slops £1.13/- the balance of years wages account.

A fine morning & blowing fresh from the SW. Mr Mark & Ferguson dined with me on board the Hope at 1 o'clock. Got the last keel down in the morning at 3 o'clock pm move ship out but having a foul anchor could not get to sea. Much damage done but on the middle sand & much stove. With Bell Jarvis in the evening.

A beautiful spring morning. The Hope got to sea early. Wind NW. Paid Foy boat 13/- Went with Mr & Mrs Tinley to Newcastle. Signed the Hope's cargo bill £176.7.7 The Dmans refused to change less than 21/- to upheld & have I conceded treated me exceptional ill. Dined & stayed all night with D Dixon. Wrote to William.

Most beautiful weather. Rather frosty & wind SSE & SE. Came down to Shields by steamer & changed my cloths. Received a letter from William with one to J Tinley. Returned by steam to Newcastle & again dined and stayed all night with D Dixon. Mrs Coll Dixon dined with us

A damp & unpleasant cold morning, blowing fresh from the SE. Some loaded ships put back. Gave J Tinley, William's letter. My cold so much worse today & allofother so unwell that I was obliged to lay up & take physic.
Weather very wintery and cold. Wind E by NE & snow showers. Dined at home. Mrs Scott very ill
Finer weather but the wind still from the SE. Confined myself entirely to the house in consequence of my cold.

Frosty weather. Wind changed to NW. Walked to the newsroom about 2 o'clock & read the papers. Wind in the afternoon changed to about N by E & NNE. The Lady Jane sailed for the fishery. Gave Mrs Scott her ¼ year annuity £75
A fine day, rather cool. Wind ENE to SSE. At the newsroom & walked to Milburn Place with Mr Mark. Mrs Dixon came down to see Mrs Scott & dinner. Attended the whist club for the last time this season.
A fine day but cold. Wind SSE. At the Mulstrum in the morning. Dined at home.
A fine morning but still cold & frosty. Wind SSE. Dined at home. Took grog on board the Brodwick. R Peach. Drank tea & attended the whist club at H Harry's
A continuance of cold dry weather. Wind E by S. Attended morning service with Dale at Tynemouth Barracks & heard Mr Mark preach to the soldiers. Dined at home. With Bell Jarvis in the evening.

A damp morning having been a little rain. Wind E. Went over to Sunderland with Captain Bunbury & Jackson of the 80th. Allen Davies of the artillery to dine at the Mulstrum & spent a pleasant day. The Hope got to London on Friday afternoon.
A wet morning & cool. Wind NE with showers of snow towards the middle of the day. Jackson & I returned from Sunderland. Dined at Mr Matthews, a party.

A cold winter's morning. Wind NE having been a good deal of snow during the night. Wind changed to NW with heavy showers of hail & snow during the day& night. Dined at home. In the evening at a party at Mr Mathews

A continuance of cold weather with showers of snow & wind NNW. Although a heavy swell upon the bar & occasionally breaking, several ships got to sea. Dined at home. In the evening at the Jarvis's with Bell.

Exceedingly cold weather & frosty. Wind variable between SE & SSW. Dined at home & at a party at Mrs Recds in evening. Sent to William their promissory notes at 12.18 & 24 months to Messrs Lees for £400, 400 & 450 dated 11 feb 1828

A clear frosty morning. Wind NW. received a letter from William of the sale of the Hope at 38/6 8/3 for Town by = to 7 freight eneserable work. Dined at home. Slept all night with Bell Jervis at her sisters.

A beautiful mild morning. Wind WNW. Got home to breakfast after sleeping with Bell Jarvis. The wind in the afternoon changed to SE. Several ships sailed for America & the Baltic. The XYZ Ld the soles run. Dined with J Tinley, Ian Carr married to Sam Barton & got home this morning attended the whist club at H Dales.

A damp morning wind SSE. Turned out very wet. Wrote to William. Wind changed in the afternoon to SE. Found myself very queer this morning in consequence of late hours & last night at the Dales. Stayed in the house all day. In the evening at the newsroom & called at the Mulstrum & gave Bennett a turn.
A dull wet morning. Wind E. Engaged in the house reading until 12 o'clock. Called upon J Hearn about his bell for the Hope, but he was not at the sail-loft. Dined at home.
A very wet morning. Wind East & been much rain during the night. Dined with ben Wright & a party ra bard. Then Stephen & spent a very pleasant evening.
A dull thick morning & turned out wet. Wind NW. Heard from Mr Stephenson the Hope was out on Monday & going to take in dung. Dined at home.

A dull morning. Wind S by E & heavy sea upon the bar. Bowies Brittania arrived in the harbour this morning without the Captain Mr W Bowie on board. Supposed to have jumped out of the cabin window when off the bar. Dined at home. Mrs Dixon joined me & returned home in the evening.

Weather moderating and fair having been very strong all night. Wind about E by S. Several ships arrived this morning. Among them the Hope having left London on Tuesday. A schooner loaded with grain got upon the hard Sand, the sea higher than has been this winter. Went to Newcastle & fixed the Hope to load Townty main again the price 20/ chat & to be applied 8/6 freight. Returned by steam to dinner. Wind changed to SW & then to SE.

A fair morning. Wind WNW. About 11 o'clock began to rain. Drew £40 out of Chapmans to pay wages & hadesmens bells for the Hope. Mr Mark sit took our dinner on board. Wind got to ESE again. Attended the whist club at R Pearts. Wrote to William.
A very wet morning. Wind SSE. Received a letter from William weth the Hope. Balance note $40.11/- & £50 lent = £90.11. Went to church. Dined with J Tinley. Mr & Mrs Carr & Jane Kelsoe there.

A tremendously heavy storm & fall of snow all day & wind SE. Mr Smith & Fanny unexpectedly arrived some busy body having sent a "message" to Togston in my name, that Mrs Scott was not expected to live more than two or three days. Dined at home & at whist club in the evening

Rather a dull morning. Wind blowing fresh from SW & W. Several ships sailed for America but no loaded vessels got out. A heavy sea being upon the bar. Moved the Hope from the crane to a tees in South Shields. The river on the north side being so crowded Dined at home. Joined a party on board the Harmony. Mr Peark in the evening. With Bell Jarvis. Paid into Chapmans. The bill for £90.10/-

A beautiful morning & blowing fresh from the SW. On board of ship Mr Allen & Mary & Bell Jarvis. Danced on board with me. Drew a draft for self for £15 & paid into the account of Exors £20. Paid Mr Lough an average for Hope Club £19.2.1. In the evening the wind changed to SSE blowing hard all night with rain.

This morning dry weather but still blowing hard all night & still continuing from SSE & S by E. The Hope moved down to a tier below the library to load up. Dined at home. Wrote the secretary of the Hope Club to reduce the value of the Hope to £1600.

A very wet morning. Wind SW. On board the Hope. She got two keels down today making 15. Dined on board. Dr Drewery & W Peart with me. A great many ships got to sea this afternoon. The wind changed to S & S by E. Poor R Brown died today. A serious loss to his family.

Good Friday. A most beautiful morning. Wind NW. Did not go to church in consequence of poor Robert Brown's death. On board the Hope. She got the remainder of her coals down & sailed this afternoon. Towed out by a steam boat, the wind being from the SSE. Dined at home & afterwards went with H Harry to Mr Sadlers at Whittle Point to take wine in the evening at Nancy Jervis

A fine morning, but has been rain early. Wind WNW. Paid the pilot of the Hope £1.15/. Paid Twigel Bragier for the Hope £12.13/-. Call upon & saw about Richard's funeral. Walked to Tynemouth. Dined at home. In the evening suppered at the Albion upon some oysters, given by A Cunningham. With Ann!!!!!!

A wet morning. Wind NW. Signed the Hope's cargo bill £166.5.1 & returned it to Geo Dunn& Sons. Continued raining heavily until 4 o'clock when it cleared up. Dined at home. With Bell Jervis in the evening. Turned out a very rainy night.
Finer weather. Wind about N by E. Turned out a most beautiful & warm day & favourable for Tynemouth Races. Immense number of people out. Dined at home

Rather a dull morning. Wind SSE. Dixon & Befry came down from Beaton & the foreman & I attended the remains of poor Rich Brown to the grave with his three youngest boys. I returned with them to dine & stay all night at Benton.

A cold morning with a dry easterly wind. Walked down to Shields. Dined at homer & afterwards went to Tynemouth races, very few people there & not worth going to. Drank tea with Mr Tibbs. With Bell Jarvis in the evening

... as every man must do, who keeps there grand maxim in view "Do onto others as you would they should do unto you", he who attends to this well , never get far wrong & thank god so far I feel I can apply the quotation "mens conscia recti" to myself indeed . I am made to feel it by the kind & friendly manner in which every person receive me I hope I deserve it, I do not know that I ever did an injury to anyone certain never intentionally.

However there is one person whose conduct has indeed been that of a friend & such a friend as seldom is met with & I cannot omit recording it here & were I ever to forget it should indeed be ungrateful & unworthy of every kind feeling. John Tinley is the man who could feel for the misfortunes of another. He it was who paved the way for our emancipation from all difficulties. Where is the friend that would have acted as he did? I fear not to be found. He came forward not a friend in words but in deeds. He made not promises, nor exacted hopes & expectations, to disappoint & blast them when called upon. He saw our situation, he volunteered his services as security, without which we could have effected nothing & thus has the primary cause of our accomplishing all that has been done. He thought he knew us & I hope has not been deceived. This is what I call friendship, true & sincere, not according to the worldly acceptation & profanation of the word, but friendship in the true spirit & meaning of the word.

I yesterday, the last day of the old year, dined with this my excellent friend & accompanied him Miss Barton A party to the ball & spent a very pleasant evening & thus ended the old & began the new year merrily. I hope it is a good omen. Today I again dined with J Tinley to meet Mr Waldie to a very agreeable party.
The weather changed, a fine mild day & rapid thaw wind W to NW. Dined at Mr Wrights. Several ships sailed

Another cold morning. Wind easterly. Walked to Tynemouth. Dined with J Tinley. In the evening called upon Mr J Young & had a long conversation both with him about taking our dividend without surveying. Also he did not seem so determined in his opposition. He desired me to see H Dale & talk to him.

A continuance of cold weather & ENE wind. Dined at home & afterwards went with H Harry & R Peart & drank whisky on board the Ardineaple steamer Captain Cunningham. On our return when the boat reached the shore, Cunningham stumbled & falling upon me, we both rolled overboard. Got a good dunking. Wrote to Mrs Scott of my determination not to make her an allowance.

A beautiful morning but still cool & wind NE & ENE. Walked with H Harry to Tynemouth. Dined at home. Received a letter from William of the arrival & sale of the Hope on Wednesday at 27/- = to 6/6 freight. This well I'm upheld 8/6. Answered the letter desiring him to tender the Hope to the Gafs Co. to carry coal at £9 a keel or 21/6 freight Newcastle cha. Attended the whist club at Tibbs. Got £5 of Chapman. Paid steam boat for Hope 30/- aformenbec 20/- washing 31/6

A beautiful morning. Quite summer weather. Wind S & changed before 12 o'clock to SE. Attended morning service. Dined at home at 2 o'clock & afterwards walked to Tynemouth with H Harry. On our return had a bottle of port at the George. With Bell Jarvis in the evening.

A showery morning. Wind N by W. In the house all the morning. Mrs Dixon brought Emma down again. Dined at house. In the evening went up to the castle & played a rubber at Dacres rooms. With rum I think!!!

A showery morning & blowing fresh from the N & W by N and increased to a very heavy gale of wind varying between NNW and NNE which brought on a tremendous sea, a small sloop in coming in got upon the Heard Sand. Dined at home.
The gale has continued all night with showers of snow with a tremendous sea. Wind continues the same as yesterday. The gales abated towards evening. Dined at home. In the evening with Bell Jarvis

A fine morning & again calm Weather. Wind NW by N. Went to Newcastle by steamer to dine with Mr R Arsey in Eldon Square. Spent a very pleasant day & returned to Shields. In the evening took Mr Dacres & RA with me. Tom Smith & his mother arrived at Dockwray Square today.

A fine morning. Wind NW walked about the town with Tom Smith the principle part of the morning. Dined at home & took a walk to Tynemouth after dinner. Accepted In Hearn's bill for £34.7/- at 3 months dated 27 April, due 30 July, for repairing Hope's sails. A most extraordinary bill.

A pleasant morning blowing rather fresh from NW by W. Walked with Tom Smith down to Low Town & afterwards to Alec Sadlers at Whitle Point. Dined at home & after tea again walked to Whitle Point but the sloop had not come down.
A beautiful day & a little frost in the air. Wind WNW. A few ships sailed. Dined at home. A letter from William & answered

A fine mild morning after a few showers of rain during the night. Wind W by S. Tom Smith, Emma & I went to church & after [the] service, Tom & I walked up through the country to Benton, dined & stayed all night. A very windy day & unpleasant walking.

A pleasant morning. But still blowing hard from the NW. Amused ourselves for a short time in the plantations with the beagles. Mrs Dixon took us into Newcastle in the carriage. Tom Smith transacted his business there & we afterwards walked down to St Anthon's to see a sloop he had purchased for his colliery. Returned to Shields by steam to dinner.

A fine spring morning with showers. Wind SSW. Several light ships arrived. Tom & Mrs Smith left us this morning for Benton. Dined at home. Accepted a bill at 3 months dated 16 April for polices & Insurance 1 & 2 coal voyages in general Premium Club £13.7.10. With Bell Jervis in the evening

A beautiful morning. Wind SW. Called upon & spent an hour with Fergusson the artist. Dined at home. Afterwards walked to Tynemouth with Fergusson to sketch the ruins. In the evening at Davies Rooms at the Castle

A pleasant spring morning. Wind NNW. Changed during the day to NE & again at night to W. Took a walk round by Cullercoat Fields & Tynemouth. A beautiful summers day. Dined with Jackson 80th Regiment at the Castle. H Dale, Dacres, RA. Newton & a Lieutenant Hamilton Brown there. (with 1st term)
A wet morning . A fine mild rain. Wind W by N. Called upon Fergusson Dined at home. The Hope arrived this evening after a fine passage. Left Gravesend on Wednesday morning.

A fine spring morning. Some showers during the night. Warmer growing weather at last. Wind W by N. Mr Fergusson & I went to Newcastle by steam on the quay, but could do nothing for the Hope. Called upon Inspector Hodgson & dined with him at his brothers. Returned to Shields in the evening. With Bell Jarvis, remained with her until 4 o'clock in the morning. Received from Geo Dunn & sons £27 being the difference between the freight made & that upheld =rig: 8/6
A most beautiful morning & summers weather SE. Went with Emma to church. Dined at home at 2 o'clock. Took wine with H Harry. Walked to Tynemouth in the evening.

A dull morning. Wind ESE. Turned out a very fine day. Went to Newcastle by steam but did not fix the Hope. Returned home to dinner. Walked to Tynemouth in the evening. Paid the men their wages & gave Stephenson a draft for £45

A fine morning. Wind NE. Paid into Chapmans £27 the balance of sales & our ship Hope for £69.5/-. Went to Newcastle again & fixed the Hope to load Gamlington Walls at 9/6 freight by spout clear of brokerage & the freighters to pay two keel dues should she not load up. Dined on board the Choice with H Harry & A French. Wrote to William. The Hope dis lorry is to go past him to millis & roth
A very fine morning & rather frosty. Wind W by N. At church in the morning. Dined at home. Mrs Scott much better
A most beautiful morning. Wind SE. The Hope gone up to the spout this tide. Walked with Captain Webb up to the Hope & dined on board
Another fine day. Wind W by N. Changed to SW. Went by steam to Newcastle. Gave the fitter the Hope's monthly bill. Called upon J Hodgson & returned to dinner. In the evening a little rain.

A dull morning but fine spring weather. Wind NE. Mr Mark, Mr Sadler & I walked up to Cramlington Spout. Found the Hope hauling off & she shortly after proceeded down the river having only taken in 14 keels. Dined with Mr Sadler. With Bell Jarvis in the evening.

A beautiful summers morning. Wind ENE. Received a letter from William agreeing to offer Younger 10/- in the £. Drew £20 out of Chapman. £15 for Stephenson & £5 for self. Drew £5 more in the afternoon. Stephenson wanting £20. Dined at home. In the evening called upon A Dale to propose to join Younger's 10/- in full. Dale sacfe for Younger, who I afterwards found much to my relief of mind had agreed to our proposal. Spent the evening with Mr Allen. With Bell Jervis.

A beautiful morning. Wind SE. The Hope was loaded on Friday but we could not go to sea in consequence of Young business. Determined not to sail until the morning tide. Walked to Tynemouth with H Harry. Took a warm bath. Dined at home. H Harry & Mr Dadler took wine with me. Wrote to William of my intention to sail ...

At 3 o'clock am got under way & sailed from Shields with a westerly breeze & fine weather. At 10 o'clock am becalmed off Sunderland, the wind having got round to SE. Between 1 & 2 o'clock the breeze freshened a little but we made little way, being ebb tide. At 10 o'clock we went to bed, the ship being abreast of the Tees

has been blowing pretty fresh all night from the SE & SSE. Got up at 8 o'clock am. The ship abreast of Huntcliff Foot. The wind the same but moderate & fine weather. Anne very unwell, but more frightened not having been at sea before. Towards evening wind very calm again. Turned in at 10 o'clock. The ship in a very little wind.

A beautiful morning. Wind NE. Turned out a 8 o'clock am. The ship off Robin Hoods but the ebb tide & heavy SE swell setting against us drove us back to Whitby. In the afternoon with the fload a better breeze spring up & set us ahead again & 10 o'clock pm bed time, we were off Scarborough. A fine moonlit night.

Turned out at 8 o'clock am been a fresh breeze all night from NE. Got round the Head at 5 o'clock am. A fine morning but rather dull. Had a good sun. About 9 o'clock Cromer. At 10 o'clock turned in being marhasborough. Ann Stokes 1st time.

Got up at 8 o'clock am. Very thick weather, but a fine breeze at NE, then appeared to be off Yarmouth behind the sands. We ran until about 1 o'clock pm when we took in studding sails & stood in for the land, which we made a little to the northward of Aldeburgh. The weather clearer from thence. We took our departure to run down raren . About 4 o'clock it turned out a beautiful clear day. At 6 o'clock pm abreast of Orford. At 10 pm being dark, brought up abreast of the Hook of the middle. At a little after 12 o'clock went to bed. A fine moonlit night. With Ann Stokes again!!

A fine day and frosty, Wind WNW. Got the fore rigging over the mast head & the main mast out & found it much decayed both foot and head & fear we shall be obliged to have a new one. Ordered a new bowsprit of Morton & Thompson. Dined at home & spent the evening with N Bird

At 3 o'clock [in] the morning they got the ship under way, with a light breeze from the NE. At 7 o'clock I got up & went upon deck, past through a large fleet of light ships. At 8 o'clock got the flood with a little more wind. Again passed a great number of light ships. Between 5 & 6 o'clock brought up a little blow Gravesend. The crew went to bed early. Ann & I walked the deck until after 10 o'clock. Sat up until 12 o'clock. Went to bed to Ann

Got up about 7 o'clock. A most delightful morning. Wind unfortunately changed to W so that at the early morning tide, we could not move, There also being very little of it. After breakfast dressed myself & landed at Gravesend about 11 o'clock, waited until about 1 o'clock before I could get a coach. Got to town at 4 o'clock pm. Left the ships papers at the office & got to Nottingham Place at ½ past 5 o'clock. Found them all well & glad to see me. Bob Marsh & his father dined with us. Heavy rain in the afternoon.

A fine morning, but blowing hard from the N by E. William & I walked into the city. Called upon Bob Marsh only a short time at the office, when Stephenson brought Ann up. I walked with her to Grays Inn, showed her St Pants, went round by Oxford & Regents street & Ann feet being very sore we after buying a pair of easy shoes, took a coach & drove to new inn. Dined with Bob Marsh & afterwards we all went to the pit at Covent garden Theatre. Ann much astonished at the size & splendour of the houses. We saw Romeo & Juliet performed by C Kenneth & Mrs Smithson. Then afterwards the Devils Elixir, not worth seeing. Ann & I slept at the Fountain in Catherine Street

A beautiful day. Wind still fresh from the N by E. We got breakfast at 11 o'clock & afterwards walked into the Green park round by the Kings Place by Pall Mall to Somerset House & saw the exhibition. Ann much pleased with her mornings amusements took & left in Grays Inn. Walked into the city. Attended Changes, did nothing with the ship & walked to Nottingham Place to dinner. The Hope could not be sold today.

Another beautiful morning. Wind blowing fresh at N by E. Called upon Mr ward. Walked into the city. On my way saw Ann. Attended the coal market with much difficulty they sold 58/2 of the Hope's cargo. Walked out of the city. Saw Ann again. Called upon Richmond found him looking well, though still lame. Returned by Regents He to Mr Lee to dinner. Bob marsh with us.
A continuance of fine weather. Wind NE. Wrote to Mr Vernon to send Inspector Galbraith to London. Walked into the city. Attended changers. Did nothing. Dined with Richmond.

A dull morning but fine weather. Wind still NE & ENE. Mr Lee drove me into the city. Attended the local exchange. Sold 63 more of the Hope's coals. Went to the Royal Ex. Could not fix. Walked out of the city. Dined at Mr Lees. Mr & Bob Marsh & F Barclay there.

Another cloudy morning. Wind NE. Walked into the city. Called upon Bob Marsh. He & his father walked with me down to the Hope. Saw the St Catherine Docks in our way & the most perfect & comfortable perhaps of thing of the sort all the warehouses & upon so good a place. Had lunch on board & I afterwards attended changes but did nothing for the ship. Walked out of the city with Inspector Chapman & dined with him. His brothers the captain, Thomas, Ben, Mr Graham & a Mr Day there.

A dull cloudy morning. Wind about N. Went with the Miss Lees to the chapel in Vern Street. Afterwards called upon Mr & Mrs Lumley in Gower Street. Mr Lee very unwell, consumption, going to leave this home. Called upon Mr Linskill. Went to see Mary & Emma in Sloan Street & then to the park. Dined with Mr ward & spent a pleasant day.

A very dull morning & light rain. Wind NW. Walked into the city. At the coal exchange the remainder of the Hope sold. Attended the Royal Exchange but could not fix the Hope. Walked to Mr Lees to dinner. Bob Marsh dined with us.
A beautiful day. Wind WSW but changed to SSW towards the evening. Got the Hope upon the blocks & the flat up to light water mark caulked. Condemned the main mast. Dined at home

A most beautiful morning. Wind NW. Walked into the city. Saw Ann. Fixed the Hope for Petersburg with Mr Hubbard ar 26/-. & iow for fellow. Walked to Mr Lees to dinner. Bob Marsh there, he & the guests having been to Kensington gardens

A fine morning & very hot. Wind NW. Rode into the city. Went to the Bull at Alegate & saw Ann Stokes set off for Hford. Went to the ship with William, Bob Marsh & Vincent , dined on board. Returned to Aldgate to meet Ann. Took her to Astleys theatre & afterwards slept at the Fountain

... upon one of which, Yelagin. We landed & walked through the plantations, the walk of which are beautiful, in good order & under the management of an English Lumana & and attached to a very fine palace of the Emperor that stands close to the water. Near it is a bridge which we crossed to the opposite Island of Kamenny, at the end is a handsome theatre, placed there to be near this summer retreat of the Emperor's. This is a very fashionable theatre & attended principally by the court, but I believe open to all. Here they perform French, Italian & German operas. These islands are the property of the Emperor & noblemen. The grounds most beautifully laid out & always open to the public. The Russians being much more ceribal in this respect than John Bull. They delight in seeing the people strolling about the grounds & have seats placed in all directions for their accommodation. We then proceeded through these fairy grounds to the island of Krestovsky Island where Mr Dye has a cottage for the summer. Here we took tea with his family & late in the evening returned to Petersburg which we did not reach till after 1 o'clock in the morning exceptionally tired with our walk

Got up at 11 o'clock. Breakfasted at the Fountain & saw Ann safe to her aunty. Walked into the city. Called at the country house. William gone. Returned to Nottingham Place with Mr Lee. Went with the Lees to dine with A Patterson at Clapton, a party. A very fine but extremely hot day. Wind WNW & NW. Received a letter from Mr Vernon of J Galbraith setting off for London.

A continuance of fine weather. Wind NW. Mr Lee drove me into the city. Walked down to the ship upon Dowland's Ways. The painters finished painting the cabin & busy with the sides. Made a port hole into the state room. Moored the ship down in Duke Shore & got ballast. Took boat to the tower & walked from thence to Mr Lees to dinner
A fine morning & a fresh breeze from NW. Walked into the city with William. Got a new hat at Olipharts. Called for Bob Marsh & we afterwards went by water to the Hope. Walked home to dinner

A fine day. Wind WSW. Got the Hope flats finished caulking & blocks stowed. Brought a new mainmast of Miles Forster at £7.10 per load less discount = £20.11. Dined at home. At Mrs Clarks in evening a party

A fine day, but weather cooler. Wind NE. I went to the Roman Catholic Chapel in Warwick Street & much pleased with the ringing. Went to the park, met Bob Marsh & proceeded to Kensington Gardens. A great crowd of fashionable company there & many beautiful women. Dined at Mr Lees.

A dull morning. Wind NW. A good deal of rain after a breakfast. Walked into the city. Brought a filtering machine for the ship. Gave Stephenson £25. Settled the freight account with William & received the balance £30.4/-. Called at the Russian consul for passports. Dined at Richmonds. Hard J Jobling Chambers & there. When I got home, found J Gilbraith had arrived.

A fine morning, but rather dull. Wind NNE. Later J Galbraith & I took a coach from Nottingham Place for the city with our cloths for the ship's boat with four hands at Billingsgate to carry all our things to the ship. Called upon the Russian Consol. The party with one Vinccent carrying ½ dozen wine with us took a waterman at the Customs House & went down to the ship to dinner. In the evening attended Greenwich Fair which was not so crowded as I have seen it & letto run. I called upon G Watts. William, Lee & Vincent left us & Bob Marsh J.G. & I returned to the ship a little after 10 o'clock to sleep. Bob & I smoked a cloud, wet both eyes & turned in.

A pleasant morning. Turned out between 7 & * o'clock am & breakfasted. The ship under way with a foul wind at NNE. Bob Marsh, John Galbraith & I got a waterman & returned to London to see William again & get some of our cloths. Gave WBS a my note on detailed for £300 because int I unfortunately being considerably in his debt. We all dined in Water lane at 3 o'clock pm & at 4 o'clock embarked on board to the Hope, lying at Gallions. Had tea. Employed ourselves in the evening stowing all our cloths & away & getting things into something like shipshape. Between 9 & 10 o'clock blew a cloud, discharged a couple of glasses of gin & water & about 11 o'clock turned in, feeling my cold rather worse. With a cough at my chest. Wrote today to the Sadler declining to join him in the establishment of a paper manufactury at Shields.

Turned out a little after 7 o'clock am. Thick weather & wind very variable between E & NNW. At ½ past 9 o'clock got under way & worked down with the tide. At ½ past 3 o'clock being low water, we brought up at Grays & had our dinner. Several very fine sailing boats past us, being a race for a cup, in the following order as they returned after going round the boat at south fleet, the Einnlation , Rob Bery, Yela, Lady Luisa & Royal Eagle.

After dinner, Bob & I discerfsed a bottle of Madiera. At 7 o'clock had tea. At ½ past 8 o'clock being high water we again got under way & worked down to Gravesend where we brought up for the night at 10 o'clock, smoked two pipes, finished the like number of glasses of rum & water & at 11 o'clock went to roost. Wind very variable during the day between SE and NNW.

Got up at 7 o'clock. Every appearance of being a very after a thick foggy night. Wind about East. After breakfast Bob Marsh & I went on shore to endeavour to get each a straw hat, but did not succeed. Returned to the ship again before 10 o'clock. During our absence they had got her under way. At low water having had a fresh breeze from the E to ESE. We brought up abreast of Canvey Island, off Leigh at ½ past 2 o'clock. Had our dinner which was devoured with a pretty considerable appetite. Bob & I punished another bottle of Madeira. Took tea at 7 o'clock and at 9 o'clock again got underway with a light breeze from about SSE which carried us down to Southend when we let go our anchor for the night at ½ past 10 o'clock. Discharged a couple of glasses of rum & water & turned in at ¼ to 12 o'clock. Quite ready for a good snooze.

Should the wind continue from the eastward our intention is to go on shore & spend the day at Southend.

I woke a little after 5 o'clock this morning by the crew preparing to get underway, the wind having changed to the westward, so that our intentions of going on shore at Southend has been frustrated. Turned out at ½ past 7 o'clock. The ship not much below Southend there being scarcely enough wind to set us against the tide. A most beautiful morning & exceedingly hot. Passed the Earl Balcarras Indiaman homeward bound. A very fine vessel & also a 74 foot ship at anchor above the Hove Light. Several smaller vessels principally foreigners. Mr Has Venson proceed & be d_d to them. In company with us. A beautiful sight, the sea as smooth as oil. At 10 o'clock am driving with the tide, a dead calm. Fear we shall make but a had tide work. The wind seems much incined to get round to the eastward again. About 10 o'clock a little below the Nou Light, the wind took us all aback, changing to the ESE. After making a few tacks, we increased to a fine breeze & we proceeded down wind gradually increasing our rate to about 7 knots an hour. At ¼ to 5 & 6 o'clock pm. Passed the Suak Light. We have had a most glorious day, exceptionally hot & singing our phizogs in grand style. Bob & I again dispatched a bottle of Maderia after dinner upon deck. If we go on at this rate, I reckon our stock of wine (originally only ½ dozen) will only last three days longer. Today we dined at a little after 12 o'clock sea hours. Employed during the morning in preparing our fishing gear. My cold worse this evening & felt exceedingly chilly. Took a stiff glass of warm rum & water & went to bed. Set steering sails

During the night it has blown a steady breeze, fair for us & we have gone along steadily & pleasant at about the rate of 6 knots. After a good snooze, turned out at ½ past 7 o'clock. A most delightful morning. Not a cloud to be seen, with a find steady & refreshing breeze from SW by W. Steady sails still continued set. After breakfast read the morning service & lessons. Passed through a large fleet of Dutch fishing boats, many of them came near & wished us much to buy some fish. Dined between 12 & 1 o'clock & Bob & I punished another bottle of Madeira. Only one more left, which we have determined, if possible, to keep for next Sunday. We have not averaged this day more than 4 knots an hour.

Started a ENE course. The master & mate at 12 o'clock took their observation on latitude 53.8 North Long 3.30. Distance from the Sunk, run since 6 last evening 111 miles. Changed our course to NE.

At 9 o'clock took our rum & water & afterwards being a most beautiful moonlit night, we walked the deck for ½ an hour & at ½ past 10 o'clock turned in, at which time we had a better breeze & had increased our rate to about 6 knots.

Robecia Filtering Apparatus answered admirably yielding an ample supply of most beautiful clear & pure water, from the filthy Thames mud

Turned out at ½ past 6 o'clock. Found that J Galbraith had kept his watch last night for the first time. Have had a fair breeze all night from the SW. Continuing our course NE with steering sail set at the rate of 6 knots. Got fishing line out but could not catch nothing. The ship going too fast through the water.

Bob & I employed ourselves in painting the skiff & making her decent to go to shore in at Elsinecra.

At 12 o'clock the Captain took his observation lat 55.1 long: 4.15 having been 112 miles since 12th yesterday & 123 from our departure.

After dinner Bob & I took a single glass of grog & again set to work to finish painting the skiff. In the evening the wind changed to South. Got trysail set & main tack down. At 9 o'clock had a glass of brandy & water & turned in

Got up a little after 7 o'clock. Had a fresh breeze all night from the southward. The ship making 8 knots per hour. A continuance of most beautiful weather. At 12 o'clock took observation Lat:57.4 long: 7.17 having made 101 miles in the last 24 hours, making 284 since our departure. Employed part of the morning in painting the skiff. At near 2 o'clock saw land on our starboard bow. Off Jutland. The wind, northeast fair, is now against ...

A damp day. A little rain in the morning. Wind SE. A few ships arrived. Carpenters at work caulking the upper works. Dined at home. In the evening at whist club. Mr Macarthy called to say he was going to send the Brolog Loves, to my brother

... SE & us. The wind getting to SSE took in studding sails & stood aft of to Norway coast which we saw between 4 & 5 o'clock. Had our fishing lines out all this morning but only caught two gurnets.

A little before 5 o'clock seeing it very black to windward & a squall coming, stowed top galland sails & lowered topsails upon the Cep just as the squall took us, very heavy, but little rain. It lasted about ¼ of an hour. Got topsails hoisted again single reefed. Wind seemed much inclined to change. At one time we had it to our great delight from the westward where we squared our yards, but to our inexpressible annoyance had scarcely done when it returned to the old quarter.

During this evening a large fleet of loaded vessels upwards of 80 sail from the Baltic passed us as we let out both reefs. Walked the deck until 10 o'clock when we had our glass of comfort & turned in. Little wind from about the south

After a regular good & sound snooze, turned out at ½ past 7 o'clock.

During the night slight shower with very little wind. To our great joy when we looked up through the cabin sky light, we saw the yards square & studding sails set. Wind WNW. After breakfast & commenced a heavy rain, which continued until 12 o'clock. Saw the Shaw light at 2 o'clock.

Employed myself in painting the ship's name upon the skiff & the carpenter finishing painting the underside. Bob Marsh being too lazy to complete his work.

Wind continuing favourable & a fine fresh breeze going 5 or 6 knots. At 9 o'clock saw the Trindlew & the island of Lcefsoe bearing NW by W, distant 5 or 6 miles.

Took our warm glass of brandy & water & got to bed before 10 o'clock. Looking the sea evidently rising.

Turned out about 8 o'clock. This morning after a rather restless night. At 11 o'clock last night it began to blow heavy with sea making the wind suddenly changed to the SE much to our disappointment & increased to a regular squall. Studding sails taken in & top gallent sails stowed. Between 12 & 1 o'clock am Bob & I not being able to sleep, from the motion of the ship & precarious articles of furniture tumbling about the cabin, clothed ourselves & went upon deck. Then about day break found the people employed in double reefing the topsail & taking one reef in the main-top-sail blowing tremendously hard but clear weather. A little after 2 o'clock saw the sun rise which amply rewarded us from our want of rest, a grand & magnificent sight. This morning particularly so. Old sol seemed to have an immediate influence over the wind & waves, for from the time he made his appearance, they gradually lulled. Before 3 o'clock, Bob & I again turned in & had a sound snooze until 8 o'clock.

The master informed us that at 6 o'clock it being almost calm. The wind again suddenly changed to the SW but although fair for us for the present, we make but little way, there being a current & hard sea against us. It appeared there are no tides here & in the Baltic & which ever way the wind is, the current sets. Before we went to our roost again at 3 o'clock we saw the Riddigen lighthouse on the Norway coast, beaming mainly SE, distant about 5 miles according to my calculation. Before breakfast set top gallent sail & let out the reefs of topsails. At 10 o'clock the wind got to the westward. In the afternoon set front-top-mast studding sail. It about 5 o'clock the wind getting from the NNW ...

... set top gallent studding sail. Fine weather. The ship in excellent run & passing everything.

Saw the lighthouse on the island of Auholt bearing W by S distant about 8 miles. At this time we could not see the land. Cloud being exceedingly low

At 9 o'clock wind NW by N a fair breeze & going about 5 knots. The Koll land in sight bearing S by E distant 15 miles.

Took our glass of grog as usual & went to bed

This morning at ½ past 3 o'clock upon looking out found the ship to the southward of the Koll lights & running up to Elsineer with a fair breeze. Kronborg Castle in sight. Bob Marsh & I dressed ourselves & went upon deck. A beautiful sight. A large fleet ahead & astern of us. This weather unfortunately rather changed. A dull morning with a little rain. Particularly struck with the beauty of the Danish coast being well studded with trees & houses to the water's edge.

At 6 o'clock am passed Kronborg Castle, a fine old building with strong batteries, but from to & commanding the entrance to the Baltic which is only three miles across. Opposite to it, in Sweden stands Helsingborg, a small town. In winter this passage is frequently frozen so that the people are enabled to cross on sledges.

Brought up in Elsineer road & about ½ past 8 o'clock went on shore, breakfasted with Mr Chapman. Dined & spent the day with him. He & his father particularly kind & attentive. The whole of this day the rain has come down in torrents, particularly unfortunate as it has prevented us in going about & seeing the sights. What little ...

... splendid & magnificent. The houses all large & good & very clean. The streets the same. The dwellings of the higher classes also in fact palaces. The city is very strongly fortified & the barracks numerous & one an immense scale & capable of containing a very strong force. At present there are 9000 men garrisoned in them exclusively of sailors.

Our guide regarded much that we had not visited Copenhagen on a Sunday, when we should have seen more of the inhabitants particularly the middle and better classes who are to be seen promenading & their favourite walk, he informed us, was in the Kings gardens, behind the palace, built by Inego Jones, but not occupied by the Royal Family. They live in one of the Square formed by four Palaces particularly handsome buildings, but not upon a large scale. The King & Queen having each one & Prince Christian & his brother the other two.

They have just finished a new Palace of an immense size, for the King, the exterior only I should observe is complete. The interior being get in an unfinished state. ‘tis upon a very grand scale has a most magnificent appearance & is well situated having a large space or open part of the town at its point, through which the river or canal run, wide & deep enough to admit small craft, presumably fishing & marked boats here are also placed the theatre and various public offices. The King's library & stables & riding house attached to the Palace are of an immense size, into the latter we were admitted, indeed they appeared open to the public.

But for the stud. I can speak little in praise, the houses of which the stable was full were very small, of an inferior breed, something like Little the Hanoverian of all long tails, in fact I could have almost fancied magical looking at Astley Stud instead of The King of Denmark. Speaking of him, he appeared to be much beloved, acceptable to the poorest ...

... devoting four hours on certain days in the week to passing any complaints or receiving petitions, which he does from the parties themselves, not as with our King through a minister which by the bye I think the proper way, the King of Denmark makes himself too common in the respect though he constantly attains his object, the love of his people. He keeps up very little state and presumably the city the same as any private individual without any attendant. We did not see him. He & the family being at their country residence in Jutland.

At ½ past 11 o'clock am returned to Mr Ryan's extremely heated & rather tired with our walk & after refreshing ourselves with a glass of his good medicine & water & thanking him for his attention, we got into our boat & again embarked at about 12 o'clock. Whilst the crew were getting the anchor up, Bob, Inspector G & I undressed, jumped overboard & had a most delightful bath. By the time we had got on board again the ship was under way, with the wind at SE, not very favourable for us. After making two or three boards, blowing by this time, a fresh breeze, we go through the grounds & at 3 o'clock the pilot left us between the islands of Saltholm & Dragør, the extreme point of Jutland. Met a fleet of loaded vessels running down to Elslnem at 5 o'clock pm. Passed Falsterbo on the starboard tack, close hauled, wind about ESE. At ¼ past 8 o'clock tacked Moen Island bearing SW distant about 6 miles. A clear frosty looking sky, wind, current & heavy swell against us & no appearance of a change this night. At 9 o'clock Bob and I took one glass of comfort & went to bed.

Turned out at ½ 7 o'clock. Found the ship still in sight of Falsterbo, having been working to windward all night & made but little progress, wind fast. After breakfast read the service & lessons of the day. Just before I got upon deck, the XYZ passed us homeward bound, with a fine breeze & studdingsails set. We continued working to westward the whole of the day. At 9 o'clock took our gin & water & went to bed.
A fine morning, but turned dull towards afternoon & damp wind veered from E by S to S by E. Dined at home. A party at Mrs Stephen's at Tynemouth in the evening

A continuance of fine weather but wind still from the east & rather cool. Towards the afternoon the wind gradually decreased & became much warmer, so that we are in hope it will die away & shall have a change. This working to windward in the Baltic is much more tiresome than anywhere else. The current also being always against you. In the evening became quite calm. At 9 o'clock took our tumbler of whisky toddy & went to bed. The Swedish coast very fine & pretty, well wooded.

Turned out before 8 o'clock & most beautiful morning & although calm during the night, the sea so smooth, that the ship with the little air there was, has, as the Captain terms it, been sliding through the water. To my surprise, found Bornholm in sight. The north of the island bearing east distant about 10 miles SE by E which is about an hour changed to SSW. Set foretopmast & maintop gallant studding sails.

... The slightest air possible during the whole of the day & making such little way that we were enabled to catch a couple of coldlings by our lines going near the bottom. At 6 o'clock pm a slight breeze sprung up from the NNE which run us pretty near against the north end of Bornholm, where at 9 o'clock it suddenly changed to against us, but died away to a dead calm. Had our whisky & water & turned in. Bornholm a very fine island as sun with the glass.

Turned out at 8 o'clock after a sound snooze. After a dead calm, the whole of the night, at 6 o'clock this morning a breeze sprung up from NW & when we got upon deck, found we were gradually loosing slight of the island. Got studding sails set, but not at any time going more than four knots, sometimes not so much.

Most beautiful weather, but the sun not so scorching as yesterday. Accompanied the whole day by thousands of large dragon flies that flew about & alighted upon our rigging which was at times covered with them. At ½ past 8 o'clock, went below & had our rum & water & when we went to bed at ½ past 9 o'clock, the wind continued favourable & a fine breeze.

... knots. At ¼ past 4 o'clock supposed to two abreast of the south end of the Ireland of Gotland & when we going with a fine NW breeze at the rate of 7 ½ knots. Suddenly & in a moment, taken all aback, got lower & topmast studdingsails in, wind in the courses of a few minutes, flying all round the compass in the most extraordinary way. At last sumed to settle at east.

A large ship upon our weather bow. Supposed to be a republican frigate. The captain amused himself today in painting the covering boards & waterways. The men this afternoon employed in washing the beef, the whole of which is unfortunately very much tainted. In the course of the evening the wind got to the WSW so that we laid up ENE going on 3 & 4 knots. At 8 o'clock took our grog & turned in at 11 o'clock. Wind more favourable

Got up this morning at a little after 7 o'clock. Bob & I had some difficulty in making our minds up to turn out, the morning being so tremendously wet. The rain coming down in torrents with heavy thunder & lightning, one peal so close to us that it sounded as if it was our top gallant mast head. In fact we were enveloped in clouds, thunder & lightning, much too near to be agreeable. This deluge of rain has continued since 4 o'clock. However the wind was fair for us, a fresh breeze at SW & giving 6 knots, our course NE by E. At 9 o'clock the rain eased & by 10 o'clock we had fine weather, warm wind the lamed & going 5 ½ knots, with studding sails set. At 12 o'clock we were by observance in lat: 58.3 long: 20.50. Having come 110 miles since yesterday at noon. Little or nothing has ...

... occurred today worthy of note. Since the morning we have had most delightful weather, with a few refreshing breeze at SW & SW by W. Our course NE ½ E & going 4 7 5 knots. At 9 o'clock Bob & I finished two glasses of gin & water & at 10 o'clock turned in.

At a little after 12 o'clock last night the wind suddenly took us all aback & hearing dome noise upon deck, went up the companion ladder & found there busy getting studdingsails in & being only in my shirt as I turned out, I think I caught cold & slight attack of rheumatism in my loin. During the remainder of the night it was quite calm with heavy thunder & lightening & toward morning tremendous heavy rain which with the rheumatism & having had little sleep, prevented me getting up to breakfast. I however turned out immediately after & was happy to find the wind had become fair for us being NNE, steering an easterly course, with studdingsails set, but only going about 3 knots. Several ships in company.

At 6 o'clock Dagon Island in sight, bearing east, distance 10 miles. This island is at the entrance of the gulf of Finland & upon it stands a lighthouse in height 538 feet above the level of the sea. At noon Dageror lighthouse bore south, distance 8 miles. Until about ½ past 3 o'clock pm it rained incessantly with thick weather. Since diner a better breeze has sprung up & we have been going 4 & 5 knots.

At 4 o'clock pm the weather has cleared up & now exceedingly fine with a warm sun, a pleasant change after such a dismal morning. At 9 o'clock abreast of the island of Odensholm, distant about 7 miles, lighthouse. 111 feet high. A fine steady breeze, but going only about 3 knots with all studdingsails set. At 10 o'clock having our warm run & water, turned in

A dull and damp morning. Wind SE. Gave Captain Stephenson £10 for Trewitt to pay carpenters wages. Went to Newcastle, dined & stayed all night with Dixon Dixon. During my absence they got the Hopes mainmast and bowsprit in. Paid Lowery broker Newcastle £4.16.6 on account of W & JS

Turned out a little before 8 o'clock. Found the ship abreast of Revala distant perhaps from 15 to 20 miles. Last night fine clear weather with light breezes. This a most delightful morning with a continuance of fair wind at WSW. Course east. At 10 o'clock the Island of Kokskar within 4 miles abreast of us. Upon it a lighthouse 99 feet high. Going five knots, breeze freshening. All the morning have been going 5 & 6 knots with most delightful weather. The ship sailing remarkably fast & passing everything in company.

At ¼ past 5 o'clock pm saw the Island of Gogland right ahead, distant about 20 miles & at 8 o'clock passed close under the north end of the island which has a most beautiful appearance being exceedingly high and mountainous & mainly covered with the spruce pine excepting in some spots when you see the rock , it is itself in fact one huge rock, not a particle of earth to be seen & producing only the now about mentioned a well as we could judge by looking through the glass & we were within a mile of it considerably. This island is about 6 miles long & forms a fine breakwater to the NE end of the gulf of Finland. For after we passed it we found the sea quite smooth. On the highest part of the island there is a lighthouse which can be seen at the distance of 12 miles & also another on the extreme Northern point, round which is the best channel for ships.

At ½ past 8 o'clock Bob, Stephenson & I punished a couple of glasses of rum and water each, being rather a cool night & likely the last. Turned in at 10 o'clock. Bob & I each to a sketch of the island of Gogland which we flatter ourselves we shall make very interesting.

This evening going 7 knots.

We were called up this morning by Stephenson between 3 & 4 o'clock to see a line of Russian men of war which were laying to, consisting of a 3 decker four 74s & 2 frigates. Fine looking vessels but laying in great disorder. A beautiful morning. Clear weather, wind west, going 5 knots. The people have been employed in the hold since 11 o'clock last night heaving ballast & got about 60 tons thrown overboard. John Galbraith has been very busy aft-section. Then & completely knacked up.

The wind dying away, we did not reach the Russian guard ship until 5 o'clock or after. It Where the officers came on board & gave us what papers were necessary, after asking numerous questions to enable us to pass into the note at Ceomstald which we laid alongside of between 6 & 7 o'clock, Stephenson, Bob Marsh & I landed & here our troubles with the d__d Russian commander. We had to go the gauntlet through two of these officers at the mole lead by producing our papers, which were detained, answering numerous questions, as to our object in visiting the country, in what capacity we came & & & . We then went to Mr Bookers who is the English local here & agent to all the English merchants at Petersburg, to support our vessel, but found we were too late.

Mr Bookers however wrote to the merchants of our arrival desiring them to advertise Bob & me, in the newspapers, which it appear is always done with strangers for about a fortnight before they can leave the country again, an absurd & one of these vexatious customs, the object of which is to put the nation upon their guard in cases we should be in their ...

Got up at 8 o'clock. A beautiful morning & exceptionally hot. Found a great many Shields ships laying in the mole amongst them the Gordeson, Cholmley, the Wellington, H Daeghton & & Bob Marsh & I went on board & had our breakfast with H Deyghtow & his wife. The master & J Galbraith went on shore early to Mr Booker to report the ship & vansack

... all necessary business. Bob & I remained on board all day, expecting the collector every hour to search the ship & independently of which the heat was so great that we did not feel much despaired to move. We got an awning aerown over the main boom & kept ourselves as cool as we could. The collector did not come on board until 6 o'clock in the evening, a pompous, haughty Russian & like all the rest, lazy & will not move an inch out of the way to seron anyone.
