I find there is a very bad feeling at present towards the English. He or rather his officers searched the ship, but put his seals upon the hatches again. For packages he did not search, only counted them & ordered his officers on board not to take them off till the morning when people might deliver the ballast.

We again had a stroll about the town & ramparts. The homes of the people are very cleanly, though certainly some, such as the shopkeepers are more so than I expected. But the labouring classes are a dirty, lousy surplus, leftover & miserable set of slaves, little removed from beastly. In every shop there is a panting or fresco of our saviour or the virgin & in various parks of the town were erections in which was placed what they intended I suppose to be representations of our saviour & the virgin or some saint decked out in a most ridiculous style with linsel. They were the most hideous likenesses to the human face that there could be. Before each was a candle which was kept constantly burning & how every one of the poor ignorant devils on payment stopped crossing themselves, bowing & seeming to repeat ...

Another fine morning. The heat not quite so oppressive, but still warm enough.

After wasting some time, the officers came on board from what they call the Potash & taking a list of our luggage, describing each article & accompanied by us carried everything on shore to the Custom House. Here after wasting a considerable time, until their excellences the collector & clerk thought proper to move their stumps, the whole of our luggage was examined & every article in our boxes turned topsy-turvy. We mentioned our intention of going to Petersburg, and that we should want our luggage. They wished us mesely to take out a shirt or two & a few things, but we told them there was nothing there but what we absolutely wanted & could not do without & at last after some hesitation, they gave us our orders for the whole to be delivered to us the next morning. Having me sea sheets & on board a white shirt with a few other things stowed away, I was not so badly off by our boxes being so many days under seal, but poor Bob Marsh had not been quite so provident & was obliged to continue wearing a shirt & which he had had on ...

... several days before. From the Customs House we went to Mr Cramps, an Englishman, interpreter to the Russian Admiral from whom we got fresh papers, paying him 5 Rubles.

After dinner, Bob John Galbraith & I landed upon the mole head which we thought would be the coolest place & here lounged the whole of the afternoon amusing ourselves by watching the departure of ships & the passage to & fro for the various boats & craft of the haleires. During this time Stephenson was on shore buying Calkwood for broken stowage, which I have determined to load upon my own account, the freights here for it being low. After tea, wrote a letter to William to go buy some vessel bound to London & then we took our usual evening's lounger about the town, had our grog & went to bed

Turned out very early. The morning having to be on board the steam boat at 9 o'clock. After breakfast went on shore to the Custom House, got all our luggage & an officer to accompany us to the steamer or otherwise it would have had to be searched again before we put it on board. The gunr desk & we left at Mr Williamsons a very respectable shopkeeper's until our return. At 9 o'clock we sent asked for Petersburg having a beautiful morning for our ...

... you behold some Palace or public building which for grandeur & beauty & magnificence are far exceed my powers of description. The Winter Palace is by far the finest building of the sort I ever saw. Its size is immense, as for St James compound to it, is like a peg size compared with Wanstrand. In fact London is not to be mentioned with Petersburg & if I mistake not Regent Street & the other new streets now forming are bad copies of the streets & buildings in Petersburg.

The admiralty is a noble building of great extent having three sides is built that next to the river being open & the square forming a fine yard there they build their men-of-war.

Next to & above the Admiralty stands the Emperors Winter Palace. A very splendid building, having four sides & forming a hollow square exceedingly large & commanding though it is, the Hermitage.

Here I must stop for I find it impossible to enter into a complete description of every place & building one sees, they are so numerous.

Bob & I attended Change about 4 o'clock & a splendid building it is & I should imagine one of the finest rooms in Europe. Here I was introduced by Mr Dye to our merchants Mr Hubband & Gillibrand. Offered 30 tons of copper for ballast at 10/-. Wrote to Stephenson about it. Dined at ½ past 5 o'clock at Mr Wilson where we met about 121 others specifically I should thank American Captain Did mot much like rather one company or over dinner. In the cool of the evening we ...

Turned out this morning a little before 8 o'clock after a sound slump. But still excessively tired. The weather horrendously hot, staid quietly in the house until 1 o'clock. Accompanied Bob marsh to call upon Mr Wishaw, introduced to him. Very polite. Then walked over to the Island & called upon Changes. Not liking our quarters with Mrs Wilson & having to pay 8 rubles per day whether we dined there or not, Bob & I passed the time until Change houses in looking for other lodgings where we could have a bed & breakfast & be at liberty to do dining, but without success, not being able to speak the language & having no person with us that could understand.

Went to change where we met Mr Dye & afterwards walked home with him to dinner. His partners Mr Lumley & a Mr Leidsey from Leeds dined with us. He gave us a very good feed & moderate quantities of wine & at 8 o'clock got into a boat & rowed across the River to the island ...

Another fine day & continuance of hot weather. Bob & I after breakfast again sallied out in search of lodgings & were fortunate enough to see Mr Lindsay. A the wonder of his quarter. The house in kept by a yorkshireman of the name of Webster, a horse dealer. Here we succeeded in getting two rooms at 2 rubbles a night, in the larger one which I propose taking, having a small bed in for John Gabraith my bed is concealed by a large screen which when drawn round it, leaves the other part of the room for us & answers the purposes of a breakfast parlour.

J Galbraith arrived this morning by the steam boat & Mr Webster brought him up to the lodgings. Bob & I went to the office & got our passports returned. We afterwards accompanied Mr Lendsay who got our names put down at the Club formed of English & German merchants much upon the same plan as the clubs in London, tis a large building, formally the residence of a nobleman upon whom the Quay principally occupied by English merchants. The suit of rooms very splendid & most elegantly furnished. Here after changing, we dined & always intended doing so when not otherwise engaged. The company being Saturday, was not numerous, but we sat down to a very handsome dinner which I understand cost about 2 ½ rubbles
A beautiful spring day. Wind S. Returned to Dockwray Square, found Mrs Scott not quite so well. Walked to Tynemouth. Dined at home

... a head, exclusive of wine.

In the evening we took a stroll. On our return to our lodgings, rather tired, & thirsty, finished a bottle of beer, a couple of glasses of grog & went to bed.

Got up about 8 o'clock after a good night's rest in very comfortable & clean beds.

At 11 o'clock went to the English Church belonging to the E: Factory. The duty done by Mr Law, brother of Lord Ellenbro & Chaplin to the Embassy. This church is next to the clubhouse & the interior extremely elegant & neat. The exterior has the appearance of a private dwelling distinguishable from the rest by a statue of Hope on the top

Dined at the lodgings at 4 o'clock that we might get to the gardens of Krestovskiy after dinner & went to the gardens. On our way caught in a horrendous shower of rain with thunder and lightning. The gardens not very crowded no doubt in consequence of the wet, which also prevented the people dancing & us of a great deal of amusement. There were their bands, one military in the gardens, but the best was in front of the master of the Hunt House, and a horn band in a boat. This band is composed of a great number of men & each plays his separate note having a horn of one key, it is the finest thing I ever heard & had a delightful effect upon the water. We did not stay...

A showery morning, but cleared up towards the middle of the day. We set off with the intention of hearing the service at the Casen Church, but loitering on the way, were too late. The church however was open being a holyday & most splendid & gorgeous it is. The paintings of the different saints etc. are very well done & the most magnificent pillars of granite, highly polished, that can be imagined, each if one stone, there are about 100 of them. Here are deposited flags & keys of towns taken from the enemy at what was no little gratification to our pride, not an English colour amongst them. After a long stroll, we returned to res for dinner. Dined at the club. A very small party. Principally gentlemen. Left the table immediately after dinner & walked about the remainder of the evening. Had our grog & went to bed at 11 o'clock.

A beautiful morning & hot. J Galbraith returned to Kronshtadt by the steamer. Bob, I Mr Lending & his friend walked out after breakfast to the "Champ de Mars" expecting to see the troops reviewed, it being the Emperor's birthday, but there were none out. This is a most spacious place, well gravelled & large enough for the review of 60,000 men at a time. ‘tis a noble parade. Next to it are the gardens to the Summer palace in which the Emperor Paul was appointed. Then we passed through & were much pleased with the order in which they are kept & laid out, the walks are ornamented with various busts & statues beautifully executed in marble, in imitation of Versailles I understand, but inferior. Next we came to the palace of archduke Michael, lately built for him upon his marriage. A magnificent building & said by Doctor Grenville to be the triumph of modern architecture.

From there we proceeded to the Church of "Our lady of Cagan" where we found a great crowd of people. Here we found them engaged in offering up "Te Deum for a Victory". As well as being the Emperor's birthday, there was some expectation of the Archduke Alexander, the Emperor's eldest son being present, but he did not make his appearance. The singing was beautiful. We next went to the Cetadle & saw the interior of the Church when all the Emperors & Empresses are buried. We saw their tomb which all covered with silk most richly embroidered in gold, with the Imperial Eagle etc.

After this we viewed the smale collage in which Peter the Great resided when he first determined upon building the ...
Dined at home with Mrs Scott a very quiet day. Damp unpleasant weather. H Hurry & J Elder surveyed the Hope & valued at from £1000 to £1100. Wind SW. Wrote to William
A pleasant day wind SW. A large fleet got to sea. Got the main rigging over the mast head. Dined at Mrs Mathews to meet the Milners. Gave captain Stephenson £5 for petty expenses

A continuance of hot weather. The first thing after breakfast was to go with Mr Lindsay to the Hermitage, the interior of which is most splendid. A suit of apartments throughout communication with each other & every room filled with the paintings of all the old & first masters & in the centre of almost every room was a vase of imimeange sege & most beautifully executed. This backing forms a square, as indeed do all the Palaces & in the centre upon the roof of the first floor they have made a very pretty garden, a retired spot for the perpermeal family & the trees in it so large in each a place. Attached to the Hermitage, the Emperor has a very neat private theatre which we ...

... did not see to advantage being under repairs. It would require two or three days to examine manually all that this Plaice contains. The admirer of the fine arts, the antiquarian & mineralogist may find many days employed in this building. From this after having had a lunch, we crossed the water to the "Hotel de Miner" where we spent two hours very agreeably in examining the models of all sorts of machinery. The Siberian mines of gold & silver, the glenichs specimens, mineral produced by them. One specimen of malachite the largest & finest in the world, weighing a ton & a half. It is said the Emperor has offered its weight in silver some say in gold & when the celebrated professor Homburg first entered the room, he was in such ecstasy at the sight of it, that he actually dropped to his knees and was helped at. Under the gardens of the institution they have made a mine, a representation of the Serbian gold & silver mines. It is of considerable extent the same size & the different stratas shown. Each having a candle, we were led through the various windings of this interesting place & much satisfied. We also had a fine view of the city at the top of the observatory. At this institution there are a great number of cadets educated for the Corp of Sappers & mines.

Mr Thilkey who was to drive us to his country house about 9 miles down ...

A fair morning. Mr Linsey, his friend, Bob & I started at 8 o'clock in a barrack for the Imperial Palace of Sarskoi & Pavhousky, about 22 versts off, where we arrived in about 2 ½ hours. Sarskoi is a summer palace & surpasses everything we have yet seen for brilliance & splendour. It is grand & magnificent beyond the possibility of just description. Every room is most richly guild with the finest gold and I showed surprise at an immense expenditure at one time. The roof & all the exterior ornaments were done in the same way, but ‘tis said that Catherine when much in want of money, made an agreement with a rich Jew, who advanced her a certain sum, for the purpose of stripping the gold off the exterior. Nothing can exceed the attention of the Chapple. The furniture is exceedingly rich & handsome & great taste is displayed ...

... throughout. The grand dining room is a noble apartments & of great size and there is great comfort neatness & cleanliness in the Emperor & Empress's private apartments. The grounds which are very extensive being about the diameter of five miles, are laid out with great taste & judgement & kept in high order & beautifully interspaces with wood & water. In the plantations is a summer or private dining room built by Catherine & elaborated by her making it the scene of her private armoires. In the centre of the building, upon the finest floor is the dining room & that night not having the attendance of servants, the table was worked by machinery & upon a bell being rung, the whole descended to a room below & there replenished, or if merely a clean plate was wanted, the plate stand, alone went down. But of each corner of the dining room was a cabinet intended no doubt for beds or couches. But when we were there, the whole was under repair & consequently not furnished.

The Palace of Jarskoi not being large enough for the whole of the family, another upon a smaller & less magnificent scale was built in the grounds. A plain but handsome mansion. There are also a number of houses at a short distance from the Palace, built after the Chinese fashion forming a small village ...

The weather still continues particularly fine. Did not go out this morning till after 11 o'clock when Bob & I went to the Aliex officer for our permit of residence for which we each had to pay 10 rubbles. We then went to the museum where we saw a great variety of minerals surgeal preparations, stuffed animals of all sorts, a number of things in ivory beautifully turned, with the lathes all the workmanship of Peter the Great.

Dined with Mr Dye where we met a Mr Atkinson, Mr Bush & Mr Linsey. Mr Dye kindly asked us to dine with him again at his country house that we might see some fete that is to take place in the neighbourhood. Left Mr Dye's early being foreign port night. Took a stroll with Mr Lindsey & called upon a friend of his. Got home a little after 10 o'clock, finished a glass of grog & went to bed

A fine morning, but windy & dusty. This being the [day] of St Peter & St Paul, is a general holiday here & services in all the churches. Mr Lindsey his friend Mr Miggete, Bob & I walked out at 12 o'clock for a stroll. Looked into the Catholic Church where they were just concluding the service, their singing seemed to be good. Returned to my lodgings about 3 o'clock, leaving Bob to prolong his walk & had a snooze being tired. Dined at the German Club at ½ past 5 o'clock. In the evening Bob & I ...

After breakfast walked to the Roman Catholic Chapel to hear the singing which was very fair. A great many people there. Bob & I perfectly disgusted at the superstition of both the Catholic Religion, their bowings, protestation & kissing the feet * gassment of the different saints. In the ceremonies & forms they do not appear to differ much.

Dined today with Mr Wishaw at his house on the Wybury Island. We were nearly an hour after our time, Mr Wishaw very stupidly not having given us proper directions to enable us to find his house out. After dinner accompanied the ladies in a boat to the opposite side of the river. Unfortunately we were late & could not use the hothouse. They seem to be expensive. Here was a military band & a good deal of company.

After breakfast Mr Bartleuace of the David just arrived from Grangemouth & I took a donkey & drove over to Mr Dryers whose partner Mr Gray had chartered the David & introduced him. Then drove to the news key ...
A fine day. Wind SW. Engaged on board ship. Dined at J Tinly & went to the assembly in the evening which was numerously attended

... prospect. On our way home seeing painted over something like cellars "English Wind cellar" & fancying them to be upon the same plan as the Shades in London, we walked in, being very thirsty with the head & ordered some Madeira. We presently suspected that the gentleman was a Wine Merchant & would have come out again, but he desiring us to walk into his office put a bottle of very fine wine before us, which we made a hole in. We then would have paid him for it, but he would not allow us, said he perceived we were strangers & was extremely happy to see us. He was exceedingly polite & kind indeed. But we were certainly placed in an unpleasant predicament.

Mr Lindsey, Bartholomew, Bob & I at 5 o'clock took a donkey & drove out to Mr Dye's country house where we dined & in the evening went to the Gelagin Palace to see the grand fête, it being the Emperor's birthday & such a scene I never beheld. Crowds of people & carriages innumerable, the walks & roads were literally choked up with them. Bands playing & singing. All sorts of national music. Five works which we could not see very well for the crowd. The river also had a very gay & animated appearance, being covered with boats filled with people in their best holiday dresses. This fate takes place in the grounds attached to the Palace which altogether is a most beautiful place. We did not arrive at our lodgings until 1 o'clock in the morning.

Breakfasted early this morning & at 9 o'clock, Bartholomew, Marsh & I set off for the arrival to the Govenor of which a Baron Gode we had a letter of introduction from Mr Wishaw. We found him at home & in a very polite gentleman's manor he talked English fluently, indeed I believe is an Englishman. Unfortunately for us he was so much engaged in business just now that he could not accompany us. He gave us an order to see everything tomorrow & at the same time told he would give such orders that everything should be shown & explained to us & that we should be accompanied by some person who could do us.

Being so far on the road, we then bent our course towards the Monastery of St Alexander Nevsky. The heat was so oppressive we were obliged to go at a snail's pace & then we were almost melted. It is a very fine church. The Westminster abbey of St Petersburg, & it with its grounds which altogether are extensive are surrounded by a high wall & various large buildings which I suppose are for the monks and priests to live in. Several of there drones we saw lounging about. The interior of the Cathedral exceedingly fine, particularly the dome & avof there are several good paintings. One or two by Reuben. There is the shrine of St Alexander Nevsky finely executed in selour & of large size, containing two tons of salour. In their ...

... place all the most celebrated Russian Generals and Statesmen are buried there & there monuments are to be seen. But there are none I think particularly striking for their sculpture. Bob & I walked viv our return home as far as the market near the Casan church in search of beads in imitation of coral for the Lees, saw some, but could not drive a bargain. Came away without them. Took a drogty home, more than a mile. Dined for 60 Kapelles = 6 English. Dined at Mr Websters. Mr Lendglig joined us.

After dinner took a drokty to go to the theatre, but not with an adventure on the way. Made a call & bestowed our charity, thankfully received. Lots of gratification. Found our way to the ____ theatre, a dismal place & very dirty. The painters brush & mutton fals or gash much required. The performance very fair & music excellent.

Got to our lodgings about ½ past 10 o'clock. Took a glass of grog & turned in. Pretty considerably tired

Immediately after breakfast to drivzkeys & went to the Arsenal where we found the Baron had been as good as his word. A soldier was in waiting for us, who took us over the different departments. They were very busy making brass cannon. The machinery for boring & polishing them very beautiful. Several rooms ...

An exceedingly close & hot morning. Had a shower or two of rain, but if anything rather warmer afterwards. Bob & I called to take leave upon Mr Dye, Mr Thilky, Mr Gellebrand & Mr Wislaw. The great linen from whom we had received attention & civilities. The heat so oppressive we remained at home. Mr Lindsley with us. By the evening went again to the market.

On our way, stopped at one of the Russian baths, where I think we were more astonished than by anything we have yet seen. There were crowds of people going & coming from the bath. Fortunately for themselves, it being considered a religious ceremony, they frequently get their carcases washed or rather purified or otherwise they would be eaten up with verusin for they never think of washing themselves. But on these occasions, as it is, so filthy are they, that they swarm with lice. They do not team themselves as formally men & women together, but among the lower orders each sex have their separate bath, where they parbait themselves by scores. The men we saw first, some ...
A wet morning, but by the time we had breakfast, it had cleared up. Paid our account for lodgings etc & got on board the steam boat at 9 o'clock & proceeded to Cronstad, where we ...

... arrived before 12 o'clock. Had to take our luggage again to the Customs House to be searched. A mere matter of form, for they only opened the boxes without turning the things over & after a little trouble & delay, we were allowed to carry all on board, accompanied by an officer. Employed ourselves during this afternoon in stowing our traps away & putting everything in order.

After tea the captain, Marsh & I went on shore, called at the butchers & baker & spent the remainder of the evening at a friend's where we had some wine. Got on board again between 11 & 12 o'clock.

Taken 250 casks of tallow on board

An exceedingly fine spring day. Wind SW. Went to Newcastle in the morning. The new register not ready. The old one & certificate not having been sent from Shields. Got £20 of J Tenley on account S W & J Scott

Another lighter came down last night with the remainder of our tallow.

After breakfast, Bob, JG & I went on shore to order some boots etc. Met with Mr Bartholomew. Went with him & had our dinner on board the David. He left by the steam boat for Petersburg at 5 o'clock. Bab & I went with Stephenson to the Butchers to see the beef salted & afterwards took a stroll.

Got in 120 casks of tallow this day.

A rainy morning. Cleared up about 10 o'clock. Dressed ourselves & went on shore to the English Church, just in time to hear the communion service & sermon. Dined on board at 1 o'clock. Had a good sea pie & some roast mutton, which enjoyed much. In the afternoon went on shore, excepting Bob, took some mead to cool us, a very agreeable & refreshing drink made of honey & ginger, not unlike ginger wine. Looked at the Neger market, a very curious and busy scene, crowded with people bargaining & selling. A great many sailors there, regular jacks, very amusing to hear them. Went in the evening to the gardens, which are open to the public on a Sunday. The walks are very prettily laid out & shaded with young trees. A great many of the fashionables of Cronstat where promenading & an excellent military band played for about a couple of hours.

Got on board early

Fine weather. Passed our time in preparing for the voyage in making what purchases we wished. Dined with Mr Bartholomew on board the David. Took a walk in the evening. Agreed to go to Peterhoff tomorrow with Mr Bartholomew.

A fine morning. Could not get to Peterhoff without our papers, which Stephenson required to clear the ship. Stayed to give it up. Dined on board the David. Turned out a rainy afternoon. Came down in torrents. Engaged to take tea with Mr Ross but the rain prevented us. Did not leave the ship.

A fine morning blowing fresh from the Westward. Several ships arrived. Among them the Herald Yacht with Lady Heytesbury on board, the wife of the British ambassador. We ourselves are cleared and ready for sea, but wind bound. Brought four pairs of boots & two pairs of slippers for which I only gave 30 rubbles equal to about 25/-. Dined on board. Brought seven Caviar for jrbling. Richmond etc. Drank a glass of punch with the Ross & afterwards called at ____.

Much annoyed with a swollen face arising from a decayed tooth & cold. Walked round the man of wars mold & went on board one of their new 74's. the Russian fleet returned from a cruise to be inspected by the Emperor, who it is reported has returned to Petersburg
Still wind bound, blowing fresh from the SW. Suffered a great deal of pain during the night from my tooth & my face swollen to a giant size. Could with difficulty eat. In no ...

Fine weather but still a fresh westerly breeze, which detains us. Relieved from pain by the flannel & hartshorn, but my face still much swollen. Remained on board & upon the mole head all the morning.

Mr Bookers clerk called to demand 15 rubbles brokerage for the copper. Went on shore at 5 o'clock to see him upon the subject. It appears I treated with a broker & nob the merchant or I supposed, the brokerage therefore due. Desired Mr Booker to request Mr Hubbardth to pay it & I should settle it in London, having no Russian money left. Amused ourselves on the mole head all evening

Blowing very hard during the whole of the day from the westward. Several ships arrived having had fine passages of 13 days from London. Amongst them the Sceptre, Coui Greenhod. Several laden ships having hauled out made the roadshad very throng. On the mole head all the morning. Mr Lendaley came down in the steam boat & brought me ec ...

... packet from Mr Dye, a present for Emma Galbraith. Mr L took a glass of grog with us & we afterwards accompanied him on board. The Chase, captain Thompson arrived today in 13 days from Hull, and had supper.

A beautiful morning, but exceptionally hot. The wind having got round to the north & an appearance of changing. We after breakfast hauled out of the mole but being quite calm were obliged to get a boat ahead & toe the ship down to the guard ship. Cleared at the guard ship about 12 o'clock & proceeded with a leading wind, but little of it.
Another fine spring day. Wind SW. Dined at home & at the whist club in the evening. Mrs Smith left us for Togston. Brought a trysailmast & gib boom for £4.12.6 & got them on board

A fine morning, rather dull. The ship working windward, the wind having unfortunately changed during the night direct against us being west. Continued binting about all day without making any way. For little to the eastward of Seascar Island. In the evening we again got a leading wind & before bed time, getting more to the northward, we were enabled to set lower fore & topmast & studding sails with a fine fresh breeze

A very thick wet disagreeable morning, been raining nearly all night, but thank God, with a fine fresh breeze from the eastward. The ship making good way passed the north end of Hogsland this morning at 6 o'clock. Continued raining all day from 5 ½ to 6 ½ knots. When we went to bed at a little before 10 o'clock we were abreast of Revel, still blowing fresh from the East.

Turned out this morning at ½ past 7 o'clock. Weather changed being quite calm, the alterations took place last night at 12 o'clock with heavy rain, thunder & lightning, which & I did not hear being on a very comfortable birth & sound asleep. In the course of the morning, when off Hanger Head, the wind got to the north (at 2 o'clock wind east) enabling us again to set studding sails, steering a WSW course.

Amused myself all day in reading Roderick Random and Peregrine Pickle. Turned in at 11 o'clock after having our grog. Little wind.

Turned out before 8 o'clock. A fine morning. A light breeze at ENE going about 3 or 3 ½ knots. Studding sails set. About dinner time it began to rain & continued very heavy until 3 o'clock. When we passed round Dago Island & entered the Baltic. At ½ past 5 o'clock the wind changed to west ...
In the evening light winds & inclined to calm. Turned in before 10 o'clock after a glass of grog

Fine weather and light breezes from WNW. During the whole of the morning mainly calm, barely going 2 knots with rather a strong sea. In the evening about 5 o'clock the wind got to the ENE & increased to a fine breeze. The ship going about 4 & 5 knots & from midnight to 4 o'clock the wind blew so fresh she increased her rate to 6 knots. This fine breeze continued all night.

Got up at ½ past 7 o'clock. A fine morning. After a few hours rain & a beautiful breeze the whole of the night. At 8 o'clock am the wind changed to SE obliged us to get in lower studding sails. At 2 o'clock the wind got to S by W strong breezes & hazy weather & rain, very cold, more like November than August. At 6 o'clock close in with Gothland Ostergarmholm light house N ½ W distant about 12 miles. Tacked ship blowing fresh with a heavy head sea. Between 9 & 10 o'clock discussed our grog & turned in.

This afternoon the Dido of Hull captain ____ passed astern of us. We hoisted our colours & he answered

Got up at our usual hour. Finer weather, wind NE & strong sea, but still cool. At noon by observation lat:57.8N Wind WNW. The strong sea preventing us making more than 2 or 3 knots. Read service & lessons for the day. In the afternoon wind NW & blowing fresh, only going from 3 to 4 knots. A few ships in company. Amongst them Bowies Malvina. At 4 o'clock took in top gallants sails. Bob & I very tired of this slow work.

Between 9 & 10 o'clock finished a couple of glasses of warm grog & turned in hoping to sleep better than last night. The tallow casks making a most infernal creaking. Obliged to get the state room port light caulked, a pretty considerable quantity of water having come in & wet my bed
A fine day day. Wind N by E. Finished with the rigging. Dined at home. At Mrs Greenhows in the evening

A very fine morning & clear weather, still blowing fresh from the NW which has continued the whole day, with a heavy sea which has prevented us making more than 3 knots. Amused myself the whole of the day reading Peregrine Pickle. At 4 o'clock pm wind got to W by N. At 5 o'clock pm tacked ship & stood across towards Gothland again. By observation at 12 o'clock lat:55.52 Reefed topsail at 2 o'clock pm

A delightful change. Now beautiful weather. Wind NW & W. Light breeze & sea very much fallen, only going about 2 knots. At 12 o'clock by observation at lat:55.47N. Employed myself all the morning in preparing the wood for a dog kennel. At 2 o'clock pm the wind got to the WSW course NW. At 5 pm set studding sails, top masts & main top gallant. Sea quite fallen & a fine fresh breeze at 6 o'clock wind S course W by S going 5 knots at 10 o'clock discharged our grog & turned in for the night, ship going 5 ½ knots

Another beautiful day. The ship making good way about 4 ½ knots with a fine breeze at SSE going free. We can perceive the Islands of Ertholmene & Bornholm with the glass. The ship much to my annoyance very leaky. Obliged to pump every hour. At 1 o'clock pm passed close to Ertholmene. With a fine breeze at S by E. Studding sails set. These are small rocky islands belonging to Denmark about 11 miles from Bornholm. Upon the largest is a lighthouse, a few small batteries & houses. On the south side a very good harbour I understand. The other two islands are mostly rocks & ...

Turned out this morning at the usual hour. Coppers hot & rather feverish, took a seidletz, very pleasant answering a double purpose. A beautiful morning. Summer returned. A light breeze at SE. At noon by observation in lat 55.10N. Kept our reach the whole of the day. Wind NW. At 8 o'clock tacked ship. Reigen Island bearing S by W distant 10 or 12 miles.

A cloudy morning & fresh breeze at NNW & N. Employed myself all the morning in drawing. At noon clear weather but still a fresh breeze. Falsterbo light bearing WNW distant 8 miles. A large fleet of ships passed us upward bound. At 5 o'clock tacked ship a little to the southward of Moea Island after which it became quite calm until 9 o'clock when we got a light air from the NNW. Afterwards most favourable. At 10 o'clock after our grog we turned in, the ship proceeding quickly towards Drags in the island Verf Amag

Hearing the master speaking a ship, I turned out before 7 o'clock. It was Hutchenson's Ajax bound to Wybury, several other ships passing us. Hazy weather & light rain, wind WNW. At ½ past 7 o'clock got a piolet onboard & at 8 o'clock passed Drago. At 10 o'clock got there through the Grounds when the piolet left us off Copenhagen proceeding with a fine breeze for Elsinore. The weather cleared up & turned out a fine warm day, giving us a beautiful view of the coast. Brought up at Elsinore at 3 o'clock & went on shore. Received a letter from William informing me of Mrs Scott's illness, not expected to live long & his intention of going to Shields on the 11 th August in the steam boat with C Richmond. Took some wine with warm chapurars & afterwards walked out to his fathers house who kindly sent to ask us when he heard of our arrival to go & drink a ...

Turned out at the usual hour & found the ship off the Koll having got underway at 9 am with a fresh breeze at W by S, proceeding at the rate of 6 or 6 ½ knots during the whole of the day. Passed Anholt at about 6 o'clock in the evening
Clear weather but blowing very fresh from WSW. Obliged to reef & double reef the topsails & slow the trysails. Could make no way against both wind & current. Lat: by obs 58.2 N

Continuance of clear weather & wind still prevailing from the SSW & SW. Could make no way at 1 o'clock pm & just after taking of position into some port in Norway an extremely heavy gale of wind came on from ...

... the west which soon caused a tremendous sea. Obliged to him too under close reefed topsails until about 4 o'clock when we wone ship & lay too under close reefed main topsail. What with the howling of the wind, the rolling & tossing of the ship & creaking of tallow casks besides being leaky & upon a lee shore, we had spent a most uncomfortable day. Did not attempt to go to bed, indeed mine was so damp I could not, but I lay down upon the captains about midnight all standing
A beautiful day. Wind N. Went to Newcastle & signed bond for Register. Dined at J Tindley, a large party. Paid carpenters £9.12/- - Riggers £7. Wrote to William

Spent a miserable night, having had little or no sleep. Looked out about 5 o'clock. The gale as heavy as ever & without any appearance of change, although the sky very clear. At 11 o'clock Masskand Castle in sight distant about 4 leagues, when we determined no longer to contend with the winds but bore away for Gottenburg & in the course of half an hour those wise few that did not follow our example at ½ past 3 o'clock we reached Wings sound & before 5 o'clock brought up in the harbour of Warga, a small channel between two docks, rejoicing with the prospect of obtaining a good nights rest.

A fine clear day, but still blowing hard from the westward.

After breakfast, Bob the Captain J Galbraith & I landed. One of the fishermen's yawls (large size) fine sea boats & safe & sailed up to Gothenburg where we spent the day in seeing the town, which is much better than I expected & larger, the country around entirely rock, having a novel wild & beautiful appearance altogether being interspersed with valleys & rivers which were the only spots that could be cultivated & were made the most of. They had one of their annual fares which lasts eight days, but did not seem well attended. After having had our dinner at one of their inns, considering the country very comfortable, we again embarked at 4 o'clock& the winds being against us, we had a turning passage of it, & did not reach the ship until near 8 o'clock.

And after having our tea blowing a cloud & discussing a glass of grog, turned in before 10 o'clock

Turned out at ½ past 7 o'clock. In the middle of the night it became quite calm & the wind changing to the eastward enabled us to get underway. Between 8 & 9 o'clock & to leave a place that I never again wish to see under similar circumstances. As the wind changed with the moon, it will carry us safely to England ...
... should it continue. At 6 o'clock passed the Scaw Light with a fresh breeze & every appearance of it increasing, the sea making very much. Turned in at about our usual hour

Got up this morning at a little before 8 o'clock after a very boisterous night, the wind having increased to more than half a gale with a tremendous sea, right aft so that we made good way, though at the sacrifice of our comfort. Everything above & below being wet & in confusion. At 5 o'clock this morning a tremendous heavy sea pooped us, stove & carried away our jolly boat & alarmed us so much fearing it had stove in the dark lights & if it had so happened we of course should have been waterlogged. Knowing the delicate state of the archboard, where she was making a great deal of water, the fear of another heavy sea striking us kept me in a very uncomfortable state the whole of the day. Towards evening however both wind & sea fell considerably. We have been going today from 6½ to 7 knots. Ship laboured very much & made a deal of water. We consider we have got this evening considerably to the westward of the Naze of Norway, say 50 miles.

A great deal of water having come into ...

More moderate weather. Wind NE. A fine breeze. Ship going about 4 knots. Let reefs out of the top sails, set top gallants sails, square mainsail free, topmasts liering sail & gib.

Read the duty & Lessons of the day.

The mainsail being split, unbent it & got up another. The breeze rather freshened. This afternoon at NNE & B by E. In the evening took a reef in each topsail & stowed topgallant sails.

Between 9 & 10 turned in, being by my calculation about 100 miles from the Land

Got up this morning much disappointed at not finding ourselves within 20 miles of land, which we should have been had the wind continued as it was last night. But unfortunately it has changed in the night to NW & NW by W & we are now only going 3 knots. The weather fine, but cloudy. Hope we shall have a change before night for I'm anxious to land at Shields.
We are now about 80 miles from the land, returning about SW. Continued this course. Ship making a deal of water.

A dull couldy morning with rain fresh breeze etc W by N going only 3 ½ knots. At ½ past 6 o'clock being thick hazy weather we made Huntcliff foot at least we concluded it to be so. This at first we thought it Tynemouth. We lay the ship to with her head off.

This morning thick weather the land in sight like a fog bank, but clearing away we found it for certain to be Huntcliff foot, bearing west about five miles. During the morning light wind variable & in the afternoon calm with tremendous heavy rain, thunder & lightning. At night the wind being from the NE light breeze & I very unwell with scumalign. The ship short of Stocks as water coals & pump gear out of order & considering she might reach shields, by daylight, we determined to work to windward & turned in for the night.
A fine but cold day. Wind N by E. At church in the morning. Walked to Tynmouth in the afternoon. Dined at home

Turned out this morning between 5 & 6 o'clock found the ship turning to windward off Marsden Rock blowing hard from N by E. The wind having increased during the night with a high sea. At about 9 o'clock, the breeze increasing & no chance of us reaching Tynemouth of getting on shore. Even if we had, we bore away for London much to our chagrin & disappointment having had Shields Dockwray Square etc in view & not able to ...

Got up at ½ past 7 o'clock. A fine morning. Most moderate weather. Wind N by W night after Studdington set Just passed the Floating light, having made good way during the night. Had a good night's rest, but much plagued with the rheumatism

Passed Cromer at 1 o'clock with less wind Between 8 & 9 o'clock in the evening abreast of Harborough endeavouring to get through the gateway, but falling calm were driven back by the tide. With much trouble got the ship head round to the westward & a light breeze springing up, stood a crop to the land. At 10 o'clock went to bed. Tide turned & the captain intending to work up to Winterton & anchor, the wind being from the SW.

Went upon deck at 8 o'clock. Found the ship outside the sands nearly as far as Lowestoft turning to windward with the wind at WSW. It seems that last night soon after we turned in, the wind suddenly got to the W & WNW where they squared the yards, set studdingsails & ran out of harbour gateway.

The wind increasing from the WNW stowed topgallant sails, reefed topsails, afterwards stowed square mainmast & bore away & at 12 o'clock when off Southwold, bore away for Yarmouth, passing through St Nicholas Gateway, where to my inexpressible horror and alarm we nearly struck upon the north end of the Croton Sand, the captain, me, taking the last buoy for the buoy of a wreck in the rocks. The lead was thrown. The mate called out ½ 3 then ¼ 3 – 3 but when it came to ¼ less 3 my state fear & agitation, for the safety of the ship, was not to be envied, expecting every moment she would strike & had she, the least that could have happened would most likely have been to deliver the cargo & repair, being already very leaky, but she probably might have gone down in deep water or have drifted on the sand to leeward where the mast probably have been lost. However the next throw of the lead the mate called ¼ 3 & then ½ & 4 fathoms was a wonderful relief to me. Such was agitation that I could almost have cried indeed I wouldn't say that the big tear did not stand in my eye but I ...

Turned out after a food nights rest at 8 o'clock. The gale as heavy as ever with rain. (Sent top gallant yards driven & struck the mast)

At 11 o'clock finer weather & some appearance of clearing up having had a glimpse of the sun.

Wrote a letter to William & Mr Clark of the Duke of Clarence coming on board. We all went on shore at 12 o'clock to put the letter into the post. Walked about & saw a little of the town of Yarmouth with which I was much pleased. After having some bread & cheese, portion & a glass of grog, we left the jetty about 4 o'clock ...
... reached the ship in about ½ a hour after a heavy pull. Still blowing very hard. Mr Clark took tea with us in the evening. The weather much improved both sea & wind having fallen.

Still blowing very hard from I believe the WSW. About 9 o'clock a most tremendous squall came off the land, a perfect hurricane, enough almost to throw the masts out of the ship. But fortunately it did not continue over ½ an hour. It changed the wind however to WNW when a number of the ships immediately began to get under way. Although continuing to blow hard & having a very unsettled appearance.

It was the contention of the master to have gone on shore & brought what previsions & water he wanted but the change of wind & other ships getting under way, colliers like, he must follow the example & at 10 o'clock having first been on board the Duke of Clarian & borrowed a bag of bread, we also up anchor & ran out of the gateway. But we had not been long outside before we repented, for it came on a heavy squall, blowing & raining like fury & very thick. We however kept all our canvas standing excepting the mainsail & continued our course to the SW. Towards evening the weather clear & more moderate & at 8 o'clock, having reached Orford refs wind about W by N we bore up & ran into Aldeburgh roads where we brought up for the night in a snug roadstead.

Many other ships following our example. Blew a cloud, discasted a glass of grog & turned in before 10 o'clock

A fine clear morning, but wind not at all abated, about WNW & the night has been so boisterous with rain, that the master & all the vessels in company have not thought it prudent to move. The people employed in sending down the Royals & setting up the short topgallant masts. Seeing about board a ship near us, we were in no little alarm, lest it should be one of the preventative service & were in a devil of a brush to get our goods and challis stowed away. It however proved a false alarm, being only a pilot boat. Got under way at 12 o'clock & turned to windward with a fresh breeze. At 9 o'clock pm brought up abreast of the hook of the Gunfleet for the night

By daylight this morning. They got the ship underway at low water. When we got up at 8 o'clock the weather much pleasanter & continued fine all day. At noon brought up at high water abreast of Whitaker Beason. Wind SW. At 5 pm, low water, we again got under way, but were much delayed by a ship giving us a foul birth, the consequence was it became dark before we could work through Shoe hole & see the mouse buoy, where unfortunately it also turned very squally & blowing a gale of wind. We were working towards the nose light & should have got well up but the overhaul of our gib giving way the ship would not steer & we were obliged, though not unwilling by ...

... to bring up, being on good riding ground between the nose light & the buoy of the mouse.

At ½ past 11 o'clock we got into bed. Blowing a gale & a dismal night

Turned out between 6 & 7 o'clock & soon afterward got underway. Still blowing hard from about the WSW lasting at 12 o'clock & after it blew a perfect hurricane, however we rode well & I slept very sound. A large Garth that we saw to leeward of us yesterday without his main topsail, is this morning upon the Maplin sand, having no doubt missed stage last night. Several smacks near him. This lide we worked up as high as Southend & brought up glad to get into such a good roadstead. At 6 o'clock, low water, the gale heavier & night coming on, we did not think it prudent to get under way. At 8 o'clock we had a warm glass of Hollands & water which we enjoyed. The first we have had for some time, having run out of coals.

I forgot to mention that yesterday while we brought up abreast of the Whitaker, we lowered our boat & went on board the Eliza of South Shields, Captain Young who kindly supplied us with two or three baskets of coals & a cask of water in return we gave him a spare for a topgallant studding sail boom in dial plank & a bottle of Hollands.

He also took a box of Russian slippers & a keg of caviar, to return to us in London. We fearing the officers might seize them

A cold morning. Wind N by W. Went to Newcastle. Dined & stayed all night at D Dixons. Accompanied Tom & Bill Smith to the Theatre. Got Hopes new Register & sent it off to London with Smiths dock bill. Wrote to William. Drew £5 of Chapmans for own use. Tendered the Hope to the Hope Club for £1000
Turned out before 8 o'clock. The gale increased & blowing so hard that we cannot get underway. In the middle of the night it was tremendous & we ...

Turned out at ½ past 6 o'clock. When I got upon the deck found the ship under way. Weather much moderated with a fine stiff breeze from the northward which carried us up to Gravesend in about a couple of hours, where we took on board a carbonhouse officer & proceeded. At about 12 o'clock we came to an anchor at Blackwall after a fine run, having made only one tack the whole of the day. Our watersman, whose boat Bob & I got into soon after we anchored with all our luggage on board, who allowed us to take it out of the ships, which few would have done & rowed up to the Tower Stairs, took a coach & drove up to the New Inn calling in Philpot Lane on our way, where I found there letters from William

Glad once more to get under a comfortable roof. When I had written a letter to William & we had ...

... made ourselves decent & comfortable Bob & I walked up to George in the Red Lion Square where we made & enjoyed a hearty dinner of pigeon & veal pies & cold mullion, discharged a good glass of punch & returned to Chambers. With the appearance of Mrs Furmedye, Bob's laudress, I made myself a good perch for the night with Bob's mallrafs in the corner of his room, turned in & enjoyed an excellent nights rest, although the bed was rather a hard one.

Thus ends our Petersburg voyage which upon the whole we have enjoyed, but we could have dispensed with the tumultuous bad weather we experienced. Thank God we have got back safe & without any accident worth mentioning to the ship.

Got up much refreshed. More moderate weather. Wind NE rather cloudy. We fully intended to have gone to church, but Bob & I took up so much linin in the washing & cleaning ourselves that it was past the hour before we were aware of it. Turned out a very fine day. We called upon Mr Ward who had gone to Paris will William. Walked through St James park up to Hyde Park where we strolled till 6 o'clock. Very few people or carriages there. Town exceedingly thin from thence came we went to Mr Piazza Covent garden & enjoyed a comfortable dinner & a good bottle of old port. Returned to Chambers between 10 & 11 o'clock & went to bed.

A cloudy morning, rather cool. Wind NE. Walked into the city. Called at the office, nothing there. Proceeded after being at Chapmans to St Catherine's docks. The ship got safe in yesterday. Stephenson noted a protest this morning, the ship having been so leaky. Found Mrs Stephenson on board, eat some dinner with them. Attended chambers. Walked westward & called upon Jobling.

A dull day & showery. Walked into the city & down to the docks. Found them employed in moving the ship to a birth & then began to deliver her cargo before I left. Went to chambers & afterwards walked westward. Dined with Jobling in the Adelphi, only ourselves. Spent a pleasant day. Got rather too much wine. Slept all night in Villiers Street

A fine day. Wind NW. Called upon Jobling. He drove me down to Woolwich to see the Lumley's. Eat some cold meat with them & returned to the ship at Greenwich to dinner, where Tom Jobling joined us. Left the ship about 7 o'clock & drove to town. Had a glass of brandy & wine with Jobling & got to bed at ½ past 10 o'clock

A fine morning. Wind NW. Bob Marsh & I walked into the city & thence on board the Hope where we dined. The people busy getting the tallow out. Returned to Philpot Lane where we stopped until 6 o'clock with Mary Ann first time. Walked out of the city to chambers & remained all evening. Received a letter from William which came yesterday. Did not answer it.

Another fine day. Wind the same. Bob & I again walked into the city & to the Hope where we lunched. Got all the tallow out today & expect to deliver the copper. Returned to Philpot Lane where I met with Mr James Gale from Carlow. With Maryann again. Took a Greenwich boat at the tower Stairs & went down to Watts, where I dined & stayed all night.

A fine morning. Rather cold. Wind N by W. Went to the county Court in the morning with Mrs Dixon & Bill Smith. Heard judge Bailey deliver his charges to The grand jury & returned to Shields by steam. Dined with J Tindley. Mrs Scott much better & downstairs

A dull cloudy morning, with a slight shower or two of rain. Wind I think about WSW. Watt prevailed upon me to remain till Monday. Amused ourselves during the morning fishing for eels near Bugsby's Hole. Had poor sport, patience exhausted. A great many large ships passed us from foreign, with some collisions. Dined at 6 o'clock & in the evening played a rubber of whist

A cloudy morning. Wind SSW. I accompanied Miss Watt to church, but might as well have been at home for anything I heard of the sermon. A large consignment Dined at 6 o'clock. Mr Philips. Watt's landlord dined with us. Spent a quiet evening. It began to rain soon after church & continued heavy all day which confined us to the house.

A showery day, at intervals, at intervals very fine. Wind about SE. Got into a Greenwich boat at ½ past 10 o'clock & landed at Catherine dock. Found them busy with the lathwood which was sold on Thursday to Mr Martin at £16.5/- a fathom. Had not been long on board when Bob Marsh came. We had our dinner & afterwards walked up to Philpot lane where I found a letter from William of his intention to be in town by the Highflyer in the evening.

Called at J Chapmans & from the state of the coal trades, the coal owners having again restricted the vends, raised their price 5/- & refusing either to freight or uphold, I almost determined to send the Hope to memel at 21/- & load for timber. Shall settle tomorrow.

Bob & I called upon J Hodgsons & afterwards took a walk up Regent Street. Brought a new Hat at Oliphants & a pair of trousers at Laffins. At ½ past 8 o'clock went to the Cock in Fleet Street & eat some oysters & at 10 o'clock met William & Lea at the White Horse in Fetter Lane having just arrived from Shields by the Highflyer. A very wet night

Showery. Wind SW. William & Lea called at new Inn & we went into the city together in a coach. Called at Chapmans but did not freight the Hope, thinking to send her to Shields. Walked down to the ship. William took J Galbraith to Nottingham Place with him. I & J Hodgson ...
.. got into a stage at 6 o'clock & went down to Greenwich & dined with G Watt, it being his wife's birthday. Returned to town in the evening.

Finer weather. Wind about SW. Nothing particular occurred today. Attended chambers. Sam Harry offered me 21/- pload for Hull, having had a letter from Henry, that such freights could be obtained. Agreed to wait till tomorrow when Henry would be in town. Walked to the Blue Ports in Cork Square where we all met & dined.

Showery weather. Wind S W. Took a cab into the city and afterwards walked to the docks. Found the people employed hauling the ship out, intending to take her down to Dukes shore. Received from Stephenson £89.7.6 for the lathwood. With Maryann. Attended chambers. H Harry never made his appearance. Did nothing. Went by a Paddington stage to Nottingham Place where Bob Marsh & I dined with William & enjoyed ourselves much.
A cold Day. Wind N by E with snow showers. Dined at home. A very heavy sea upon the bar

A fine morning. Wind SW. Walked into the city early. Called at Chapmans at 10 o'clock & fixed the Hope for memel at 21/- & load for a full cargo of timber. Found Mr Mewburn at the office, tis a long time ...

A fine morning. Wind NW William, J Galbraith called at the New Inn & I walked into the city with them.

In the afternoon we got upon a Paddington stage & went up to Nottingham Place & thence to the Zoological gardens, which are much improved. Dined at 6 o'clock with Mr R Chapman in John Street, Bedford Row. Mr Hancock, Mr Graham & another gentleman there. Spent a very pleasant day.

On my return to chambers found Bob marsh reading. Asked him to allow me to remain in his chambers for the few days I stopped in town, but much to my surprise he refused, which hurt me not a little. After living nearly three months with me on board the Hope. It was doing me but a trifling favour & without either inconveniencing or expense to himself, I could not have expected & I know not how he could possibly make his mind up to treat me with so much unkindness. However I shall not forget it in a hurry. I pronounce him to be a mean and shabby fellow

A pleasant morning wind. Feeling exceptionally annoyed & hurt by Bob Marsh's conduct, I got up early & left his chambers. Indeed had it not been so late I should have done so last night. Breakfasted with William in Nottingham Place. We afterwards went to vere St Chapel. In the afternoon we walked to Sloan Street & we called at Mrs Locks to see Mary & Emma. On our way home had a stroll in Hyde Park. Very few people there. Vincent Fitzmanian & Bob Marsh dined with us. We intended to have given the latter a hint that his company could be dispensed with, but did not, as it might have caused much unpleasantness. I determined however to tell him what I thought of his conduct, but had not an opportunity. He shall yet hear more about it. A very wet night

A cloudy morning. Wind WSW. Went into the city upon a Paddington stage coach rather early, to pack a hamper of special madeira up for Mr Chapman of Elseineur. J Galbraith & I thence walked down to Dowson's dock to the Hope, where we dined. The people busy caulking & repairing some soft places where she has been leaking. Left the ship between 4 & 5 o'clock. Brought new umbrella

A dull showery day. Wind W by N. Went by a Paddington dray into the city. Stephenson called at the office having got his dispatches. Surprised to find that Chapmans had given him a copy of a charter which did not agree with that I signed, having Stavers introduced. Called at Color's office & saw the original charter & found it outlined. Exceedingly surprised & angry that such a thing should be done without my knowledge or sanction & the more surprised that Chapmans should permit it. A most unjustifiable act, nay worse. Walked down to the ship, the people getting on very well or it seem to be giving her a good caulking. Dined on board. J Galbraith & I walked home by Fleet Street, Regent Street etc...

A very wet day & been raining heavy all night. Wind NE. Took a Paddington dray to the city. Called at Chapmans & agreed to take 500 staves and not more unless the master wished. The agent giving me a letter pledging himself to that effect. On the Coal Exchange nothing particular there. Did not find a ship to take me to Shields. Took a coach & carried all J G's cloths down to the ship. Found her just hauled out of dock. Had some beef.

Packed my clothes up ready to tranship. William, J.G. & I walked up home calling at Mrs Carfs & at the Cock in the Fleet Street where we had some oysters & brandy & water. Stephenson gave me his accounts.

A dull morning. Wind NE. Took a Paddington stage into the city. Stephenson up, but not cleared for want of papers relative to the sum, from the West India docks. J Galbraith & I walked down to the ship. Dined on board. Got our ballast alongside. Put all my cloths etc. on board the Peggy, captain Hunter, intending to take my passage to Shields in her. She hauled out of the Regents Canal & proceeded down the river to Purfleet to ballast. William & I walked up to the city, calling at Chapmans respecting the clearing papers.

Been raining very heavy all night. Weather thick. Wind NE. Packed my cloths up. Took a packing coach & went down to the office. Paid £4.12. for 23 gallons of rum at 4/ per gallon. William paid it out of £30 I gave him to place to my Chapmans account. William & I got on board the Pearl Gravesend boat. He accompanied me as far as Woolwich where he landed & I proceeded to the ...

Been blowing a gale of wind from the NNE all night & continued with rain all day. Amused ourselves during the morning strolling about Purfleet & playing at billiards. Got our ballast on board & hauled from the wharf about 5 o'clock. Weighed anchor & sailed down to the Tower. Hope when we brought up for the night. Blowing a gale of wind. Finished a couple of glasses of whiskey punch, smoked a pipe & turned in at 9 o'clock

Went to Newcastle by coach to see Dixon Dixon for the purpose of having some conversation with him, respecting his promise of assisting me, but it being Millington Colliery pay day, he was so late in returning home I had no opportunity of speaking. I however invited myself to dine & stay all night tomorrow. Got home to dinner at 5 o'clock Fine day & cold. Wind NW
A winters day, frosty, with snow showers, Wind NE. A heavy sea upon the bar The surveyor saw the Hope's keel. Paid R Brown £6.5 for trysail etc. Dined at home. Whist club in the evening

A very fine morning. Wind about NNE. Got under way about 6 o'clock & ran down to the Warp where we brought up about ½ past 9 o'clock am. Turned out an uncommonly fine day & warm. About 12 o'clock the wind got to the NNW then NW & after dinner to W by S & WSW. When we got our anchor up, but being little wind, did not make much way. At about 8 o'clock being dark & not able to see the buoy of the middle, we brought up for the night. Several ships in company.

At 9 o'clock smoked a pipe, wet both eyes & turned in. A good deal annoyed at not being able to proceed, there being a fine breeze.

Been blowing fresh all night & still continues at SE with small rain. The ship remaining down river with a strong ebb tide at the rate of about 10 knots, having got underway at day light between 5 & 6 o'clock. At 10 o'clock am abreast of Aldeburgh. Clearer weather. Top mast & lower studding sails set. Passed through the Broads about 1 o'clock with a fine breeze. At about 8 o'clock pm abreast of Happisburgh. Took our pipe & nip & turned in at 9 o'clock. A beautiful star light night. Wind about W by S

Turned out at ½ past 7 o'clock ship abreast of Darlington, having had a fine run all night. Wind W by S & W SW & beautiful weather at noon got round Flamborough Head close in shore. A delightful sail. Passed Scarborough about 2 o'clock & at 3 o'clock where off the south cheek of Robin Hoods Bay, had a small shower of rain, but soon cleared up & we had fine weather again & being close in shore enjoyed a most beautiful view of the coast & country. Passed Huntcliff Foot before dusk with a continuance of the breeze at about W. At 11 o'clock brought up off Tynemouth Bar, being past high water, we could only attempt to go in.

A beautiful morning. Wind about W by N. At 7 o'clock a steam boat came alongside & afterwards towed us into the harbour, where Mr White & I landed & went up to Dockwray Square to breakfast. Found Mrs Scott much better than I expected & able to get into the drawing room. Took an early dinner with Mr Tinley. Sat with neuf for some time in the evening & took tea with Mr Tinley.

Much mortified and unhappy at being informed by Ann Maxwell of her being with child to me. What the end of it be, I cannot divine, but it makes me miserable that I should have been such a fool & madman to have committed such an act. Such a break of hospitality, such shaming & disgraceful conduct. I am ashamed of myself.

A beautiful morning. Wind North. Engaged writing nearly all the morning. Mrs Dixon unexpectedly came down, dined & left us in the evening. Much confusion in the house.

Poor Ann Maxwell being obliged to acknowledge herself in a family way. Consequently Mrs Scott discharged her & she left the house. A strong suspicion I believe, but not known that I am the father. This day passed over without any further discovery & I hope I shall be able to keep it a secret in all events from Mrs Scott. In a devil of a stew.

Settled with Robert for payment of moly recovery. Wrote to William at Windsor. Mr French died suddenly

Another beautiful day. Wind ESE & SE. Nothing further transpired respecting this unfortunate business with Ann Maxwell. Mrs Scott has not spoken to me about, though I believe ‘tis her intention. I gave her every opportunity by dining at home & sitting with her, for I'm anxious it was over, for this suspense is unpleasant.

Saw Ann Maxwell in the evening & gave her a sovereign

A dull morning. Afterwards turned to rain. Wind SW & WSW blowing strong. Engaged all the morning in the office making up the Hope's Petersburg voyage. Dined at home. Mrs Scott put the question to me whether I was the cause of Ann Maxwell being with child, which on her (Mrs Scott's ) account being in so precarious a state of health, I denied. Therefor if she hears of it through some kind officious friend & anything happens, be the blame upon their shoulders. I shall not be the cause.

With Ann Stokes this evening

The Childers, Captain Moriay came into harbour

A fine morning. Wind SW blowing fresh during the day. Sent a letter by Mr J Haker's ship, the Ajax, to Elsineus, directed to Mr In Brown, Copenhagen, that I forgot to deliver when there. Attended church in the morning. Walked with Mr Allen to Tynemouth in the afternoon & afterward dined with him

A dull morning. Wind N by W & cold. Received a letter from C Richmond asking me to go to Burnhopeside tomorrow. Answered it & fixed Sunday to be there. Dined at home & in the afternoon took a walk with Mark Webb & Mr Robinson, the latter with his guardian
A fine morning, but cool. Wind N by W & a sea upon the bar. Heavy rain during the day. Dined at home. Drank tea & played a rubber at I Craig's
Weather changed. Wind NW. A shower of snow in the morning & afterwards turned over a wet day. A few ships got to sea. Dined at home A letter from William
A dull morning. Wind NNW. Took a walk with Mark. Dined at 12 o'clock. Mr French buried this afternoon, aged 82. Drank tea & spent the evening with Mr Tinley

A beautiful morning. Wind WNW. Received a letter from William & another from Richmond putting off my visit until Thursday next. Went over to South Shields & called upon ____. Received the butcher for William. Returned & took a walk to Cullercoats. Dined at home at 2 o'clock. The children sailed this afternoon. At the whist club in the evening.

A dull morning. Wind NE. Afterwards turned out pleasant. Captain Webb & I walked to Whitley Park & called upon Mr J Wright. Returned by Cullercoats & the sands through Tynemouth. Dined at 2 o'clock. At the Mallard soon in the afternoon. At ½ past 7 o'clock went to meet Ann but she was not at the place of appointment. Drank tea & spent the evening with Miss Tinley. Playing at cards with the boys. Wind changed. Rained in the evening to SE

A dull morning after a rainy night. Wind NW. Wrote a letter to Stephenson to meet him at Elsineur which I gave to H French to put on board some vessel at Hull bound to the Baltic. Dined at home at 2 o'clock. J Tinley returned from Liverpool, called in the evening & took a cup of coffee with him. Met Ann at ½ past 7 o'clock

The early part of the morning very fine but afterwards turned dull & like rain. Wind WNW blowing hard in the afternoon at W. Went to church in the morning. Mrs Dixon Fanny & Bell Smith came down to see Mrs Scott. In the afternoon walked down to Tynemouth & dined at 5 o'clock. Note from William. Metcalf, Henry & his wife there & Mr & Mrs J Dale in the evening
A dull morning having had rain during the night. Wind W by N & cots. Dined at home at 2 o'clock. In the evening with Ann. Took supper & a glass of punch with Allen

A fine morning but cold. Wind NW by N. Walked with Mark to the New Quay & afterwards with Mrs Tinley up Preston Lane. Dined at J Tinley. He treated us with turtle soup, spent a pleasant day. Present the vicar, William & H Metcalf, J Fenwick, J Dale & myself
A fine morning, cool. Wind NW. Dined at home. Walked with captain Webb to Tynemouth in the evening. Called at Miss Marr's & saw Emma G. At night blew hard with heavy rain & sleet. Wrote to William

A very stormy morning. Exceptional wet & heavy sleet showers. Wind about N. Got breakfast early & took the steam boat to Newcastle & at 10 o'clock got into the Express coach & went to Durham. When we arrived a little after 12 o'clock Richmond had sent his man and gig for me but by some mistake the man supposing I had not come, returned to Burnhopeside without me at ½ past 12 o'clock. I therefor started & walked out to dinner.

A very fine day & frosty. Richardson & I out shooting all the morning. The birds very wild & we only got two braces. Kit rode a pony, not being able to walk much. Joe out this morning exercising the hounds, preparing to begin the season tomorrow.
A very fine day. Wind WNW. Went to Newcastle. Put the Hope upon Willington List. Dined at home & at party in the evening at Mrs Richmond's. Wrote to William. Got cooks new hearth on board

A beautiful day & very mild. Wind about WSW. Went out at 10 o'clock with the hounds, harriers. Kept by Joe Richmond. Not much sport, being a bad scenting day, found three or four hares but only killed one. Joe mounted me upon his favourite mare, Daphne, an excellent hunter. She carried me beautifully & I performed wonders, taking several leaps without a "spill". A Mr Wylane joined us & stayed for dinner. Rich Grunwell & a Mr Potts came in to wine & we spent a pleasant evening. Joe is now enabled to keep the hounds at Burnhopeside

Another beautiful mild day. Wind about West. Got up this morning. Very stiff and aching from the exercise of yesterday. Mr Richmond, Joe & I walked to Lanchester Church. Heard the service & saw the natives. Returned home by the Greenwells of the Ford. Saw Mr White & family of Woodlands at church, lops kindly invited us to dine with him next week. Dined at 3 o'clock without company. Took a stroll after our wine, spent a quiet evening & got to bed early
A pleasant morning. Out shooting until dinner time, but poor sport. I killed a brace. Only had three shots. Mr Greenwall 3 birds. Mr G dined with us. Played a rubber in the evening

A dull morning having been a good deal of rain during the night. Wind about SSW. We breakfasted with Mr G Greenwell at ____, a party there to hunt. Went out with the harriers, but I did not follow them having a fair commanding view from the top of the hill. They had a plenty of running & found a great many hares, but being several plantations they made their escape into them. Turned out very well. We all returned & dined at Lanchester at C Lumley's public house. Sat down nine to dinner. In the evening played whist, A very stormy night. A deluge of rain. Continued playing until 3 o'clock in the morning in the hope it would clear up, instead of which, the rain was so heavy that the river overflowed its banks & covered the green so that we were compelled to remain all night.

A very wet day. Still raining, very heavy. Wind I think NNW. Walked to Burnhopeside to breakfast. Bressed & Joe Reshar, Allen Hutchinson & I went with Mr Potts, who came for us in his carriage to Mr Whites at Woodlands where we dined & spent a very pleasant & jolly day & after supper returned to Burnhopeside. Kit & Miss R stayed all night at Mr Whites

A beautiful morning. Wind ___. Excessively jacked & tired from the good living of the last two days. Took a walk with my gun, thinking the exercise would do me good. Shot a brace of birds. Dined at home & completely knocked up. Edward White dined with us.

A fine morning, rather cloudy. Jow & Kit out with the hounds. I went out shooting & walked about the whole of the day. Killed only one bird. Dined at home & in the evening Joe & I went to Mr Kell's at Lanchester (the suryion) with whom we drank tea & played a few rubbers. We got home about ½ past 1 o'clock in the morning
A mild day with a fresh breeze from NW by N. A few light ships arrived. At church with fanny Smith in the morning. Walked to Tynemouth in the afternoon with J Tenley. Dined at home

A delightful day. After breakfast wrote to William & R Snowdon of my intention to be at Shields on Tuesday or Wednesday. Walked out with my gun until dinner time. Only killed one bird which I lost. Dined & spent a quiet evening at home.

A most beautiful morning, quite like a summer's day. Mrs Richmond & Loo went to church. Kit & I took a ride to Durham & got back to dinner at 3 o'clock. Nicholas Greenwell & Reverend Thompson dined with us.
A fine day. Wind SW. Employed myself in sketching most of the morning. Kit & I took a ride before dinner. Dined & spent a quiet evening at home.
A dull morning & showery. Wind S by W. Out with my gun. But did not get a shot. Kit & Joe out hunting. They had good sport. Spent the evening at home.

A fine morning. Wind SE. Prepared to set off for Shields, but after breakfast it set in such a determined rainingday that we could not think of moving. I therefore remained at Burnhopeside. Spent a quiet evening at home.

A dull morning after a very heavy fall of rain during the night. Wind NW. After breakfast Kit & Joe went to see the Lambleton hounds throw off at Flags & James, Kits servant, drove me in the gig to Durham, where I had to remain all day, the coach not passing through till evening. Showers during the whole of the morning, but in the intervals I strolled about to see all my old haunts etc. Things much in a "status quo". I could perceive few alterations or improvements. Called upon SKeene. At 8 o'clock took a gig & got to shields at ½ past 9 o'clock & went to the whist club for an hour. Received a letter from William.

A dull misty morning. Wind NW & N by W

Accepted balances bill at 4 months for the Mesa at premium £20-2.6 due 20th Jan

Went to South Shields & paid Rids & Oliver their dividend upon G Morrisons estate. Dined at house. Wrote & enclosed a soverign to Mrs Scott Crathorn. H Harry & I drank wine together at the Commercial & afterwards eat some oysters at Janes

A very fine morning. Wind WNW. Towards afternoon it got round to SSE. Several ships got to sea. The lady Jane arrived from Greenland with 9 fish. Called at MisJarre & saw Emma. Also upon M & Ino Matthews. Dined at home. Mrs Scott not quite so well today. Took a walk in the evening with A. S__k_s (Ann Stokes)

A fine morning. Wind NW. Attended morning service & heard an excellent sermon by Mr Hollengsworth of Bolton, after which £24 was collected for the Judgement Sick Society. In the afternoon J Tinley, the boys & I walked to Tynemouth & being a most beautiful day as great many people were there. Dined & spent the evening with the Tinleys, it being Mrs T's birth & wedding day
A delightful day very mild wind NNW. Dined on board the Hope. Had A French & A Nicholson to dinner. A letter from Mrs Y

Another beautiful morning. Wind about West. Went over the water with H Harry to see Mr S Walkers patent lever to the old windlass worked, but it was unshipped. Wrote to C Kirkmond about the price of mineral timber. Mrs Dixon down to see Mrs Scott, rather more gracious than before. She invited me to Benton.

Dined at home. Drank a couple of tumblers of whiskey toddy with Allen & went to the theatre to see Madam Vestris perform Latitea Harog in the Billes Shalagen & Apollo in Midas. A pretty good house, about £37 in
Most delightful weather. Wind NW. Mrs Glover called & I paid her dividend upon G Morrison's estate. Walked to Tynemouth & called upon Mr R Airey. Dined at home. Saw Ann Maxwell in the evening
Went to the theatre & saw Madam Vestris again. She & her sister Miss Bartolozzi performed for the benefit. About ___ in the house

A dull morning. After a rainy night & wind NE, changed now to NNW. During the day variable between W by N & NNE and cold. A sea upon the bar. Amused myself drawing all the morning. Dined at home. Received from Robert £7 on WBS account for newspapers sent Commercial Rooms & £1.18.6 on account of Emma Galbraith's.

The Grenville Bay & Love arrived from Greenland well fisked. H Harry & I had a bottle of port together at the George. With Ann Stokes in the evening

A fine morning & milder weather. Wind WNW. Engaged the principle part of the morning in drawing. Dined at home at 2 o'clock. In the evening eat some oysters at Marks & afterwards attended the whist club.

A pleasant morning. Wind WNW. Again engaged the morning in drawing. Dined at home at 2 o'clock. H Harry & I went to the Commercial & punished two bottles of port. His treat having heard of the safe arrival of the Choice at Hull from Wybarz making the voyage in two months. In the evening at Mrs Lays at Tynemouth. Drank tea & played a rubber.

A fine morning. Rather cool. Wind changeable between NNW & NNE. Sea high, having blown very hard early this morning from NE. Emma Galbraith came to spend the day with Mrs Scott. Took a walk with her round by Preston Lane etc. Dined at 5 o'clock with Allen, J Craig, J Wright, W Harrison & Robinson of the 80th there. Spent a pleasant day & won of W Harrison £6

A beautiful day. Rather frosty. Wind NNW. The sea still continues heavy upon the bar. Attended morning services.

Received a letter from WBS & another from Captain Stephenson dated aneruel 17th Oct & expecting to sail next day. London on the 15th drawn upon Chapmans for expenses £93.4/- which I consider heavy.

Dined at home at 2 o'clock & afterwards took a walk to Tynemouth with H Harry. Mrs Scott not so well. Indeed the Dr considering her getting considerably worse. The disease having extended to the armpits.

At the Mulstrum.
A fine mild morning. Wind SW. Attended the justice room until dinner time. Dined at home at 2 o'clock. Played at billiards with Ben Wright until 10 o'clock. Several ships got down.

Another mild morning. Wind WSW. A number of light ships arrived this morning. N Boswell arrived the morning in his ship the William Shand, a fine vessel, about 280 tons coppond called on board. Dined at home. H Harry & I took wine together at the Commercial with Bill Jervis in the afternoon.
A beautiful day & extremely mild. Wind WNW. Dined at home

A beautiful morning. Wind NW. Captain Webb & I took a walk round by the sands to Cullercoats & returned by the fields. Dined at the house at 2 o'clock. Mark came in after dinner & took a bottle of port with me. With Bill Jervis. In the evening at the whist club

A fine mild morning with the appearance of rain. Wind WSW. Dined at the George Tavern with William Harrison who had last a diciseen upon the death of Major Wergs. He (WH) saying that the major was killed at Corunna when it was at St Sabastian's. Had an exceedingly pleasant day & excellent dinner & wine. Present J Tinley, Captain French, Mr West & Mr Robinson of the 80th Regiment, Mr Allen, William, Tom & Benj Wright, I Craig, Mr Christie of London, Mr Harrison & myself

A most beautiful morning. Wind NW. The air rather frosty. Intended going to Newcastle with H Harry but prevented by a most disturbing letter from captain Stephenson of the Hope dated Elsinore the 24th Oct informing me of the loss of poor J Galbraith. He having fallen overboard from the maintop sail yard when reefing pitching upon the top in his fall, poor fellow, his career has been short but ‘tis all for the best.
